articles.title: A
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter A makes the sound /a/. It is an open vowel, like the 'a' in 'father', but shorter. Listen to it in (apă) /ˈa.pə/, which means water. Listen again in (casă) /ˈka.sə/, which means house.

## How to say it

Open your mouth wide. Let your jaw drop. Keep your tongue low and flat. Keep your lips relaxed and not round. Let the air come out freely.

## Reading rules

A always has the same sound. It does not change when the word is stressed or not stressed. Compare (masă) /ˈma.sə/, which means table, and (acasă) /aˈka.sə/, which means at home.

## Common mistakes

Do not make A weak when it has no stress. Say it clearly in every syllable. Do not say it like the 'a' in 'cat'. Keep your tongue flat and your mouth open.
articles.summary: A is a clear, open vowel. It sounds the same in every position.

articles.title: Ă
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter Ă makes the sound /ə/. It is a short, weak vowel. It is like the last sound in 'sofa'. Listen to it in (mamă) /ˈma.mə/, which means mom. Listen again in (măr) /mər/, which means apple.

## How to say it

Open your mouth a little. Keep your tongue in the middle of your mouth. Keep your lips relaxed and flat. Do not round them. Make the sound short and quiet.

## Reading rules

Ă always has the sound /ə/. You will see it often at the end of feminine words. Examples are (casă) /ˈka.sə/, which means house, and (apă) /ˈa.pə/, which means water.

## Common mistakes

Do not say Ă like a full /a/. The mouth is less open. Do not mix it up with Â and Î. They sound different. Keep Ă light, and do not stress it.
articles.summary: Ă is a short, relaxed vowel. It is very common at the end of words.

articles.title: Â
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter Â makes the sound /ɨ/. This sound does not exist in English. It sounds like 'i' in 'bit', but with the tongue pulled back. Listen to it in (cânt) /kɨnt/, which means I sing. Listen again in (pământ) /pəˈmɨnt/, which means earth.

## How to say it

Say the sound 'ee'. Keep your lips flat and spread. Now pull your tongue back a little, without moving your lips. Keep your mouth almost closed. The sound comes from the middle of the mouth.

## Reading rules

Â and Î have exactly the same sound. Use Â inside a word. Use Î at the start or at the end of a word. Examples with Â are (român) /roˈmɨn/, which means Romanian, and (România) /roˈmɨ.ni.a/, which means Romania.

## Common mistakes

Do not say 'oo' or round your lips. Do not say a clear 'ee' with the tongue forward. Do not use Ă instead of Â. Keep your lips flat, and your tongue back.
articles.summary: Â is a back vowel that is written inside words. It sounds the same as Î.

articles.title: B
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter B makes the sound /b/. It is like the 'b' in 'big'. Listen to it in (bun) /bun/, which means good. Listen again in (băiat) /bəˈjat/, which means boy.

## How to say it

Close your lips. Let the air build up. Open your lips quickly. Use your voice. Put your hand on your throat, and you will feel it vibrate.

## Reading rules

B has the sound /b/ in every position. It is the same at the start, in the middle and at the end of a word. Listen to it at the end in (alb) /alb/, which means white.

## Common mistakes

Do not turn B into /p/ at the end of a word. Keep your voice on until the end of the sound. Say (alb) /alb/, not 'alp'.
articles.summary: B is a voiced sound made with both lips, like the English B.

articles.title: C
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter C makes two sounds. Before A, Ă, Â, O, U and consonants, it is /k/. Listen to it in (casă) /ˈka.sə/, which means house. Before E and I, it is /tʃ/, like 'ch' in 'church'. Listen to it in (ceai) /tʃaj/, which means tea.

## How to say it

For /k/, touch the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth. Then release it with only a little air. For /tʃ/, start with your tongue behind your upper teeth. Release it with a hissing sound, as in 'church'.

## Reading rules

C before E or I is always /tʃ/. Listen to (cine) /ˈtʃi.ne/, which means who, and (zece) /ˈze.tʃe/, which means ten. Sometimes the E or I is silent. It only shows the soft sound, as in (ceas) /tʃas/, which means clock. To keep /k/ before E or I, write CH, as in (chei) /kej/, which means keys.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /s/ for C before E or I. Do not say /k/ either. Say /tʃ/. Do not blow out a lot of air on /k/. Romanian /k/ is softer than English /k/ at the start of a word.
articles.summary: C has two sounds. It is /k/ before most letters and /tʃ/ before E and I.

articles.title: D
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter D makes the sound /d/. It is like the 'd' in 'day'. Listen to it in (dor) /dor/, which means longing. Listen again in (da) /da/, which means yes.

## How to say it

Touch the tip of your tongue to the back of your upper teeth. Hold the air for a moment. Release it and use your voice. Keep your tongue forward, not on the ridge behind your teeth.

## Reading rules

D has the sound /d/ in every position. Listen to it in the middle of (cald) /kald/, which means warm. Listen to it at the start of (dulce) /ˈdul.tʃe/, which means sweet.

## Common mistakes

Do not make D quiet at the end of a word. Keep your voice on. Do not put your tongue too far back. Keep it on your upper teeth.
articles.summary: D is a voiced sound. Your tongue touches your upper teeth.

articles.title: E
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter E makes the sound /e/. It is like the 'e' in 'bed', but cleaner and shorter. Listen to it in (elev) /eˈlev/, which means student. Listen again in (perete) /peˈre.te/, which means wall.

## How to say it

Open your mouth a little. Smile slightly. Keep your tongue forward and fairly high. Keep the sound steady. Do not move your tongue or lips while you say it.

## Reading rules

E is usually /e/. In a few very common words, E at the start sounds like /je/, like 'ye' in 'yes'. Listen to (el) /jel/, which means he, and (este) /ˈjes.te/, which means is. E is also part of groups like EA and EI. They have their own articles.

## Common mistakes

Do not add a glide at the end, as in the English word 'day'. The sound must stay the same from start to end. Do not make E weak like Ă.
articles.summary: E is a clear, short vowel. In a few common words at the start, it sounds like 'ye'.

articles.title: F
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter F makes the sound /f/. It is like the 'f' in 'fun'. Listen to it in (foc) /fok/, which means fire. Listen again in (față) /ˈfa.tsə/, which means face.

## How to say it

Put your upper teeth on your lower lip. Push air through the small space. Do not use your voice. The sound is a soft, steady hiss.

## Reading rules

F has the sound /f/ in every position. Listen to it in (cafea) /kaˈfe̯a/, which means coffee. Words with PH are not Romanian. Romanian writes F, as in (fotografie) /fo.to.ɡraˈfi.e/, which means photograph.

## Common mistakes

Do not use your voice. If you do, it becomes /v/. Do not close your lips together. Use your teeth and your lower lip.
articles.summary: F is a soft hissing sound made with the lip and the teeth.

articles.title: G
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter G makes two sounds. Before A, Ă, Â, O, U and consonants, it is /ɡ/ like 'g' in 'go'. Listen to it in (gură) /ˈɡu.rə/, which means mouth. Before E and I, it is /dʒ/ like 'j' in 'jam'. Listen to it in (ger) /dʒer/, which means frost.

## How to say it

For /ɡ/, press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth. Release it with your voice on. For /dʒ/, press your tongue to the ridge behind your upper teeth. Release it slowly with a buzzing sound.

## Reading rules

G before E or I is always /dʒ/. Listen to (girafă) /dʒiˈra.fə/, which means giraffe. Sometimes the E or I is silent, as in (geam) /dʒam/, which means window. To keep hard /ɡ/ before E or I, write GH, as in (ghete) /ˈɡe.te/, which means boots.

## Common mistakes

Do not say hard /ɡ/ before E or I. Do not say /ʒ/, the sound in 'measure'. Say /dʒ/, as in 'jam'. Do not whisper the hard /ɡ/. Keep your voice on.
articles.summary: G has two sounds. It is hard /ɡ/ before most letters and soft /dʒ/ before E and I.

articles.title: H
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter H makes the sound /h/ before vowels. It is like the 'h' in 'hat'. Listen to it in (hartă) /ˈhar.tə/, which means map. At the end of a word, or before a consonant, it is /x/, a rough sound from the throat. Listen to it in (duh) /dux/, which means spirit.

## How to say it

For /h/, open your mouth and push air out from the throat. Do not use your voice. For /x/, raise the back of your tongue toward the roof of your mouth. Push air through the small space. The sound is rough, like clearing your throat gently.

## Reading rules

H is /h/ before vowels. Listen to (horă) /ˈho.rə/, which means a folk dance. H is /x/ at the end of a word. Listen to (valah) /vaˈlax/, which means a Wallachian person. H is also part of CH and GH. Those groups have their own articles.

## Common mistakes

Do not drop the H. Say it in every word. Do not make the final H silent. Keep a little rough air at the end of (duh) /dux/.
articles.summary: H is a breathy sound. At the end of a word it is rougher.

articles.title: I
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter I makes the sound /i/ as a full vowel. It is like 'ee' in 'see', but shorter. Listen to it in (inimă) /ˈi.ni.mə/, which means heart. Before another vowel, I is a glide /j/, like 'y' in 'yes'. Listen to it in (iarbă) /ˈjar.bə/, which means grass.

## How to say it

For the full vowel, smile and keep your tongue high and forward. For the glide, say the sound 'y' very quickly. For the soft I at the end of a word, whisper it. Your lips stay in the shape of a small smile.

## Reading rules

At the end of a word, after a consonant, I is very weak. It softens the sound before it. Listen to (lupi) /lupʲ/, which means wolves, and (bani) /banʲ/, which means money. After a vowel, I is a short glide. Listen to (pui) /puj/, which means chick.

## Common mistakes

Do not say a full 'ee' at the end of (lupi) /lupʲ/. Whisper it. Do not say the glide in (iarbă) /ˈjar.bə/ as a full vowel. Say 'y' and move on.
articles.summary: I has three jobs. It is a full vowel, a glide, or a soft whisper at the end.

articles.title: Î
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter Î makes the sound /ɨ/. This sound does not exist in English. It is like 'i' in 'bit', but with the tongue pulled back. Listen to it in (înger) /ˈɨn.dʒer/, which means angel. Listen again in (încă) /ˈɨn.kə/, which means still.

## How to say it

Say the sound 'ee'. Keep your lips flat. Now pull your tongue back a little. Do not round your lips. Keep your mouth almost closed. The sound is short and tight.

## Reading rules

Î and Â have the same sound. Use Î at the start of a word, as in (înot) /ɨˈnot/, which means swimming. Use Î at the end of a verb, as in (a hotărî) /a ho.təˈrɨ/, which means to decide. Inside a word, Romanian writes Â.

## Common mistakes

Do not say 'oo'. Do not say a clear 'ee'. Do not use Ă instead of Î. Keep your lips flat, and keep your tongue back.
articles.summary: Î is the same sound as Â. It is written at the start and at the end of words.

articles.title: J
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter J makes the sound /ʒ/. It is like the 's' in 'measure' or 'pleasure'. Listen to it in (joc) /ʒok/, which means game. Listen again in (plajă) /ˈpla.ʒə/, which means beach.

## How to say it

Round your lips a little. Raise your tongue near the ridge behind your upper teeth. Push air through the small space. Use your voice. You will feel a soft buzz.

## Reading rules

J always has the sound /ʒ/. Listen to it at the start of (jos) /ʒos/, which means down. Listen to it in the middle of (ajutor) /a.ʒuˈtor/, which means help.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /dʒ/, the sound in 'jam'. That sound is written with G before E or I. Do not say /ʃ/, the sound in 'ship'. Keep your voice on.
articles.summary: J is the soft buzzing sound in 'measure'.

articles.title: K
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter K makes the sound /k/. It is only used in words from other languages. Listen to it in (kilogram) /ki.loˈɡram/, which means kilogram. Listen again in (karate) /kaˈra.te/, which means karate.

## How to say it

Press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth. Release it with a small burst of air. Do not use your voice. Keep the sound short.

## Reading rules

K is always /k/, even before E and I. Listen to (ketchup) /ˈket.ʃap/, which means ketchup. Romanian words use C for this sound. K appears in names and loanwords, such as (kiwi) /ˈki.wi/.

## Common mistakes

Do not make K soft before E or I. It stays hard. Do not blow out a lot of air at the start of a word.
articles.summary: K is only used in foreign words. It has the sound /k/.

articles.title: L
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter L makes the sound /l/. It is clear and light, like the 'l' in 'let'. Listen to it in (lup) /lup/, which means wolf. Listen again in (mal) /mal/, which means shore.

## How to say it

Touch the tip of your tongue to the ridge behind your upper teeth. Let the air flow around the sides of your tongue. Use your voice. Keep the sound bright.

## Reading rules

L has the same sound in every position. It is clear at the start, in the middle and at the end of a word. Listen to (cald) /kald/, which means warm, and (luna) /ˈlu.na/, which means the moon.

## Common mistakes

Do not make L dark and heavy at the end of a word, as in the English word 'full'. Keep your tongue forward. Say a clear /l/ every time.
articles.summary: L is a clear sound. The tongue touches the ridge behind the upper teeth.

articles.title: M
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter M makes the sound /m/. It is like the 'm' in 'mom'. Listen to it in (mamă) /ˈma.mə/, which means mom. Listen again in (om) /om/, which means person.

## How to say it

Close your lips. Let the air come out through your nose. Use your voice. You can feel your lips vibrate.

## Reading rules

M has the sound /m/ in every position. Listen to it at the end of (om) /om/ and in the middle of (masă) /ˈma.sə/, which means table. Keep it clear at the end of a word.

## Common mistakes

Do not open your lips too early. Keep them closed until the sound ends. Do not drop the M at the end of a word.
articles.summary: M is a nasal sound made with both lips.

articles.title: N
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter N makes the sound /n/. It is like the 'n' in 'no'. Listen to it in (nor) /nor/, which means cloud. Listen again in (nou) /now/, which means new.

## How to say it

Touch the tip of your tongue to the ridge behind your upper teeth. Let the air come out through your nose. Use your voice. Keep the sound short and clear.

## Reading rules

Before K or G, N changes to /ŋ/, like 'ng' in 'sing'. Listen to (bancă) /ˈbaŋ.kə/, which means bank, and (lung) /luŋɡ/, which means long. In all other places it is /n/, as in (luna) /ˈlu.na/, which means the moon.

## Common mistakes

Do not say a hard /ɡ/ after /ŋ/ in (bancă) /ˈbaŋ.kə/. The sound ends in your nose. Do not drop the N at the end of a word.
articles.summary: N is usually /n/. Before K or G it sounds like 'ng' in 'sing'.

articles.title: O
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter O makes the sound /o/. It is like the 'o' in 'more', but pure and steady. Listen to it in (om) /om/, which means person. Listen again in (copil) /koˈpil/, which means child.

## How to say it

Round your lips. Keep your tongue in the back of your mouth. Open your jaw a little. Keep the lips in the same shape for the whole sound.

## Reading rules

O usually has the sound /o/. In some groups it becomes a quick glide. Listen to (soare) /ˈso̯a.re/, which means sun, and (noapte) /ˈno̯ap.te/, which means night. Those groups have their own article, OA.

## Common mistakes

Do not close your lips at the end, as in the English word 'go'. The sound must not glide to 'oo'. Keep your lips still.
articles.summary: O is a pure, rounded vowel.

articles.title: P
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter P makes the sound /p/. It is like the 'p' in 'spin', with very little air. Listen to it in (pâine) /ˈpɨj.ne/, which means bread. Listen again in (cap) /kap/, which means head.

## How to say it

Close your lips. Let the air build up. Open your lips quickly. Do not use your voice. Hold a small piece of paper in front of your mouth. It should hardly move.

## Reading rules

P has the sound /p/ in every position. Listen to it at the end of (cap) /kap/ and at the start of (pom) /pom/, which means tree. Keep it short.

## Common mistakes

Do not blow out a strong puff of air, as in the English word 'pin'. Do not make P voiced. If you use your voice, it becomes /b/.
articles.summary: P is a quiet sound made with both lips. It has very little breath.

articles.title: R
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter R makes the sound /r/. It is a quick tap or roll of the tongue. It is not the English 'r'. Listen to it in (rac) /rak/, which means crab. Listen again in (mare) /ˈma.re/, which means big.

## How to say it

Touch the tip of your tongue to the ridge behind your upper teeth. Let the air push it so it taps once or rolls. Use your voice. Say 'butter' fast, and you will find the tap in the middle.

## Reading rules

R is /r/ in every position. Say it at the start of (rac) /rak/, in the middle of (mare) /ˈma.re/ and at the end of (soare) /ˈso̯a.re/, which means sun. Never drop it at the end of a word.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the English 'r' with the tongue curled back. Do not say the sound from the throat. Keep your tongue tip forward. Do not drop R at the end of a word.
articles.summary: R is a quick tap or roll of the tongue. It is said in every position.

articles.title: S
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter S makes the sound /s/. It is like the 's' in 'sun'. Listen to it in (soare) /ˈso̯a.re/, which means sun. Listen again in (masă) /ˈma.sə/, which means table.

## How to say it

Put your tongue behind your upper teeth, close to the ridge. Push air through the small space. Do not use your voice. The sound is a steady hiss.

## Reading rules

S is always /s/. This includes S between two vowels. Listen to (casă) /ˈka.sə/, which means house. In the English word 'rose', the S buzzes. In Romanian it does not.

## Common mistakes

Do not make S buzz between vowels. Do not say /ʃ/, the sound in 'ship'. That sound is written Ș. Keep your voice off.
articles.summary: S is a clear hissing sound. It is never a buzzing /z/.

articles.title: Ș
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter Ș makes the sound /ʃ/. It is like 'sh' in 'ship'. Listen to it in (școală) /ˈʃko̯a.lə/, which means school. Listen again in (oraș) /oˈraʃ/, which means city.

## How to say it

Round your lips a little. Raise your tongue toward the roof of your mouth. Push air through the space. Do not use your voice. The sound is a soft, long hiss.

## Reading rules

Ș always has the sound /ʃ/. Listen to it at the start of (șapte) /ˈʃap.te/, which means seven. Listen to it at the end of (oraș) /oˈraʃ/. The letter has a small comma below it. It is not the same as S.

## Common mistakes

Do not read Ș as S. Do not say /tʃ/, the sound in 'church'. Say a smooth /ʃ/ and hold it a little. Do not use your voice.
articles.summary: Ș is the 'sh' sound. It is written with a small mark below the S.

articles.title: T
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter T makes the sound /t/. It is like the 't' in 'stop', with very little air. Listen to it in (tată) /ˈta.tə/, which means father. Listen again in (carte) /ˈkar.te/, which means book.

## How to say it

Touch the tip of your tongue to the back of your upper teeth. Let the air build up. Release it quickly. Do not use your voice. Keep the sound short.

## Reading rules

T has the sound /t/ in every position. Listen to it at the start of (tren) /tren/, which means train. Listen to it in the middle of (frate) /ˈfra.te/, which means brother.

## Common mistakes

Do not blow out a strong puff of air. Do not touch the ridge with your tongue. Use your upper teeth. Do not use your voice, or T becomes /d/.
articles.summary: T is a quiet sound. The tongue touches the upper teeth.

articles.title: Ț
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter Ț makes the sound /ts/. It is like 'ts' in 'cats'. Listen to it in (țară) /ˈtsa.rə/, which means country. Listen again in (viață) /ˈvja.tsə/, which means life.

## How to say it

Say a quick /t/. Then let the air slide into an /s/. Do this in one fast move. Do not use your voice. The sound is one short unit.

## Reading rules

Ț always has the sound /ts/. You can use it at the start of a word. Listen to (țară) /ˈtsa.rə/. You can also use it in the middle and at the end, as in (munți) /munts/, which means mountains.

## Common mistakes

Do not read Ț as T. Do not say /tʃ/, the sound in 'church'. Say /ts/. Do not split it into two slow sounds.
articles.summary: Ț is the 'ts' sound. It is written with a small mark below the T.

articles.title: U
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter U makes the sound /u/. It is like 'oo' in 'moon', but shorter. Listen to it in (unu) /ˈu.nu/, which means one. Listen again in (lup) /lup/, which means wolf.

## How to say it

Round your lips tightly. Pull your tongue back. Open your jaw only a little. Keep the lips round for the whole sound.

## Reading rules

U can also be a quick glide, like 'w' in 'wet'. This happens next to another vowel. Listen to (nou) /now/, which means new, and (rău) /rəw/, which means bad. In these words U is very short.

## Common mistakes

Do not say 'you'. Romanian U does not start with a 'y' sound. Do not make the lips wider. Keep them round.
articles.summary: U is a rounded vowel. Before another vowel it can be a quick 'w'.

articles.title: V
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter V makes the sound /v/. It is like the 'v' in 'van'. Listen to it in (verde) /ˈver.de/, which means green. Listen again in (val) /val/, which means wave.

## How to say it

Put your upper teeth on your lower lip. Push air through the small space. Use your voice. You will feel a buzz on your lip.

## Reading rules

V has the sound /v/ in every position. Listen to it at the start of (vino) /ˈvi.no/, which means come. Listen to it in the middle of (nouă) /ˈno.wə/, which means nine, and at the end of (sclav) /sklav/, which means slave.

## Common mistakes

Do not turn V into /f/ at the end of a word. Keep your voice on. Do not say /w/ with round lips.
articles.summary: V is a voiced sound made with the lip and the teeth.

articles.title: W
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter W is not part of normal Romanian words. It is used in loanwords and names. In older loanwords, it sounds like /v/. Listen to it in (watt) /vat/, which means watt. In newer English words, it sounds like /w/. Listen to it in (weekend) /ˈwi.kend/, which means weekend.

## How to say it

For /v/, put your upper teeth on your lower lip and use your voice. For /w/, round your lips and say a quick 'oo' that slides into the next vowel. Keep your teeth away from your lip for /w/.

## Reading rules

There is no single rule. Words from German often use /v/. Words from English often use /w/. Listen to (web) /web/, which means web. Check a dictionary when you are not sure.

## Common mistakes

Do not use W in a native word. Do not always say /w/. Some loanwords keep the older /v/. Listen to how the word is said in Romanian.
articles.summary: W is only used in foreign words. It can sound like /v/ or /w/.

articles.title: X
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter X makes two sounds. Most often it is /ks/, like 'x' in 'taxi'. Listen to it in (text) /tekst/, which means text. Between vowels, in some words, it is /ɡz/. Listen to it in (examen) /eɡˈza.men/, which means exam.

## How to say it

For /ks/, say /k/ and then /s/ with no pause. For /ɡz/, say /ɡ/ and then /z/. Use your voice for the second one. Keep both sounds in one smooth move.

## Reading rules

Words that start with EX and a vowel usually use /ɡz/. Listen to (exemplu) /eɡˈzem.plu/, which means example. Other places use /ks/. Listen to (taxi) /ˈtak.si/, which means taxi.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /ks/ in (examen) /eɡˈza.men/. Say /ɡz/. Do not split X into two slow sounds. Say it as one quick unit.
articles.summary: X sounds like /ks/ or /ɡz/, depending on the word.

articles.title: Y
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter Y is used in loanwords and names. Before a vowel, it sounds like /j/, like 'y' in 'yes'. Listen to it in (yoga) /ˈjo.ɡa/, which means yoga. At the end of a word, it can sound like /i/. Listen to it in (hobby) /ˈho.bi/, which means hobby.

## How to say it

For /j/, raise the middle of your tongue toward the roof of your mouth. Then glide into the next vowel. For /i/, smile and keep your tongue high and forward.

## Reading rules

Y has no single rule. Before a vowel it is usually /j/, as in (yen) /jen/, which means yen. At the end of an English loanword, it is usually /i/. Check the word in a dictionary when you are not sure.

## Common mistakes

Do not use Y in a native Romanian word. Romanian writes I there. Do not say a long English 'y' sound. Keep it short.
articles.summary: Y is only used in foreign words. It can sound like 'y' or like 'i'.

articles.title: Z
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter Z makes the sound /z/. It is like the 'z' in 'zoo'. Listen to it in (zi) /zi/, which means day. Listen again in (zece) /ˈze.tʃe/, which means ten.

## How to say it

Put your tongue behind your upper teeth. Push air through the small space. Use your voice. You will feel a buzz.

## Reading rules

Z always has the sound /z/. Listen to it in the middle of (varză) /ˈvar.zə/, which means cabbage. Listen to it at the start of (zahăr) /ˈza.hər/, which means sugar.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /s/. Keep your voice on. Do not say /dz/. The sound is a clean buzz.
articles.summary: Z is a voiced buzzing sound.

articles.title: Q
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter Q is not part of normal Romanian words. It appears in foreign words and names. It can sound like /k/ or like /kv/. Listen to it in (Qatar) /kaˈtar/, which means Qatar. Listen again in (quasar) /kvaˈzar/, which means quasar.

## How to say it

For /k/, press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth. Release it quickly. For /kv/, say /k/ and then /v/ right after it. Keep both sounds short.

## Reading rules

Q is almost always followed by U in Romanian writing. The group QU usually sounds like /kv/, as in (quasar) /kvaˈzar/. In some names, Q is only /k/, as in (Qatar) /kaˈtar/. When in doubt, check the word in a dictionary.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the English /kw/ as in 'queen'. Romanian says /kv/. Do not expect Q in common words. It is not used for native Romanian sounds.
articles.summary: Q is rare. It appears in foreign words and names.

articles.title: A
articles.body:
## The Sound of the Letter A

The letter **A** in German represents two distinct vowel lengths: short `/a/` and long `/aː/`. Unlike in English, German **A** never shifts toward a schwa or a diphthong like the vowel in 'cat' or 'cake'. It remains a pure, open central vowel very close to the 'a' in 'father', differing primarily in duration and tension.

## How to Pronounce A

Open your mouth moderately wide with your jaw relaxed and lowered. Rest the tip of your tongue gently behind your lower front teeth, keeping the body of the tongue flat in the floor of the mouth. For the long sound in `Abend`, sustain the tone with steady tension, while for the short sound in `Apfel`, cut the airflow quickly with a crisper release.

## Spelling Rules for A

A single **A** is pronounced short when followed by two or more consonants, as in **Apfel** or **Kamm**. It is pronounced long before a single consonant, at the end of an open syllable, when doubled (**Aal**), or when followed by a silent **h** (**Zahn**). Remember that all German nouns, including those beginning with **A**, must always be capitalized.

## Contrasting Sounds and Pitfalls

Contrast the long `/aː/` in **raten** with the short `/a/` in **Ratten**, where vowel length completely changes the word's meaning. A common trap for English speakers is reducing an unstressed **A** to an indistinct schwa sound at the end of words. Keep vowels like the final **a** in **Sofa** crisp and clearly articulated.
articles.summary: The letter name is A, as in the word Apfel.

articles.title: B
articles.body:
## The Sound of B

In German, the letter **B** usually sounds just like the English voiced `b` as in *ball* when it appears at the start of a syllable. However, when it stands at the end of a syllable or word, it undergoes final devoicing and turns into an unvoiced `p`. This means that words like *ab* actually end with the crisp sound of `p` rather than a soft `b`.

## How to Pronounce It

Press your upper and lower lips firmly together to temporarily block the airflow. For the regular voiced sound `/b/`, vibrate your vocal cords as your lips part to release the air. If the letter is at the end of a word or syllable, do not vibrate your vocal cords, resulting in a clean, sharp `/p/` sound without puffing too much air.

## Spelling and Patterns

The letter **B** is written with standard Latin forms as uppercase **B** and lowercase **b**. It frequently appears initially (*Buch*), medially (*haben*), and doubled (*Ebbe*). A double **bb** marks the preceding vowel as short and is always pronounced as a single consonant sound.

## Sound Differences and Traps

Compare the voiced `/b/` in **Buch** with the devoiced `/p/` in **gelb** or **Urlaub**. A very common mistake for English speakers is continuing to pronounce a voiced `b` at the end of German words. Make sure to clearly devoice syllable-final **b** into `p`, so that *Dieb* sounds just like *deep* without aspiration.
articles.summary: The letter name is Be, as in the word Buch.

articles.title: C
articles.body:
## The Sound of C

On its own, the letter **C** is almost exclusively found in loanwords in German, so its sound depends directly on the word's origin. Before back vowels or consonants it usually sounds like a regular English `k` as in *cat*, whereas before front vowels like *e* or *i* it commonly takes the German `ts` sound identical to the letter **Z**. In certain modern English or French borrowings, it may also sound like a soft `s` or blend into common digraphs like **ch**.

## How to Pronounce It

For the hard variant `k`, raise the back of your tongue firmly against your soft palate, build up air pressure, and release it crisply. When pronouncing it as `ts`, start with your tongue tip pressed against the back of your upper teeth as if making a `t`, then instantly release it into a sharp hissing `s`. Keep your lips relaxed and neutral for both sounds.

## Spelling Patterns

Purely native Germanic words rarely use a solitary **C**; native roots rely almost entirely on digraphs like **ch** or **ck**. Standalone **C** marks international vocabulary taken from Latin, Greek, French, or English. It capitalizes normally at the beginning of nouns or sentences (like **Café** or **Cent**), but native German spelling reforms have historically replaced many older Latin **c** spellings with **k** or **z**.

## Variants and Common Pitfalls

Notice the contrast between **Computer** (`/kɔmˈpjuːtɐ/`) with a hard `k` and **Cent** (`/tsɛnt/`) with a crisp `ts`. English speakers often make the mistake of pronouncing words like **Celsius** or **Cent** with a soft English `s` instead of the required German `ts`. Always check whether the following vowel is front or back, and default to `ts` for Latinate academic and financial terms.
articles.summary: The letter name is Ce, as in the word Computer.

articles.title: D
articles.body:
## The Sound of D

In German, the letter **D** typically represents a voiced alveolar plosive `/d/` at the start of words and syllables, very similar to the English 'd' in *door*. However, when it appears at the end of a syllable or word, a process called terminal devoicing (*Auslautverhärtung*) turns it into a sharp, voiceless `/t/`. Unlike English speakers, Germans pronounce `/d/` with the tongue firmly against the upper teeth or alveolar ridge, producing a crisper sound.

## How to Pronounce D

Place the tip of your tongue against the alveolar ridge directly behind your upper front teeth to completely block the airflow. For the voiced `/d/` at syllable beginnings, gently vibrate your vocal cords as you release the tongue. If the letter stands at the end of a syllable, stop the voicing entirely and release the air with a crisp `/t/` burst.

## Spelling Patterns

The letter **D** is written as uppercase **D** and lowercase **d**, appearing frequently in native German vocabulary and loanwords. Double **dd** occurs occasionally after short vowels, as in *Pudding* or *Widder*, maintaining the `/d/` sound before a following vowel. Remember that word-final spellings with single **d** are phonetically pronounced as `/t/`, yet spelled with **d** due to related inflected forms like *Bäder* from *Bad*.

## Variants and Common Pitfalls

Notice the stark contrast between syllable-initial `/d/` in *Danke* and syllable-final `/t/` in *Hund* `/hʊnt/` or *Bild* `/bɪlt/`. English speakers frequently forget *Auslautverhärtung* and produce a voiced, soft English 'd' at the end of words, which sounds unnatural in German. Always ensure that words ending in **d** receive a clean, voiceless `/t/` unless an inflected vowel suffix follows.
articles.summary: The letter name is De, as in the word Danke.

articles.title: E
articles.body:
## The Sounds of 'E'

The German letter **E** represents several distinct sounds depending on stress and syllable structure. When long, it sounds like a tense, pure `[eː]` similar to the vowel in 'café', while the short version is an open `[ɛ]` like the vowel in 'bed'. In unstressed grammatical endings, it weakens to a neutral schwa `[ə]`, and before an unstressed final 'r' as in '-er', it merges into a subtle open vowel `[ɐ]`.

## How to Pronounce It

For the long `[eː]`, spread your lips wide into a gentle smile, keep your tongue high and tense toward the front of your mouth, and avoid gliding into an English 'ay' diphthong. For short `[ɛ]`, drop your jaw slightly and relax your tongue muscles. When saying the unstressed `[ə]` at word endings, relax your vocal tract completely and produce a very brief, effortless central murmur.

## Spelling and Patterns

A stressed **E** is pronounced long `[eː]` when doubled (**ee**), followed by a silent **h** (**eh**), or in an open syllable. It is short `[ɛ]` when followed by two or more consonants, such as double letters (**Bett**, **hell**). Almost every grammatical suffix ending in single **-e**, **-en**, or **-em** uses the unstressed schwa `[ə]`.

## Contrasting Sounds and Common Mistakes

English speakers often mistakenly turn long `[eː]` into the diphthong `[eɪ]`, turning *Tee* into 'tay-ee'. Another common error is over-pronouncing the final unstressed **-e** as an English 'ee' (making *bitte* sound like 'bit-tee') instead of using the muted schwa `[ə]`. Notice how the vowel quality changes between the tense long sound in **Beet** `[beːt]` and the lax open sound in **Bett** `[bɛt]`.
articles.summary: The letter name is E, as in the word Elefant.

articles.title: F
articles.body:
## Sound Value

The German letter **F** represents the voiceless labiodental fricative `/f/`. It sounds virtually identical to the English 'f' in **fish** or **leaf**. It maintains a crisp, unvoiced quality regardless of where it appears in a word.

## Pronunciation Guide

Place your upper front teeth lightly against the inner edge of your lower lip. Blow air gently through the narrow gap without vibrating your vocal cords. Keep the airflow steady and avoid puffing your cheeks.

## Spelling Patterns

The sound `/f/` can be written as a single **f**, a double **ff** after short vowels (as in **Hoffnung**), or historically as **ph** in Greek loanwords like **Philosophie**. Additionally, the German letter **v** is frequently pronounced as `/f/` in native Germanic words such as **Vater**.

## Comparison and Traps

German **F** has a consistent, stable pronunciation that rarely poses difficulties for learners. The main pitfall is orthographic rather than phonetic: remember that the letter **V** often shares the exact same `/f/` sound, so do not pronounce words like **Vogel** with a voiced English 'v'.
articles.summary: The letter name is Ef, as in the word Fisch.

articles.title: G
articles.body:
## The Sound of G

The German letter **G** most commonly represents a voiced velar plosive `/ɡ/`, identical to the hard 'g' in English *garden*. At the end of a syllable or word, it undergoes terminal devoicing and sounds like a sharp `/k/`. In the standard suffix **-ig**, it uniquely takes on the soft palatal fricative sound `/ç/` as in *ich*.

## How to Pronounce It

Press the back of your tongue firmly against your soft palate (velum) at the back of your roof mouth. Build up air pressure behind the closure, then release it crisply while engaging your vocal cords for `/ɡ/`. If it appears at the end of a word like *Tag*, release it without voice as `/k/`.

## Spelling and Patterns

**G** is written as uppercase **G** and lowercase **g**, appearing widely in native Germanic vocabulary. In standard German orthography, the suffix **-ig** is always written with a **g** despite sounding like `/ç/` before pauses or consonants (e.g., *wichtig*). Double **gg** indicates a preceding short vowel, as in *Flagge*.

## Variants and Pitfalls

Notice how **G** changes its sound based on position: compare voiced `/ɡ/` in *Garten* to voiceless `/k/` in *Tag* and fricative `/ç/` in *richtig*. English speakers often make the mistake of pronouncing **-ig** with a hard `/k/` or soft `/dʒ/`, neither of which is standard in high German. Additionally, avoid pronouncing native German **g** as an English soft 'j' sound.
articles.summary: The letter name is Ge, as in the word Garten.

articles.title: H
articles.body:
## The Sound of H

At the start of a word or syllable, German **H** is pronounced as a voiceless breath sound `/h/`, just like in the English word **house**. However, when it appears after a vowel (known as *Dehnungs-h*), it is completely silent and signals that the preceding vowel is long. It is never pronounced with friction or raspy throat clearing like the German *ch*.

## How to Pronounce H

Keep your mouth relaxed and open in the position of the vowel that follows. Exhale gently from your throat without engaging your vocal cords, producing a soft sigh. Avoid tightening the back of your tongue, ensuring no rasping or scraping sound is made.

## Spelling and Patterns

Capital **H** and lowercase **h** regularly appear at the beginning of words and roots (e.g., **Hand**, **gehören**). Inside words after a vowel, as in **Zahn** or **Stuhl**, it functions purely as an orthographic length marker. It also forms crucial digraphs and trigraphs like **ch**, **sch**, and **ph**.

## Comparing H Sounds and Pitfalls

Contrast the pronounced `/h/` in **Hut** (`/huːt/`) with the silent letter in **Schuh** (`/ʃuː/`) or **gehen** (`/ˈɡeːən/`). English speakers often try to pronounce the internal or final **h**, producing an awkward pause or aspirate where the vowel should simply flow smoothly. Conversely, French and Romance speakers must take care not to drop the initial `/h/` altogether.
articles.summary: The letter name is Ha, as in the word Haus.

articles.title: I
articles.body:
## The Sound of I

The German letter **I** represents two distinct vowel sounds: a tense, long `/iː/` and a lax, short `/ɪ/`. The short variant `/ɪ/` heard in **Insel** is very close to the English vowel in *bit* or *pin*, while the long variant sounds like the *ee* in *see*. English speakers often make the short sound too open or drawl it, so aim for a crisp, centered sound.

## How to Pronounce It

For the short `/ɪ/` in **Insel**, keep your lips unrounded and relaxed while raising the front of your tongue toward the hard palate. Do not tense the mouth muscles as much as you would for a long 'ee' sound. Keep the vowel short, letting the vocal cords produce a brief, clear resonance before moving directly into the next consonant.

## Spelling Patterns

A single **I** followed by two or more consonants typically represents the short `/ɪ/`, as in **Insel** or **Kind**. When written as a single vowel in an open syllable (like **Igel**), it is long `/iː/`. German also frequently uses the digraphs **ie** (as in **sie**) or **ih** (as in **ihn**) to indicate a long `/iː/` explicitly.

## Comparing Vowel Lengths

Contrast the short `/ɪ/` in **bitten** (`/ˈbɪtn̩/`) with the long `/iː/` in **bieten** (`/ˈbiːtn̩/`). Confusing these two vowel quantities can completely alter the meaning of a word in German. Beginners often stretch the short `/ɪ/` into a long tense vowel, so always remember to keep short vowels clipped and energetic.

articles.title: J
articles.body:
## The Sound of J

In standard native German words, the letter **J** is pronounced as a voiced palatal approximant `/j/`, exactly like the *y* in English *yes*. It does not have the harsh English *dzh* sound in native vocabulary. However, in modern borrowings from French or English, it usually retains the source language's pronunciation (`/ʒ/` or `/dʒ/`).

## How to Produce /j/

To make the German `/j/`, raise the middle body of your tongue close to the hard palate, just as if you were about to say the vowel in *see*. Keep your vocal cords vibrating and your lips relaxed and unrounded. Let the air glide smoothly through the narrow constriction without creating friction or popping.

## Spelling and Patterns

The letter **J** appears predominantly at the beginning of words and roots, preceding vowels as in *Jacke* or *Juni*. Capital **J** and lowercase **j** are standard, and it never occurs at the end of native German words. In some loanwords, such as *Jeans* or *Jongleur*, it preserves foreign sound-spelling correspondences.

## Variations and Common Pitfalls

The most critical error for English speakers is pronouncing German native words like *Jahr* or *ja* with an English *j* sound (`/dʒ/`). Always treat a native German **J** as a English *y*. Pay attention to loanwords like *Job* (`/dʒɔp/`) and *Journal* (`/ʒʊʁˈnaːl/`), where speakers switch intentionally to foreign phonemes.

articles.title: K
articles.body:
## The Sound of K

The German letter **K** represents a voiceless velar plosive, standardly transcribed as `/k/`. Before a stressed vowel, it is pronounced with a distinct burst of air (aspiration, `[kʰ]`), very much like the English *k* in *king*. When preceded by an *s* or in unaccented positions, this aspiration disappears.

## How to Pronounce K

Raise the back of your tongue until it forms a tight seal against your soft palate (velum). Allow breath pressure to build behind this closure, then release it crisply to create a sharp burst of air. Ensure your vocal cords remain completely still, as this is a voiceless consonant.

## Spelling Patterns

**K** appears frequently at the beginning, middle, and end of native and loan words like *Katze* and *Kino*. After short vowels, the sound `/k/` is almost always written with the digraph **ck** (as in *Bäcker* or *Ecke*). Additionally, the letter combination **kn-** is always fully pronounced in German, unlike in English.

## Tips and Common Pitfalls

English speakers must remember to pronounce the initial **k** in words like *Knie* (`/kniː/`) or *Knoten* (`/ˈknoːtn̩/`), as it is never silent in German. Learners from languages without aspiration (like Romance languages) should make sure to release a puff of air when **K** begins a stressed syllable. Be careful not to soften the sound into a fricative or voiced `/ɡ/`.

articles.title: L
articles.body:
## The Sound of L

In Standard German, the letter **L** represents the clear alveolar lateral approximant `/l/`. Unlike the 'dark L' common at the end of English syllables, German maintains a **clear, crisp L** in all positions. It sounds bright and fronted, whether at the start of a word or at the very end.

## How to Pronounce It

Place the tip of your tongue firmly against the **alveolar ridge**, right behind your upper front teeth. Let the air flow smoothly around the sides of your tongue while keeping the back of your tongue flat and relaxed. Avoid pulling the back of your tongue up toward the soft palate, which creates an unwanted dark English quality.

## Spelling Patterns

The letter **L** can appear as a single consonant or doubled as **ll** after short vowels, as seen in `Ball` or `hell`. Doubling does not change the core phonetic quality of the sound, but it serves as an indicator that the preceding vowel is short. It appears freely at the beginning, middle, and end of words.

## Avoiding Mistakes

English speakers must avoid using the dark velarized `[ɫ]` at the end of syllables in words like `voll` or `Apfel`. Keep the tongue arched forward so that every German **L** sounds light and European, similar to the initial sound in 'leaf'. Falling back on a hollow, English-style syllable-final L is one of the most recognizable foreign accent markers.

articles.title: M
articles.body:
## The Sound of M

The German letter **M** represents the voiced bilabial nasal consonant `/m/`. It sounds virtually identical to the English 'm' in words like *mother* or *summer*. Unlike some other German consonants, it does not change its quality at the end of words.

## How to Pronounce M

Close both lips completely to block the airflow through your mouth. Lower your velum (soft palate) so the air resonates and escapes freely through your nose while your vocal cords vibrate. Release gently into the following vowel or consonant without adding an extra puff of air.

## Spelling and Patterns

This sound is written as a single **m** or a double **mm**. A doubled **mm**, as in *kommen* or *Sommer*, indicates that the preceding vowel is short and lax. As with all German nouns, words starting with this letter are capitalised when used as substantives, such as *die Mutter*.

## Things to Watch For

German **M** is very consistent and rarely poses difficulties for English speakers. Avoid making the doubled **mm** noticeably longer in normal speech; it merely signals the shortness of the preceding vowel rather than a prolonged consonant. Be careful not to drop the final nasal resonance when it appears in endings like *-em* (e.g., *mit dem*).

articles.title: N
articles.body:
## The Sound of N

The letter **N** in German most commonly represents the voiced alveolar nasal `/n/`, identical to the English 'n' in 'name'. Before velar stops like **k**, it assimilates to the velar nasal `/ŋ/`, sounding like the 'ng' in 'sink'. In everyday spoken German, an unstressed ending like **-en** frequently reduces so that the **N** becomes syllabic `[n̩]`, forming its own syllable without a distinct vowel sound.

## How to Say It

To produce the standard `/n/`, press the tip of your tongue firmly against the alveolar ridge just behind your upper front teeth. Lower your soft palate to let the airstream pass freely out through your nose while vibrating your vocal cords. When pronouncing the reduced ending **-en**, keep your mouth in the position of the previous consonant and simply release the voice through your nose without adding a separate vowel.

## Spelling and Rules

German **N** can appear alone or doubled as **nn**, which serves as a marker that the preceding vowel is short and lax, as seen in **Kanne** or **Sonne**. It also combines with **g** to form the digraph **ng**, representing the single sound `/ŋ/`. Remember that all German nouns starting with **N**, such as **Name** or **Nacht**, must always be capitalized.

## Tips and Common Pitfalls

English speakers often pronounce the final **-en** ending too clearly as `/ən/`, which can sound overly robotic or artificial in natural conversation. Aim instead for a quick syllabic nasal `[n̩]` in words like **haben** (`/ˈhaːbn̩/`). Watch out also for words where **n** sits directly before **k**, ensuring you shift the articulation back to `/ŋ/` rather than pronouncing a crisp `/n/` followed by `/k/`.

articles.title: O
articles.body:
## The Sound of O

The German letter **O** represents two distinct vowel sounds depending on syllable structure: a tense, closed long `/oː/` and a lax, open short `/ɔ/`. English speakers should be careful not to glide the long `/oː/` into a diphthong like the 'o' in 'boat'; it remains completely pure and steady from start to finish. The short `/ɔ/` closely mirrors the British English vowel heard in 'lot' or 'cost'.

## How to Pronounce O

For the long `/oː/`, round your lips tightly into a small circle, keep your tongue pulled back, and tense the vocal tract without letting the jaw close further during the sound. For the short `/ɔ/`, drop your jaw slightly lower and relax the lips into a broader, looser oval shape. Ensure that in both cases, your tongue does not glide towards a 'w' sound at the end.

## Spelling and Patterns

A single **O** is typically pronounced long `/oː/` before a single consonant, at the end of an open syllable, or when doubled (**oo**) as in **Boot**. It is also long when followed by a silent lengthening **h**, as in **Kohl** or **Sohn**. Conversely, it represents the short `/ɔ/` when followed by double consonants or consonant clusters, such as in **Sommer** or **Kopf**.

## Comparing Variants and Common Pitfalls

Contrast the long, tense vowel in **Ofen** `/ˈoːfn̩/` with the short, open vowel in **offen** `/ˈɔfn̩/`. The most frequent error for learners is turning long `/oː/` into an English-style diphthong [oʊ]. Practice keeping your jaw, tongue, and lips entirely motionless while sustaining words like **Rose** and **Obst**.

articles.title: P
articles.body:
## The Sound of P

The letter **P** in German is pronounced as a voiceless bilabial plosive `/p/`. Unlike in French or Spanish, it is strongly aspirated when it begins a stressed syllable, sounding like an English *p* with a noticeable puff of air. Before vowels, make sure to release the burst crisply.

## How to Produce /p/

Bring both lips completely together to block the airflow coming from your lungs. Build up slight air pressure behind your lips without vibrating your vocal cords. Then, part your lips suddenly to release a sharp burst of air.

## Spelling and Occurrence

German **P** appears at the beginning, middle, and end of words, as well as in the doubled form **pp**, which signals a preceding short vowel as in *Kappe*. It also forms the common affricate digraph **pf** as in *Pferd*, where the lips transition immediately into the upper teeth touching the lower lip. In native vocabulary, single *p* is less frequent than *b*, but it is standard in loanwords and everyday terms.

## Contrasts and Common Pitfalls

Take care not to confuse voiceless `/p/` with voiced `/b/`, especially since German devoices final *b* to `[p]`, making *Dieb* end in the same sound as *Typ*. Learners from Romance language backgrounds must remember to aspirate the sound before stressed vowels, producing `[pʰ]` rather than an unaspirated stop. When encountering **pf**, avoid dropping the *p*; pronounce both parts tightly together.

articles.title: Q
articles.body:
## The Sound of Q

In German, the letter **Q** almost never appears alone; it is virtually always paired with **u** as the combination **qu**. Unlike the English pronunciation /kw/, standard German pronounces **qu** as `/kv/`, combining a crisp `[k]` immediately followed by a voiced German `[v]` (like an English *v*). In loanwords borrowed from French, such as *Boutique*, the final **que** simply sounds like a plain `/k/`.

## How to Say It

To produce the standard German **qu**, start by pressing the back of your tongue against your soft palate to make a sharp, voiceless `[k]`. As you release that burst of air, immediately place your upper front teeth lightly against your lower lip to voice a smooth, continuous `[v]`. Transition seamlessly without inserting any pause or vowel sound between the `/k/` and the `/v/`.

## Spelling and Rules

Native German vocabulary strictly uses **Q** followed by **u**, forming words like *Quelle* (spring) or *bequem* (comfortable). You will never see a freestanding **q** without **u** in native German roots. When capitalised at the start of a noun or sentence, only the **Q** is uppercase, while the accompanying **u** remains lowercase (*die Quelle*).

## Comparison and Common Mistakes

English speakers frequently make the mistake of pronouncing German **qu** as `/kw/` (like *quick*), saying */ˈkwɛlə/* instead of the correct */ˈkvɛlə/*. Remember to bring your top teeth to your bottom lip for a firm `[v]` rather than rounding your lips into a `[w]`. The only common exceptions are recent English imports like *Quiz*, which many speakers keep as `/kwɪs/`, and French borrowings ending in *-que*, which are simply `/k/`.

articles.title: R
articles.body:
## Sound of the Letter

In standard German, **R** usually produces a voiced uvular fricative `/ʁ/` at the start of syllables, similar to the French 'r', or vocalises into a central vowel `[ɐ]` at the end of syllables. Unlike the English curled 'r' (`/ɹ/`), the tongue tip never turns upward toward the roof of the mouth. English speakers must avoid substituting their native rhotic sound, as it sounds distinctly foreign in German.

## How to Pronounce It

For the consonant variant `/ʁ/`, keep the tip of your tongue resting behind your lower front teeth and raise the back of your tongue toward the uvula. Let the air flow gently through the narrow constriction to create a soft friction, almost like a gargling motion without water. When followed by a consonant or at the end of a word, simply relax your mouth into an open, unstressed schwa-like vowel `[ɐ]`.

## Spelling and Patterns

The letter **R** appears in both lowercase ('r') and uppercase ('R'), commonly starting words such as **Rot** or doubled as in **Wasser**. Double 'rr' indicates that the preceding vowel is short, as in **Herren**. Word-finally and in the frequent unstressed suffix **-er**, it is almost universally vocalised into `[ɐ]` rather than pronounced as a full consonant.

## Variants and Common Pitfalls

Notice the contrast between the consonant in **Rot** (`/ʁoːt/`) and the vocalised ending in **Vater** (`/ˈfaːtɐ/`). Learners frequently make the mistake of using an English postalveolar approximant or over-rolling an Italian-style trill in northern and central standard contexts. Remember that after long vowels and in unstressed endings, letting it soften into an 'a'-like sound is key to sounding authentic.

articles.title: S
articles.body:
## The Sound of S

In German, the letter **S** has three main sounds depending on its position: voiced `/z/`, voiceless `/s/`, and postalveolar `/ʃ/`. At the beginning of a word or before a vowel, it is typically voiced like the English *z* in *zoo*, as heard in `Sonne` (`/ˈzɔnə/`). At the end of a syllable it hardens to `/s/`, and when it stands before *p* or *t* at the start of a syllable, it sounds like English *sh*.

## How to Pronounce S

For the voiced `/z/` sound in `Sonne`, bring your teeth lightly together and place the tip of your tongue near the gum ridge behind your upper teeth. Push air out while vibrating your vocal cords to make a buzzing sound. Keep your lips relaxed rather than rounded.

## Spelling Rules

Initial **S** followed by a vowel is almost always pronounced `/z/` in standard German. When followed by **p** or **t** at the onset of a root syllable, it is written simply as **S** but pronounced `/ʃ/` (e.g., `Sport`, `Stein`). At the end of words or morphemes, it yields the voiceless `/s/`, contrasting with double **ss** and **ß** which denote voiceless `/s/` after vowels.

## Common Mistakes

English speakers often pronounce initial **S** as a voiceless `/s/` like in *sun*, which makes German words sound unvoiced or foreign. Remember that German `Sonne` starts with a buzz like an English *Z*. Be careful not to confuse this with word-final **S**, which devoices completely to `/s/` as in `Haus`.

articles.title: T
articles.body:
## The Sound of T

The German letter **T** represents a voiceless alveolar plosive, transcribed as `/t/`. At the beginning of a stressed syllable or word, it is strongly **aspirated** (`/tʰ/`), releasing a noticeable puff of air just like in English *tea*. In clusters such as **st** or **rt**, or before unstressed endings, this aspiration is absent or much weaker.

## How to Pronounce It

Place the tip of your tongue firmly against the alveolar ridge just behind your top front teeth to block the airflow completely. Build up slight air pressure behind the closure, then release the tongue sharply downward. Let out a crisp puff of air without vibrating your vocal cords.

## Spelling and Patterns

The letter can appear as a single **t**, a doubled **tt** (indicating that the preceding vowel is short, as in *Mutter*), or combined in digraphs like **th** (which is pronounced as a plain `/t/` in native and loanwords like *Thema*). It also pairs with other consonants in trigraphs such as **tsch** for the `/t͡ʃ/` sound. Final **t** never softens or turns into a flap.

## Watch Out for Traps

Learners with Romance language backgrounds often forget to aspirate word-initial **t**, making words like *Tier* sound almost like *Dir*. English speakers must avoid 'flapping' the letter between vowels: in German *bitten*, you must articulate a crisp, distinct dental/alveolar stop rather than the soft tap heard in American English *butter*.

articles.title: U
articles.body:
## The Sound of U

The German letter **U** primarily represents two vowel sounds: the long tense `/uː/` and the short lax `/ʊ/`. Long `/uː/` is a deep, pure sound similar to the 'oo' in 'boot', but pronounced with noticeably more lip rounding and tension. Short `/ʊ/` is close to the vowel sound heard in English 'put'.

## How to Pronounce It

For long `/uː/`, purse your lips tightly into a small, forward-projecting circle while pulling the back of your tongue upward toward the soft palate. Keep your lips rigid and do not let the vowel glide into an English-style diphthong. For short `/ʊ/`, relax the tongue slightly and keep the lips rounded but much looser.

## Spelling Patterns

A single **u** followed by one consonant or an **h** (as in `Uhr`) is generally long, producing `/uː/`. When followed by a double consonant or consonant cluster (as in `Butter` or `und`), it is almost always pronounced short as `/ʊ/`. German words do not use double 'uu' except in rare loanwords.

## Comparing Long and Short U

Contrast the long vowel in `Mut` (`/muːt/`) with the short vowel in `Mutter` (`/ˈmʊtɐ/`). English speakers often make the mistake of not rounding their lips enough, or they allow long `/uː/` to glide into a 'w' sound at the end. Keep the vowel pure, steady, and fully rounded from start to finish.

articles.title: V
articles.body:
## The Sound of the Letter V

In German, the letter **V** usually sounds like a voiceless `/f/` in native Germanic words, just like the English 'f' in **father**. However, in loanwords derived from Latin, Romance languages, or modern English, it is pronounced as a voiced `/v/` identical to the English 'v' in **vase**.

## How to Pronounce V

Place your upper teeth gently against the inner edge of your lower lip and push air through the narrow gap. For native words like *Vater*, keep your vocal cords still to produce a crisp voiceless `/f/`. For loanwords like *Vase*, vibrate your vocal cords while keeping the same mouth position to make a voiced `/v/`.

## Spelling Patterns

The letter **V** appears at the beginning of many fundamental German words like *viel*, *von*, and *vor*, where it invariably sounds like `/f/`. When found in international words such as *Verb*, *Visum*, or *Klavier*, it regularly carries the voiced `/v/` value. At the end of any syllable or word, German final devoicing forces it to sound like `/f/` regardless of origin.

## Comparing Pronunciations

A frequent mistake for English speakers is pronouncing every German **V** as a voiced `/v/`, turning *Vater* into something that sounds wrong to native ears. Contrast the native `/f/` in *vier* (`/fiːɐ̯/`) with the borrowed `/v/` in *Villa* (`/ˈvɪla/`). Always verify whether a word is native Germanic or borrowed to choose between `/f/` and `/v/`.

articles.title: W
articles.body:
## The Sound of W

In German, the letter **W** is pronounced as a voiced labiodental fricative `/v/`. Unlike in English, it never makes the rounded `/w/` sound heard in words like *water*. Instead, it sounds exactly like the English **V** in *vase* or *vine*.

## How to Pronounce W

Place your upper front teeth lightly against the inside of your lower lip. Push air gently through the contact point while vibrating your vocal cords. Keep your lips unrounded so you do not accidentally slip into an English `/w/` sound.

## Spelling and Occurrence

The letter **W** is extremely common in German and can appear at the beginning of words (*Wort*) or inside them (*löwe*, *zwei*). It is capitalized as the initial letter of nouns and at the start of sentences. German never doubles the letter **W** in native vocabulary.

## Avoiding Common Pitfalls

The biggest trap for English speakers is pronouncing German **W** like an English `/w/`, turning words like *Wasser* into */ˈwasɐ/* instead of `/ˈvasɐ/`. Remember that German **W** equals English **V**, while German **V** often sounds like an English **F**. Practice contrast pairs like *Wein* (`/vaɪ̯n/`) and *fein* (`/faɪ̯n/`) to solidify this distinction.

articles.title: X
articles.body:
## The Sound of the Letter X

The German letter **X** represents the consonant cluster `[ks]`, combining an unvoiced `k` followed immediately by a sharp `s`. Unlike English, where an initial **X** is often pronounced as `[z]` (as in *xylophone*), German always articulates the crisp initial `k` sound. It sounds virtually identical to the English sound in *fox* or *box*.

## How to Produce the Sound

Start by raising the back of your tongue against the soft palate to block the airflow for a brief `[k]`. Release this closure crisply and immediately slide your tongue forward behind your lower teeth. Blow air through this narrow passage to create a sharp, unvoiced hiss `[s]`.

## Spelling and Patterns

The letter **X** is relatively rare in native German words, where the sound cluster `[ks]` is more frequently written as **chs** (as in *sechs*) or **cks** (as in *Keks*). It appears primarily in Greek or Latin loanwords such as *Xylophon* and *Text*, or native exceptions like *Hexe*. In German orthography, **X** is never doubled.

## Pronunciation Variants and Common Traps

The standard pronunciation is universally `[ks]`, though in certain Latin loans like *Examen*, some speakers voice the second element to sound like `[gz]`. The biggest mistake English speakers make is dropping the initial `[k]` in words starting with **X**, pronouncing *Xylophon* with a simple `[z]`. Always ensure the initial `[k]` is distinctly audible in German.

articles.title: Y
articles.body:
## The Sound of Y

The letter **Y** (called *Ypsilon*) is not native to standard Germanic roots and primarily occurs in loanwords. Depending on origin, it usually represents the rounded front vowels `/yː/` or `/ʏ/` in words from Greek, or the glide `/j/` and short vowel `/i/` in modern borrowings. English speakers must avoid reading it automatically as a diphthong like in *sky*.

## How to Produce the Sounds

For the classic Greek sound `/yː/`, say an English 'ee' while pursing your lips firmly as if whistling. If pronouncing the consonant variant `/j/` in words like **Yoga**, let the middle of your tongue approach the hard palate cleanly, just like the English 'y' in *yes*. Keep the airflow steady without adding any friction or turning it into a 'j' sound.

## Spelling and Context

Capital **Y** and lowercase **y** appear almost exclusively in borrowed vocabulary from Greek, English, or French. You will see it internally in scientific or classical terms like *Physik* and *Analyse*, or word-initially in modern terms like *Yacht*. At the end of everyday Anglicisms such as *Handy* or *Hobby*, it consistently denotes a clean, unreduced `/i/`.

## Contrasting the Variants

Notice the stark contrast between the vowel in **Typ** (`/tyːp/`) and the glide in **Yoga** (`/ˈjoːɡa/`). A frequent mistake among learners is pronouncing words like *System* with an English short 'i' or diphthong rather than the rounded `/ʏ/`. Always check the etymology: classical terms require rounded lips, while modern international terms usually take `/j/` or `/i/`.

articles.title: Z
articles.body:
## The Sound of Z

In German, the letter **Z** is pronounced as a voiceless alveolar affricate `/ts/`, exactly like the *ts* in English *cats* or the *zz* in *pizza*. Unlike in English, it is **never voiced** like a buzzing `/z/` in native German vocabulary. Whenever you see a **Z**, always treat it as a crisp blend of `/t/` and `/s/`.

## How to Pronounce /ts/

Start by pressing the tip of your tongue firmly against the alveolar ridge just behind your upper front teeth, exactly as if preparing to say a `/t/`. Build up a small amount of air pressure, then release the tongue slightly so the air hisses out as an `/s/`. Make sure your vocal cords do not vibrate; the entire sound should remain crisp and unvoiced.

## Spelling and Patterns

The letter **Z** appears at the beginning, middle, or end of words, such as in **Zug** (train), **Katze** (cat), and **Holz** (wood). After short vowels, the sound is conventionally spelled as **tz** rather than a double *zz*, except in foreign loanwords like **Pizza**. The uppercase **Z** is required for nouns, while lowercase **z** appears elsewhere.

## Variants and Pitfalls

The standard pronunciation is strictly `/ts/`, seen in words like **Zahn** (`/tsaːn/`) and **Zeit** (`/tsaɪ̯t/`). English speakers frequently slip up by pronouncing German **Z** as a buzzing `/z/`, which sounds foreign and can cause misunderstandings. The only rare exception where **Z** sounds like English `/z/` is in recent English loanwords such as **Zoom** (`/zuːm/`).

articles.title: Ä
articles.body:
## The Sound of Ä

The German umlaut **Ä** represents an open-mid front unrounded vowel, either long `/ɛː/` or short `/ɛ/`. The long variant sounds like a stretched version of the vowel in English *air* or *bear*, while the short variant is virtually identical to the short *e* in *bed*. English speakers often confuse the long `/ɛː/` with a diphthong, so take care to keep the sound pure and steady without gliding into an 'ee' or 'uh' sound.

## How to Produce Ä

To articulate short `/ɛ/`, open your jaw halfway and place your tongue forward, just like pronouncing the *e* in *pen*. For the long `/ɛː/`, keep the mouth slightly more open than for German long **e** `/eː/` while anchoring the tongue tip behind your lower front teeth. Keep your lips completely unrounded and relaxed throughout the sound.

## Spelling Rules and Context

The letter **Ä** is formed by placing an umlaut over **A** and typically arises in plurals or inflections of words containing **A** (such as *Apfel* becoming *Äpfel*). A single consonant or an open syllable usually triggers the long `/ɛː/`, as in *spät*, while a double consonant forces the short `/ɛ/`, as seen in *hätte*. If the umlaut character is unavailable, standard German orthography replaces it with the digraph **ae**.

## Variants and Contrasts

Compare the short `/ɛ/` in **Bälle** (balls) with the long `/ɛː/` in **Bären** (bears) to train your vowel length. A frequent mistake made by English learners is drifting towards the close long `/eː/` (like in *Beere*), or inserting a glide like *ay* in *day*. Focus on maintaining an open, steady vowel posture without shifting your tongue position mid-sound.

articles.title: Ö
articles.body:
## The Sound of Ö

The letter **Ö** represents a front rounded vowel that does not exist in standard English. Long **Ö** is pronounced as `/øː/`, similar to the vowel in French *peu* or roughly like the vowel in English *bird* but spoken with firmly rounded lips. Short **Ö** sounds like `/œ/`, which is more open and relaxed, comparable to the vowel in French *peur*.

## How to Produce the Sound

To pronounce long `/øː/`, shape your tongue as if you are saying the long English vowel in *see* (`/iː/`). Without moving your tongue, tightly round your lips into a small, tense circle as if whistling. For the short `/œ/`, start with the open vowel in *bed* (`/ɛ/`) and round your lips into a relaxed circle.

## Spelling and Patterns

**Ö** is an umlauted vowel, historically formed from an **O** combined with an **E**. In stressed open syllables or before a single consonant, it is typically long (`/øː/`), often reinforced by an **h** as in *Söhne*. Before double consonants or consonant clusters, it is pronounced as the short vowel `/œ/`, as seen in *Löffel* or *öffnen*.

## Variants and Pitfalls

German contrasts the tense, long sound in *Öl* (`/øː/`) with the lax, short sound in *Köpfe* (`/œ/`). English speakers often fall into the trap of substituting the unrounded vowel `/ɜː/` (as in *fur*) or the plain back vowel `/oː/`. Always ensure your tongue remains pushed forward while your lips do the rounding to avoid sounding muffled or mispronouncing critical minimal pairs.

articles.title: Ü
articles.body:
## The Sound of Ü

The letter **Ü** represents a close front rounded vowel, which does not naturally exist in standard English. In its long form it sounds like `/yː/`, similar to the French **u** in *lune*, while its short counterpart is `/ʏ/` as in *fünf*. English speakers tend to substitute an English 'oo' sound, but **Ü** requires voicing with fronted tongue placement.

## How to Pronounce Ü

Position your tongue as if you are about to pronounce the long 'ee' sound `/iː/` as in *see*. Without moving your tongue or jaw, tightly round your lips into a small, tense 'o' shape. Blow voice through this shape to produce the pure `/yː/` sound without sliding into a diphthong.

## Spelling and Patterns

The letter **Ü** appears throughout native German words and can occur in lowercase (**ü**) or uppercase (**Ü**). If the letter appears in an open syllable or before a single consonant, it is usually long (`/yː/`), whereas before multiple consonants it is typically short (`/ʏ/`). When a German keyboard layout is unavailable, it is standard practice to transcribe it as **ue**.

## Short vs. Long Ü and Common Pitfalls

Notice the difference between the long `/yː/` in **fühlen** and the short `/ʏ/` in **füllen**. A frequent mistake is unrounding the lips, which erroneously turns **fühlen** into *fielen* (`/iː/`), or failing to front the tongue, making it sound like **buhlen** (`/uː/`). Keep your tongue high and forward while keeping your lips firmly pursed.

articles.title: ß
articles.body:
## The Sound of ß

The letter **ß** (called *Eszett* or *scharfes S*) represents the voiceless alveolar fricative `[s]`. It sounds exactly like the 'ss' in English **hiss** or the 's' in **sun**, never vibrating like the 'z' in **buzz**. Unlike a single 's' between vowels in German, which is voiced `[z]`, **ß** is always crisp, sharp, and unvoiced.

## How to Pronounce ß

Bring your teeth lightly together and spread your lips slightly into a neutral position. Place the tip of your tongue close to the alveolar ridge just behind your upper teeth without touching it. Push air steadily through the narrow gap to produce a sharp, continuous hissing sound without engaging your vocal cords.

## Spelling Rules for ß

In modern German orthography, **ß** is written only after long vowels (such as in **Straße**) or diphthongs (such as in **heiß**). It never appears at the very beginning of a word and is replaced by **ss** in Switzerland and Liechtenstein. When writing in all capitals, it is traditionally converted to **SS**, though the capital letter **ẞ** is now officially recognised.

## Comparing ß with Similar Sounds

A frequent error among learners is confusing **ß** with double **ss** or voiced **s**. Notice the vowel length: the preceding vowel before **ß** is always long, as in **Maße** (`/ˈmaːsə/`, measurements), whereas the vowel before **ss** is always short, as in **Masse** (`/ˈmasə/`, mass). Never voice **ß** as `[z]`, even when it stands between two vowels.

articles.title: А
articles.body:
## The Sound of Russian А

The letter **А** represents an open central vowel `[a]` when stressed, very similar to the 'a' sound in English *father*. However, in unstressed syllables, Russian undergoes vowel reduction, causing **А** to sound like `[ɐ]` (a shorter 'uh' sound as in *cup*) or `[ə]` (the schwa in *sofa*). It never diphthongises into the flat vowel found in words like *cat* or *face*.

## How to Produce the Sound

To pronounce the stressed sound `[a]`, open your mouth comfortably wide and keep your tongue low and flat on the floor of your mouth. Your lips should remain relaxed and completely unrounded without protruding forward. For unstressed variants, simply keep the mouth slightly less open and relax your vocal tract into a neutral, effortless position.

## Reading and Writing Rules

Uppercase **А** and lowercase **а** look identical to their Latin counterparts, making them immediately recognisable. In standard Russian spelling, **А** indicates that the preceding consonant is 'hard' (non-palatalised), contrasting with **Я**, which indicates palatalisation. Note that after the spelling rule consonants **Ж**, **Ш**, **Ч**, **Щ**, the letter **А** is written instead of **Я**.

## Nuances and Common Mistakes

English speakers often make the mistake of pronouncing unstressed **А** as a full, clear `[a]`, which sounds unnatural and foreign. Compare stressed **мама** (`/ˈma.mə/`), where the first syllable is an open `[a]` and the second reduces to `[ə]`, with **арбуз** (`/ɐrˈbus/`), where the initial unstressed vowel is `[ɐ]`. Pay close attention to word stress so you can reduce the unstressed vowels correctly.

articles.title: Б
articles.body:
## The Sound of Б

The Russian letter **Б** represents a voiced bilabial plosive, identical to the standard English `b` in 'bed'. Unlike English, however, it comes in two distinct forms: 'hard' `/b/` and 'soft' (palatalized) `/bʲ/`. Additionally, Russian regularly devoices voiced consonants at the ends of words, meaning **Б** often sounds just like a crisp English `p`.

## How to Produce the Sound

To pronounce the basic hard sound `/b/`, bring both lips completely together to block the airflow, build up slight pressure, and release it while vibrating your vocal cords. For the soft version `/bʲ/`, arch the middle of your tongue toward the hard palate at the exact moment your lips part, creating an acoustic blend of `b` and a faint `y`-sound. When producing the devoiced sound `/p/` at the end of words, keep your lips firm and avoid adding a strong puff of air (aspiration).

## Spelling and Alphabet Position

**Б** is the second letter of the Russian Cyrillic alphabet, immediately following **А**. Its printed uppercase form looks like an angular number '6' or a Greek beta with a top bar, while the lowercase **б** features an ascending loop to the right. Take care in handwriting not to confuse **Б** with **В** (which represents the `/v/` sound).

## Variants and Common Pitfalls

Listen to the contrast between hard `/b/` in **брат** (`/brat/`) and palatalized `/bʲ/` in **белый** (`/ˈbʲelɨj/`). A major trap for learners is forgetting final devoicing: a word like **клуб** is pronounced `/klup/`, never with a voiced `/b/`. Failing to soften the letter before vowels like **е** or **и** is another frequent mistake that will make your speech sound distinctly non-native.

articles.title: В
articles.body:
## The Sound of В

The letter **В** most commonly represents the voiced labiodental fricative `/v/`, very similar to the English sound in **voice** or **vine**. Unlike English, it regularly undergoes palatalization to become soft `/vʲ/` before soft-indicating vowels. Additionally, it devoices to `/f/` or `/fʲ/` whenever it appears at the end of a word or before a voiceless consonant.

## How to Pronounce В

To produce the hard `/v/`, lightly place your upper front teeth against the inner margin of your lower lip and breathe out while vibrating your vocal cords. For the soft `/vʲ/`, arch the middle of your tongue upward toward the hard palate simultaneously while maintaining light lip-to-teeth contact. Keep your lips relatively relaxed rather than excessively rounded to avoid sounding like a 'w'.

## Spelling and Rules

Uppercase **В** and lowercase **в** share the identical printed shape with the Latin capital letter 'B', which is a notorious pitfall for beginners. It never represents the 'b' sound in Russian, which is written with the distinct letter **Б**. The letter participates actively in Russian voicing assimilation, turning into `/f/` in clusters like **вход** `/fxot/`.

## Variants and Pitfalls

Notice how **вода** uses the standard hard `/v/`, while **вечер** softens into `/vʲeʨɪr/`, and **готов** drops voicing entirely to end in `/f/`. English speakers frequently confuse the glyph **В** with Latin **B**, reading it as `/b/` by accident. Another common error is substituting the English bilabial `/w/` sound for Russian `/v/`; ensure your teeth genuinely contact your lip.

articles.title: Г
articles.body:
## The Sound of Russian Г

The letter **Г** usually represents a voiced velar plosive, identical to the English `g` in "go". Before front vowels like **е**, **и**, or **я**, it softens into a palatalized sound `ɡʲ`. In common grammatical endings like **-ого** and **-его**, it takes on a surprising `v` sound instead of a plosive.

## How to Pronounce It

Press the back of your tongue firmly against your soft palate, just as you do for a standard English `g`. Build up air pressure and release it abruptly while vibrating your vocal cords. For the soft variant `ɡʲ`, raise the middle body of your tongue higher toward the roof of your mouth while making contact.

## Spelling and Alphabet Position

**Г** is the fourth letter of the Russian alphabet, corresponding structurally to Greek gamma. The capital printed form resembles a right angle, while the lowercase cursive form looks like a reversed small Latin "s" or a rounded hook. When written at the end of a word or before voiceless consonants, it undergoes final-devoicing and sounds like `k`.

## Nuances and Common Mistakes

English speakers often default to a hard `ɡ` in all contexts, forgetting that **друг** sounds like `druk` due to word-final devoicing. Another common pitfall is pronouncing the **г** in genitive endings like **хорошего** phonetically as `ɡ` rather than the correct `v`. In a few specific religious words like **Бог**, it is pronounced as a soft fricative `x`.

articles.title: Д
articles.body:
## The Sound of Д

The letter **Д** most commonly represents the voiced dental stop `/d/`. Unlike English /d/, which is alveolar and pronounced behind the upper teeth, Russian `/d/` is dental, made with the tip of the tongue touching the back of the upper front teeth. Before front vowels like **е** or **и**, it softens into a palatalized `/dʲ/`.

## Pronunciation Guide

Press the broad tip of your tongue firmly against the back of your upper front teeth rather than the gum ridge. Build up air pressure and release it with vocal cord vibration to produce a crisp, clean sound.
