Be careful not to confuse it with Hungarian **É** `/eː/`, which is noticeably more closed, longer, and higher in vowel quality.

## How to Pronounce E

Drop your jaw slightly so your mouth is moderately open, wider than for an English *say*. Keep your tongue relaxed forward with its tip resting gently behind your lower front teeth. Vibrate your vocal cords to make a crisp, short, unrounded vowel without gliding into any other sound.

## Spelling Rules and Occurrence

The letter **E** appears freely at the beginning, middle, and end of words, as in **este** ('evening') or **kefe** ('brush'). Hungarian spelling is consistently phonetic, meaning a single **E** is practically always pronounced `/ɛ/`. When a word ends in **-e** and takes a suffix, this final vowel routinely lengthens into **-é-** (for example, *este* becomes *estét*).

## Dialects and Common Pitfalls

In Standard Hungarian, **E** is consistently `/ɛ/`, though many regional dialects distinguish between open `/ɛ/` and a closer, short `/e/` (often called *zárt e*). The most common mistake for foreign learners is lengthening **E** or confusing it with **É**, which changes meaning drastically (e.g., *egy* 'one' versus *égy*). Avoid diphthongising the vowel into an *ay*-like glide at the end of syllables.

articles.title: É
articles.body:
## The Sound of É

The letter **É** represents a long, close-mid front unrounded vowel `/eː/`. It sounds very similar to the vowel in French *fée* or German *See*, but it is held distinctly longer. Unlike the English "long a" in *cake*, it is a pure, steady monophthong that never glides into an "ee" sound.

## How to Pronounce É

Spread your lips into a gentle smile, similar to pronouncing a high "ee" sound. Keep your tongue high and pushed forward against your lower teeth, raising the arch slightly lower than for Hungarian **Í**. Hold the vocal tract completely stationary throughout the duration of the long sound.

## Spelling and Occurrence

**É** is written with an acute accent over the letter **E**, which indicates both length and a completely different vowel quality from short **E** `/ɛ/`. It can occur at the beginning, middle, or end of words (such as *kávé* 'coffee'). In Hungarian morphology, a word-final **e** usually lengthens to **é** when adding suffixes, as in *fekete* becoming *feketét*.

## Comparisons and Pitfalls

The most critical distinction is between short **E** `/ɛ/` (open, like in *bed*) and long **É** `/eː/` (close and tense). Confusing them changes the meaning of words, such as *egy* ('one') versus *égy* (archaic/dialectal form) or *ment* ('went') versus *mént*. English speakers must be careful not to turn **É** into a diphthong like /eɪ/.

articles.title: F
articles.body:
## The Sound of F

The Hungarian letter **F** represents the voiceless labiodental fricative `/f/`, identical to the English 'f' sound in words like *fish* or *coffee*. Unlike some other Hungarian consonants that assimilate across word boundaries, this sound remains remarkably crisp and consistent in almost all contexts. English speakers will find it completely familiar and natural to pronounce.

## How to Pronounce It

Rest your upper front teeth lightly against your lower lip, leaving a slight gap for airflow. Blow air continuously out of your mouth across this contact point without engaging your vocal cords. Keep the friction clear and unvoiced throughout the sound.

## Spelling and Gemination

The letter **F** can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of words. When doubled as **ff** (such as in *huff* or *felfed*), it indicates a prolonged, geminate `/fː/` consonant. In hyphenation across line breaks, doubled letters remain unchanged as **f-f**.

## Tips and Common Pitfalls

Take care to keep `/f/` strictly voiceless; do not accidentally voice it into a `/v/` before vowels or sonorant consonants. Contrast pairs like **férfi** (`/ˈfeːrfi/`, man) and **vér** (`/ˈveːr/`, blood) demonstrate why maintaining clear unvoicing is crucial for meaning. The primary variation is simply length: single `/f/` versus geminate `/fː/`.

articles.title: G
articles.body:
## Sound of the Letter

The letter **G** represents the voiced velar plosive `[ɡ]`, identical to the hard 'g' in English words like *go* or *get*. Unlike in English, Hungarian **G** is never pronounced as an affricate like the 'g' in *gem* or *giant*. It retains this solid, voiced stop quality across almost every position.

## Pronunciation Guide

Raise the back of your tongue until it firmly seals against your soft palate (velum). Build up slight air pressure behind the closure while engaging your vocal cords to create vibration. Release the tongue cleanly to let the sound burst out without any added breathiness.

## Spelling and Distribution

Hungarian **G** appears frequently at the beginning, middle, and end of native words and loanwords. When doubled as **gg**, it denotes an elongated consonant sound `[ɡː]`, as in **reggel** ('morning'). It also combines with 'y' to form the distinct palatal letter **Gy**, which should not be confused with plain **G**.

## Contextual Variations and Common Pitfalls

Before voiceless consonants, such as in compound prefixes like **meg-** followed by a voiceless sound (e.g., **megkér**), **G** naturally assimilates and sounds like `[k]`. English speakers must be careful never to soften **G** into a 'j' sound before front vowels like *e* or *i*. In Hungarian, words like **gép** always start with a hard `[ɡ]`.

articles.title: Gy
articles.body:
## The Sound of Gy

The Hungarian letter **Gy** represents a voiced palatal plosive, transcribed as `/ɟ/`. It is somewhat similar to the 'd' sound in the English word *duty* or the 'j' in *jeep*, but it is a pure stop made further back along the hard palate rather than an affricate. English speakers should be careful not to pronounce it like the English 'j' (`/d͡ʒ/`), as it lacks the hissing friction of that sound.

## How to Pronounce Gy

Place the flat body of your tongue firmly against your hard palate, just behind the alveolar ridge. The tip of your tongue should point downward behind your lower front teeth rather than touching the roof of your mouth. Build up slight air pressure, then release the seal smoothly while vibrating your vocal cords to create voice.

## Spelling Rules for Gy

**Gy** is considered an independent letter of the Hungarian alphabet and alphabetises separately after **G**. When writing in capital letters, only the first letter is capitalised in sentence case (**Gy**), though both are capitalised in all-caps texts (**GY**). If geminated (doubled), it is written as **ggy** (for example, in *meggy*), rather than repeating both letters.

## Sound Variations and Common Pitfalls

Hungarian **Gy** has a single standard value, `/ɟ/`, though it automatically undergoes voicing assimilation to its voiceless counterpart `/c/` (written as **ty**) before voiceless consonants. The most frequent pitfall for learners is substituting the English affricate `/d͡ʒ/` (as in *jar*) or the cluster `/dj/`. Practice contrasting minimal pairs like *gyár* and a hypothetical *djár* to keep the sound completely smooth and palatal.

articles.title: H
articles.body:
## The Sound of H

Hungarian **H** represents the voiceless glottal fricative `/h/`, very similar to the English *h* in *house*. Unlike in French or Spanish, it is never automatically silent at the beginning of words. Between voiced sounds it often becomes voiced `[ɦ]`, and in a few words word-finally it surfaces as a raspy velar fricative `[x]` or is completely silent.

## How to Pronounce H

Open your mouth slightly and keep your tongue resting in a neutral position on the floor of the mouth. Exhale gently through your open vocal cords without engaging your voice, producing an audible puff of air. Make sure the friction comes from the throat rather than the tongue touching the palate.

## Spelling and Patterns

The letter is written as **H** in uppercase and **h** in lowercase. It appears initially, medially, and occasionally finally. When doubled as **hh**, it represents an intensified or geminate fricative sound, found mostly in loanwords or compound boundaries like *méhhas*.

## Nuances and Common Mistakes

English speakers often drop **h** in connected speech, but Hungarian requires a crisp `/h/` initially and medially (e.g., *ház* `/haːz/`, *haza* `/hɒzɒ/`). A critical trap is word-final position: some words drop the **h** entirely (*cseh* is pronounced `/t͡ʃɛ/`), while others retain a rough German-style `[x]` sound (*düh* is `/dyx/`). Do not pronounce silent final **h** unless dictionary norms specifically require `[x]`.

articles.title: I
articles.body:
## The Sound of I

The letter **I** represents a short close front unrounded vowel `/i/`. Unlike English short *i* in *bit* (which is lax `[ɪ]`), Hungarian **I** is a pure, tense sound very similar to the *ee* in *beet*, but held for a much shorter duration. Avoid centralizing or relaxing it into a lax vowel.

## How to Pronounce I

Spread your lips slightly into a relaxed smile and raise the front of your tongue high up toward your hard palate. Keep your vocal cords vibrating and your vocal tract tense without letting the tongue drop. Produce a clean, brisk sound without gliding into any other vowel.

## Spelling and Distribution

Hungarian **I** occurs freely at the beginning, middle, and end of words. It is strictly short; its long counterpart is written with an acute accent as **Í** (`/iː/`). Keep in mind that vowel length distinguishes entirely different words in Hungarian, so do not stretch a plain **i**.

## Comparing and Common Mistakes

English speakers often substitute the lax vowel `/ɪ/` as in *sit*, which sounds foreign and muffled to native Hungarian ears. Another common error is confusing short **i** with long **í**, as in pairs like *irt* (extirpates) versus *írt* (wrote). Always keep short **i** crisp, tense, and brief.

articles.title: Í
articles.body:
## The Sound of Í

The Hungarian letter **Í** represents a long close front unrounded vowel, transcribed as `/iː/`. It sounds very similar to the "ee" in English *see* or *fleece*, but it is held distinctly longer and remains pure throughout its duration. Unlike in English, Hungarian vowels never glide into a diphthong, so your tongue must stay completely stationary.

## How to Pronounce Í

To make this sound, raise the front of your tongue high towards the hard palate, keeping the tip resting just behind your lower front teeth. Spread your lips wide in an unrounded, smiling posture. Hold the vocal sound steady for roughly double the length of the short Hungarian **I**, without letting your pitch or tongue position drift.

## Spelling and Distribution

Written as **Í** in uppercase and **í** in lowercase, this letter carries an acute accent to mark its long vowel length. It can appear anywhere in a word: initially as in *így* ('thus'), medially as in *víz* ('water'), or finally as in *sí* ('ski'). It is an independent letter in the Hungarian alphabet and must never be written as plain **I**.

## Contrasting Sounds and Common Mistakes

The most critical contrast is between long **Í** `/iː/` and short **I** `/i/`, which creates distinct word pairs like *irt* ('to eradicate') versus *írt* ('wrote'). Many learners tend to shorten **Í** in unstressed syllables or diphthongize it into an English-style glide. Make sure you actively sustain the vowel duration, as shortening it can confuse native listeners or alter the grammatical meaning.

articles.title: J
articles.body:
## The sound of J

The Hungarian letter **J** represents the voiced palatal approximant `/j/`. It is identical to the English **y** in *yes* or *yellow*. In standard Hungarian, it shares the exact same pronunciation as the digraph **LY**.

## How to say it

Raise the middle part of your tongue towards the hard palate, close to the position for the vowel `/iː/`. Allow your vocal cords to vibrate as the air glides smoothly through the gap without friction. Keep your lips relaxed or adapt them to the following vowel.

## Spelling conventions

Capital **J** and lowercase **j** appear in all positions of a word, including initials, medials, and finals. Because historical sound changes caused both **J** and **LY** to merge into `/j/`, native speakers must memorize which spelling a word requires by convention. When lengthened, it is written doubled as **jj**.

## Comparing sounds and common pitfalls

Be careful not to pronounce **J** as an English soft 'j' `/dʒ/` or a French `/ʒ/`. Avoid turning it into a harsh fricative `/ʝ/`, except occasionally after voiceless consonants at word boundaries. Remember that words like *jó* ('good') and *folyó* ('river') use the exact same sound `/j/` despite their different spellings.

articles.title: K
articles.body:
## The Sound of K

The Hungarian letter **k** represents the voiceless velar plosive `/k/`. Unlike in English, it is completely **unaspirated**, meaning you release the sound cleanly without a burst of air. It closely resembles the crisp 'k' sound in the English word *sky* rather than the breathy 'k' in *kite*.

## How to Pronounce K

Raise the back of your tongue against the soft palate at the roof of your mouth to completely block the airflow. Release the contact sharply while keeping your vocal cords still. Ensure that no puff of breath escapes after the release, especially before front vowels.

## Spelling and Gemination

The letter **k** occurs frequently in all word positions, including prefixes like *ki-* and suffixes like the accusative marker *-t* after stems. When doubled as **kk**, it is held longer as a geminate consonant (as in *sokk*). Before voiced obstruents, it assimilates phonetically to `[ɡ]`, though the spelling remains **k**.

## Nuances and Common Mistakes

English speakers often make the mistake of heavily aspirating **k**, pronouncing *kék* as `[kʰeːkʰ]`, which sounds distinctly foreign to Hungarian ears. Listen to the difference between normal `/k/` in *kék* and the voiced assimilatory variant `[ɡ]` in compound phrases like *kék bálna*. Practice keeping your throat tension sharp and breath release completely suppressed.

articles.title: L
articles.body:
## The Sound of Hungarian L

The Hungarian letter **L** represents an alveolar lateral approximant `/l/`. Unlike the dark or velarised English 'l' heard in words like *ball* or *milk*, Hungarian **L** is always 'clear' and bright across all positions in a word. It closely matches the light 'l' sound heard at the beginning of English words such as *light* or *lemon*.

## How to Pronounce L

Place the tip of your tongue firmly against the alveolar ridge just behind your upper front teeth. Let the air flow smoothly around both sides of your tongue without adding any friction or throat tension. Keep the back of your tongue low and relaxed so that the sound never becomes dark or muffled.

## Spelling and Gemination

The letter **L** can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of words. When doubled as **LL**, it represents a geminate or lengthened consonant `/lː/`, as in *toll* (pen) or *áll* (to stand). In hyphenated compound words where three identical consonants would meet, the cluster is written out with a hyphen, such as *toll-léc*.

## Common Traps and Comparisons

The most common mistake English speakers make is replacing word-final or preconsonantal Hungarian **L** with a dark, hollow [ɫ], pronouncing words like *bál* or *zöld* incorrectly. Always keep the sound forward and crisp, maintaining the exact same clear quality whether the letter starts a syllable or ends it. Be careful also to hold double **ll** for roughly twice as long as a single **l**.

articles.title: Ly
articles.body:
## Sound of Ly

Historically, **Ly** represented a palatal lateral approximant like Italian *gli*, but in modern standard Hungarian it has completely merged with **j** to sound like `/j/`. It is identical to the English consonant **y** in *yes* or *yellow*. While it looks like an *L*-combination, there is absolutely no *l*-sound in its contemporary pronunciation.

## How to Say Ly

Raise the middle body of your tongue towards the hard palate, keeping the tongue tip down behind the lower front teeth. Let your vocal cords vibrate as air flows smoothly across the surface of the tongue without creating friction. Do not touch the tip of your tongue to the upper gum ridge, or you will accidentally introduce an English *l* sound.

## Spelling and Rules

Hungarian orthography retains **Ly** entirely for historical and etymological reasons, making it a famous spelling hurdle even for native speakers. When doubled, it is written as **lly** (or **Lly** at the beginning of a capitalized sentence), pronounced as a long `/jː/` as in *süllyed*. Aside from the root word *lyuk* (hole) and its derivatives, very few modern words begin with this letter.

## Comparison and Pitfalls

The main challenge is that **Ly** sounds completely indistinguishable from the letter **J** in standard Hungarian; *folyó* (river) and *hajó* (ship) use the exact same sound `/j/`. Foreign learners often make the mistake of pronouncing it like an *l* followed by a *y* (as in *million*) or like Spanish *ll*. Remember that in every single context today, it functions simply as an ordinary `/j/`.

articles.title: M
articles.body:
## The Sound of M

The Hungarian letter **M** represents the voiced bilabial nasal sound `/m/`. It sounds exactly like the English **m** in *mother* or *summer*. It is a voiced nasal consonant that remains completely consistent across almost every phonetic environment in Hungarian.

## How to Pronounce It

Close both lips firmly together while keeping your soft palate lowered so that airflow escapes freely through your nose. Engage your vocal cords to create voice as the air resonates through the nasal cavity. When opening your lips to release into the next vowel, do so smoothly without adding any puff of air.

## Spelling and Gemination

The letter is written as **M** (uppercase) and **m** (lowercase). When doubled as **mm**, it indicates a long consonant sound `[mː]`, as seen in *semmi* ('nothing') or *elem* versus *ellemmel*. Unlike in English where double letters usually just affect preceding vowels, in Hungarian **mm** must be distinctly held for roughly twice as long as a single **m**.

## Accents and Pitfalls

Native speakers of English will find the basic single `/m/` completely straightforward. The primary pitfall is ignoring length distinctions: failing to hold double **mm** long enough can sound unnatural or obscure word boundaries. Additionally, when followed by labiodental sounds like /f/ or /v/, it naturally assimilates into the labiodental nasal `[ɱ]` (as in *hamvas*), which happens instinctively.

articles.title: N
articles.body:
## Sound of the Letter

The letter **N** generally represents the alveolar nasal `[n]`, very similar to the English 'n' in *net*. When it occurs immediately before the velar consonants `[k]` or `[ɡ]`, it automatically assimilates into the velar nasal `[ŋ]`, exactly like the sound in English *sing* or *bank*. Unlike English, Hungarian consonants do not soften or reduce in unstressed positions.

## How to Pronounce It

For the standard sound `[n]`, press the tip of your tongue firmly against the alveolar ridge just behind your upper front teeth while lowering your soft palate so air flows freely through your nose. For the variant before `k` or `g`, raise the back of your tongue against the soft palate instead, allowing the nasal resonance to shift backward. Keep your vocal cords vibrating throughout the sound.

## Spelling and Distribution

Written as uppercase **N** and lowercase **n**, it appears in all word positions including beginnings, middles, and word-finally. A doubled **nn** represents a phonemically distinct long consonant `[nː]`, which must be held for roughly twice the duration of a single 'n'. Be careful not to confuse **n** with the digraph **ny**, which represents an entirely distinct palatal sound.

## Variants and Common Pitfalls

Listen to the contrast between the standard dental/alveolar sound in *nap* (`/ˈnɒp/`) and the assimilated velar sound in *bank* (`/ˈbɒŋk/`). A frequent mistake for learners is failing to hold geminate consonants, turning words like *font* (pound) into a confusion with *fonn* (to spin). Additionally, ensure you do not add a palatal 'y-glide' after plain **n** before front vowels like *e* or *i*.

articles.title: Ny
articles.body:
## The Sound of Ny

The digraph **Ny** represents a voiced palatal nasal consonant, transcribed as `[ɲ]`. It sounds virtually identical to the Spanish *ñ* in *señor*, the French/Italian *gn* in *oignon* or *gnocchi*, or roughly like the *ny* in English *canyon*. Unlike English *ny*, it is produced as a single merged palatal sound rather than an alveolar `[n]` followed by a distinct `[j]`.

## How to Pronounce Ny

Press the broad flat body of your tongue firmly against your hard palate, just behind the alveolar ridge. The tip of your tongue should rest gently behind your lower front teeth or lightly touch the gumline without bearing pressure. Lower your soft palate to let the air stream freely out through your nose while your vocal cords vibrate.

## Spelling and Rules

**Ny** is treated as a single letter in the Hungarian alphabet and can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of words. When capitalised at the start of a sentence or proper noun, only the first element is uppercase (**Ny**), but in full acronyms or all-caps text, both letters become uppercase (**NY**). When doubled, it is written as **nny** (e.g. *mennyi*), which represents a long `[ɲː]`.

## Common Pitfalls

Native English speakers often mistakenly pronounce **ny** as two distinct sounds, `[n]` plus `[j]`, as in *ten years*. Ensure that your tongue body makes broad contact with the roof of the mouth in one seamless gesture. Be careful not to confuse **ny** with plain **n**, as pairs like *bán* ('to regret') and *bány* ('mine', archaic) or *anya* ('mother') and *Anna* have completely distinct meanings.

articles.title: O
articles.body:
## The Sound of O

The Hungarian letter **O** represents a short close-mid back rounded vowel, transcribed as `/o/`. Unlike the English vowel in words like *boat* or *go*, it is a pure, steady monophthong that does not glide into a `/w/` sound at the end. It sounds very similar to the pure Spanish or Italian short `o`.

## How to Pronounce O

Shape your lips into a tight, firm circle and pull your tongue slightly back in your mouth toward the soft palate. Raise the back of your tongue to a mid-high position without touching the roof of your mouth. Keep the lips and tongue completely motionless while producing the sound to avoid creating a diphthong.

## Spelling and Occurrence

The letter **O** is extremely frequent in Hungarian and can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of words. It contrasts directly with its long accented counterpart **Ó**, which has a similar quality but lasts roughly twice as long. Always write and pronounce it without an accent to keep the vowel short.

## Comparing Sounds and Common Mistakes

Native English speakers tend to diphthongize this vowel into `[oʊ]`, which sounds foreign in Hungarian. Be careful not to confuse short **o** in words like *kor* (age) with long **ó** in *kór* (disease), as vowel length changes the entire meaning. Always keep the sound clipped, clean, and strictly monophthongal.

articles.title: Ó
articles.body:
## The sound of Ó

The letter **Ó** represents a long, close-mid back rounded vowel `[oː]`. It sounds very similar to the vowel in British English *law* spoken with rounded lips, or more accurately like a prolonged French *eau* or German *Boot*. Unlike in English, this vowel is a pure, stable monophthong and must never glide into a `[w]` sound.

## How to pronounce Ó

Round your lips firmly into an 'o'-shape and pull the body of your tongue back toward the soft palate. Keep your jaw relatively closed, higher than for English *hot*. Maintain the position steadily for roughly twice as long as the short Hungarian **O** without moving your lips or tongue at the end.

## Spelling rules for Ó

The acute accent mark (*hosszú ékezet*) always indicates length in Hungarian vowels. **Ó** can appear at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end of words, frequently functioning as a distinct word on its own (meaning *ancient*). In uppercase, the accent must be maintained as **Ó**.

## Comparing Ó with similar sounds

The most critical distinction is between short **o** and long **ó**, which changes word meanings entirely, as in *kor* (age) versus *kór* (disease). English speakers commonly make the mistake of turning **ó** into a diphthong `[oʊ]`; ensure your lips remain locked in a static position until phonation ends completely.

articles.title: Ö
articles.body:
## The Sound of Hungarian Ö

The letter **Ö** represents the short, close-mid front rounded vowel `[ø]`. It is very similar to the German short *ö* in *können* or the French vowel in *peu*, but it has no direct equivalent in standard English. English speakers often substitute it with the vowel in *bird* or *cup*, but **Ö** is strictly fronted and pronounced with rounded lips.

## How to Pronounce Ö

Start by producing the English vowel sound in *bed* (`[e]`), keeping your tongue pressed forward against the backs of your lower front teeth. Without moving your tongue at all, round your lips tightly as if you were going to whistle or say *oh*. Keep the sound short, crisp, and pure, avoiding any diphthong glide.

## Spelling and Distribution

Hungarian **Ö** is written with two dots (an umlaut) and is treated as an independent letter in the alphabet, coming immediately after **O**. It can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of words, such as in *öt* (five) or *sör* (beer). Be careful not to confuse it with **Ő**, which has two long accents (a double acute) and represents a distinctly long vowel.

## Comparing Ö and Ő

The most critical distinction in Hungarian is vowel length between short **Ö** (`/ø/`) and long **Ő** (`/øː/`). A classic contrast is *öt* (five) versus *őt* (him/her, accusative), where lengthening the vowel completely changes the meaning. Avoid unrounding your lips into an English *uh* or dragging the short **Ö** out into a long syllable.

articles.title: Ő
articles.body:
## The Sound of Ő

The letter **Ő** represents a long, close-mid front rounded vowel, written as `/øː/` in IPA. It is the long counterpart of the short Hungarian **Ö** (`/ø/`), similar to the vowel in French *deux* or German *schön*, but sustained longer. English lacks this sound entirely; it sounds somewhat like the vowel in *bird*, but pronounced with tensely rounded lips and no rhotic coloring.

## How to Pronounce Ő

Shape your tongue as if you were pronouncing a long 'ay' sound as in *say* (`/eː/`). Without moving your tongue, round your lips firmly into a tight, pursed circle as if you were going to whistle. Hold this sound steady and long, ensuring your tongue stays high and fronted without gliding into an 'ee' or 'oo' sound.

## Spelling and Length Markings

In Hungarian orthography, the double acute accent (hungarumlaut) marks a vowel as both rounded and long. **Ő** contrasts strictly with **Ö**; failing to write or pronounce the length properly can change the meaning of a word completely. It can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of words, such as in **ő** ('he/she') or **mező** ('field').

## Contrasts and Common Pitfalls

The most critical distinction is between short **Ö** (`/ø/`) and long **Ő** (`/øː/`), as seen in pairs like **öt** ('five') and **őt** ('him/her'). English speakers frequently make the mistake of reducing it to an unrounded central vowel like the 'er' in *butter* or turning it into a diphthong. Keep the lips tensely pursed and extend the duration so that native speakers do not hear the short vowel instead.

articles.title: P
articles.body:
## The Sound of P

The Hungarian letter **P** represents the voiceless bilabial plosive `/p/`. Unlike in English, it is strictly **unaspirated**, meaning you release it without any audible puff of air, similar to the 'p' in English *spin* rather than *pin*. When it precedes a voiced consonant such as **d**, **g**, or **b**, it undergoes voicing assimilation and turns into a soft `/b/` sound.

## How to Pronounce P

Close both lips firmly together to completely block the airflow from your lungs. Let a small amount of air pressure build up behind your lips without vibrating your vocal cords. Then, part your lips crisply to release the sound without blowing extra breath out afterwards.

## Spelling and Gemination

The letter **P** can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of words. When doubled as **pp**, as in *csöpp* (tiny drop), it represents a **geminate** or long consonant `/pː/`, held for roughly twice the duration of a single **p**. In compound words, the combination of two **p** letters is written out fully.

## Sound Variations and Common Pitfalls

The regular sound is pure `/p/` (as in *piros*), but in words like *népdal* (folk song), it sounds like `/b/` due to the following voiced **d**. The most common mistake for English speakers is **aspirating** this consonant at the start of words; make sure to keep it tight and clean, holding back the breath.

articles.title: Q
articles.body:
## The Sound of Q

The letter **Q** is not part of the traditional native Hungarian alphabet, but it is officially included in the extended 44-letter alphabet for foreign loanwords and proper names. It is almost exclusively found in the sequence **qu**, which is pronounced exactly like `kv` in Hungarian (the sound `/k/` followed by `/v/`). Unlike in English, the letter **u** that follows does not form a `w` glide, but a clear Hungarian `v` sound.

## How to Pronounce It

To produce the **qu** combination, raise the back of your tongue against the soft palate to make a crisp, unaspirated Hungarian `k`. Immediately release it into a voiced labiodental fricative `v` by bringing your upper teeth against your lower lip while vibrating your vocal cords. Ensure you do not round your lips into an English `w` sound.

## Spelling and Usage

**Q** only appears in Latin loans, historical family names, and foreign terminology such as **Aquincum** or **quasi**. In fully integrated loanwords, Hungarian orthography almost always adapts the spelling to **kv**, as seen in **kvartett** (quartet) or **kvíz** (quiz). You will rarely encounter **q** outside of formal or specialized contexts.

## Comparing and Pitfalls

The most common mistake English speakers make is pronouncing **qu** with an English `/kw/` diphthong or glide. In Hungarian, the sequence represents a strict `kv` where the second consonant is a sharp labiodental `/v/`. Compare borrowed spellings like **quasi** with native adaptations like **kvaterkázik** to hear the identical consonant cluster.

articles.title: R
articles.body:
## The Sound of R

Hungarian **R** represents an alveolar trill or tap, transcribed as `/r/`. Unlike the English smooth retroflex approximant or the French/German uvular throat sound, Hungarian **R** is produced by rolling the tip of the tongue against the gum ridge behind the upper teeth. In everyday speech it often consists of a single brisk tap, while double **RR** is distinctly prolonged with multiple vibrations.

## How to Pronounce R

Place the tip of your tongue loosely against the alveolar ridge, right above your upper front teeth. Exhale a steady stream of air across the tip so that it flutters or taps briskly against the ridge. Keep the back and root of your tongue relaxed so you do not accidentally produce a throat sound.

## Spelling and Usage

The letter **R** appears in uppercase as **R** and lowercase as **r**. It is extremely common in Hungarian and can occur at the beginning, middle, or end of words. When geminated as **rr** (as in *forró*), the tongue trills for a longer duration with multiple audible vibrations.

## Tips and Common Pitfalls

The most common mistake for English speakers is using the English postalveolar approximant `[ɹ]`, which sounds very muffled and foreign in Hungarian. German and French speakers must also avoid using the uvular trill or fricative `[ʁ]`. Aim for an Italian- or Spanish-style rolled or tapped `/r/` using strictly the tongue tip.

articles.title: S
articles.body:
## The Sound of S

In Hungarian, the single letter **s** always represents the sound `/ʃ/`, exactly like the **sh** in English *shoe* or *fish*. It never sounds like the English /s/ sound; learners frequently confuse this with the letter **sz**, which actually produces /s/. Additionally, before voiced consonants like *b*, *d*, or *g*, it assimilates and is pronounced voiced as `/ʒ/` (like the *s* in *measure*).

## How to Pronounce It

Round your lips slightly and push them forward into a gentle trumpet shape. Lift the blade and front of your tongue toward the roof of your mouth, just behind the alveolar ridge. Expel air smoothly through the channel without vibrating your vocal cords to produce a clear, rushing **sh** sound.

## Spelling and Patterns

The letter **s** appears freely at the beginning, middle, and end of native and loan words. When prolonged or doubled, it is written as **ss** (for example, *lassú* meaning slow). Remember that whenever you see a solo **s** in a Hungarian text, you must read it as an English 'sh'.

## Comparing Sounds and Common Mistakes

The most critical mistake English speakers make is pronouncing **s** as `/s/`, which entirely changes words or makes them unrecognizable. Compare **só** (`/ʃoː/`, salt) with **szó** (`/soː/`, word); confusing the two completely alters the meaning. Also watch out for regressive voicing in compound words such as **kisbaba** (`/ˈkiʒbɒbɒ/`), where the /ʃ/ softens into `/ʒ/`.

articles.title: Sz
articles.body:
## Sound of Sz

The digraph **sz** represents the voiceless alveolar fricative `[s]`, precisely matching the English *s* sound in *sun* or *bus*. Learners are often confused by Hungarian orthography because a plain letter *s* represents an *sh* sound `[ʃ]`, whereas **sz** is simply *s*. It remains crisp and unvoiced in nearly all contexts.

## How to Say Sz

Position the tip of your tongue close to the alveolar ridge just behind your upper front teeth without touching it. Keep your teeth close together and blow a steady stream of air through the central groove of the tongue. Do not engage your vocal cords; the resulting sound should be a sharp, clear hiss.

## Spelling and Rules

Hungarian treats **sz** as a single distinct letter of the alphabet. At the beginning of a sentence or a proper noun, only the first letter is capitalised (**Sz**), while fully uppercase text uses **SZ**. When doubled for a long sound, it is spelled **ssz** (as in *hosszú*), rather than repeating both letters.

## Comparing and Mistakes

The most frequent error English speakers make is misreading **sz** as a *z* sound or confusing it with plain Hungarian *s* (`[ʃ]`). Remember the inverse rule: Hungarian **s** is *sh*, while **sz** is *s*. Additionally, before voiced consonants like *b*, *d*, or *g*, **sz** undergoes voice assimilation and is pronounced as `[z]`, as seen in *részben*.

articles.title: T
articles.body:
## The Sound of the Letter T

The letter **T** represents a voiceless dental stop, transcribed as `/t/`. Unlike in English, it is pronounced with the tip of the tongue touching the upper front teeth rather than the alveolar ridge behind them. Most importantly, it is **unaspirated**, meaning there is no puff of breath released when saying it, sounding much like the 't' in the English word *stop*.

## How to Pronounce T

Place the tip of your tongue firmly against the back of your upper front teeth to completely block the airflow. Build up a small amount of air pressure behind the closure, then release the tongue sharply without breathing out extra air. Ensure your vocal cords do not vibrate during the initial contact.

## Spelling and Gemination

The letter is written as **T** in uppercase and **t** in lowercase. In Hungarian, it can appear anywhere in a word, including initially, internally, and finally. When doubled as **tt**, it represents a lengthened or geminate sound `/tː/`, which must be held distinctly longer than a single **t**.

## Sound Variations and Common Pitfalls

While usually pronounced as a clean `/t/`, it assimilates to a voiced `/d/` before voiced consonants, as heard in **hatvan** (`/ˈhɒdvɒn/`). English speakers frequently make the error of adding aspiration at the start of words like **tél**, which sounds unnatural to Hungarian native speakers. Be careful to keep the release crisp, clean, and strictly unaspirated.

articles.title: Ty
articles.body:
## The Sound of Hungarian Ty

The Hungarian letter **Ty** represents a voiceless palatal plosive, transcribed in IPA as `[c]`. It sounds somewhat like the *t* in English *tune* or the *c* in *cue*, but pronounced as a single, neat sound rather than two separate elements. Unlike the English /tʃ/ sound in *chair*, **Ty** is a true stop consonant articulated flat against the hard palate.

## How to Pronounce Ty

Place the flat body of your tongue firmly against the hard roof of your mouth, just behind the alveolar ridge. Keep the tip of your tongue pressed down behind your lower front teeth to prevent turning it into an English *ch* sound. Build up slight air pressure and release it cleanly without a noisy whistling or friction.

## Spelling and Rules

**Ty** is treated as a single letter in the Hungarian alphabet and alphabetised under its own heading. When capitalised at the beginning of a word or sentence, only the initial consonant is uppercase (**Ty**), while fully capitalised words write both letters as capitals (**TY**). When doubled, it is contracted to **tty**, as seen in words like *hattyú* (swan).

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

Learners frequently substitute the English /tʃ/ (as in *chin*) or an explicit /tj/ sequence (as in *stew*) for Hungarian **Ty**. Notice how *tyúk* differs sharply from *csuk* or a two-step *t-yúk*. Practice keeping the airflow completely stopped and releasing smoothly without buzzing or hissing.

articles.title: U
articles.body:
## The Sound of Hungarian U

The letter **U** represents the short close back rounded vowel `/u/`. It sounds very similar to the 'oo' in English *book* or *look*, but it is articulated with more tightly rounded lips and a slightly higher tongue position. Unlike its long counterpart **Ú**, this vowel is kept distinctly crisp and brief.

## How to Pronounce U

Pull your tongue back toward the soft palate while keeping the tongue body high in the mouth. Round your lips tightly into a small circle, pushing them slightly forward. Produce a clean, short vocal sound without letting it glide or lengthen into a diphthong.

## Spelling and Occurrence

Hungarian **U** appears frequently across all word positions, including prefixes, word stems, and grammatical suffixes. It is written as a simple **U** in uppercase and **u** in lowercase. Do not confuse it with **Ú** (long), **Ü** (front rounded), or **Ű** (long front rounded), which are entirely distinct letters with different sounds.

## Contrasting U with Similar Sounds

A frequent mistake for English speakers is making **U** too lax or lengthening it into **Ú** `/uː/`, which changes word meanings entirely, as seen in *hurok* (loop) versus *húrok* (strings). Additionally, take care not to confuse it with front-vowel **Ü** `/y/`, where the tongue is pushed forward instead of back. Always keep short **U** fully back, rounded, and clipped.

articles.title: Ú
articles.body:
## The Sound of Hungarian Ú

The letter **Ú** represents the long close back rounded vowel `/uː/`. It is nearly identical in quality to the vowel in the English word *flute* or *moon*, but it is held distinctly longer than the short Hungarian **u**. English speakers tend to diphthongize long back vowels, but Hungarian **ú** remains purely monophthongal and steady from start to finish.

## How to Pronounce Ú

Pull your tongue back and raise the back of it toward the soft palate, just as you do for a regular /u/. Round your lips tightly into a firm, puckered circle. Hold this exact tongue and lip posture while voicing for roughly twice the duration of a short **u**, ensuring that your lips and jaw do not move.

## Spelling and Distribution of Ú

The letter **Ú** is spelled with an acute accent over the Latin vowel *u* to signify its long duration. It can appear in all positions: word-initially (as in *új*), medially (as in *hús*), or word-finally (as in *bosszú*). The acute accent is phonemic in Hungarian, meaning omitting it often produces an entirely different word or a misspelling.

## Contrasts and Common Pitfalls

Be careful never to substitute the short vowel **/u/** for the long **/uː/**, as vowel length changes meaning in Hungarian. For instance, compare **húsz** (/ˈhuːs/, 'twenty') with **huszár** (/ˈhusaːr/, 'hussar'). Foreign speakers frequently shorten this sound in unstressed syllables; ensure you maintain its long, rounded quality wherever it appears in a word.

articles.title: Ü
articles.body:
## The Sound of Ü

The Hungarian letter **Ü** represents a close front rounded vowel, transcribed as `/y/`. It is essentially identical to the German short **ü** in *fünf* or the French **u** in *tu*. English lacks this native sound, so learners should take care not to substitute an English 'oo' `/u/` or 'ee' `/i/`.

## How to Pronounce Ü

Start by producing a clear, continuous English 'ee' sound as in *see*, keeping your tongue arched high at the front of your mouth. Without moving your tongue at all, tightly round your lips into an 'o' or whistling shape. Keep the vowel short and crisp without sliding into a diphthong.

## Spelling and Distribution

Written as lowercase **ü** and uppercase **Ü**, this letter carries two dots (an umlaut or trema). It can appear in any position within a word, including initially, medially, and finally. Always distinguish it from the long version **Ű**, which uses double acute accents to mark duration.

## Comparisons and Pitfalls

The most critical distinction is between short **ü** `/y/` and long **ű** `/yː/`, as in *öt* (which has **ö**) vs. words like *fül* (ear) and *fű* (grass). English speakers often unround the lips to sound like **i** or pull the tongue back to sound like **u**. Practice contrasting *tükör* (mirror) with *tik* or *tuk* to keep the tongue forward and lips rounded.

articles.title: Ű
articles.body:
## The Sound of Ű

The letter **Ű** represents a long, close front rounded vowel, transcribed as `/yː/`. It sounds exactly like a prolonged French *u* in *lune* or German *ü* in *Tür*. English lacks this specific vowel, so learners must avoid substituting standard English sounds like `/uː/` (as in *moon*) or `/juː/` (as in *few*).

## How to Pronounce Ű

Start by producing a continuous long **ee** sound as in *see*, keeping your tongue pushed high and forward against your lower teeth. Without shifting your tongue's position at all, tightly round your lips into a small, tense 'O' circle. Hold this rounded vowel sound steady for roughly twice as long as the short **Ü**.

## Spelling and Length Mark

The letter **Ű** is uniquely Hungarian, distinguished by its double acute accent (*hosszú hungaricum*), which signifies that the vowel is strictly long. The lowercase form is **ű**. It contrasts directly with **ü**, which bears a regular umlaut to show a short duration.

## Crucial Contrasts

Ensure you hold **ű** significantly longer than short **ü**, as duration alone can change the meaning of words. For example, compare **tűz** (`/tyːz/`, meaning 'fire') with **tüzet** (`/ˈtyzɛt/`, 'fire' in the accusative case), or **öt** ('five') versus **őt** ('him/her'). A common mistake for native English speakers is relaxing the rounded lips, which creates a diphthong like /juː/; keep the lips firmly rounded and static.

articles.title: V
articles.body:
## The Sound of V

The Hungarian letter **V** represents the voiced labiodental fricative `/v/`. It sounds virtually identical to the English **v** in *vine* or *river*. Hungarian `/v/` is unique in phonology because it can undergo voicing assimilation (becoming unvoiced before voiceless consonants in colloquial fast speech, though strictly standard Hungarian resists this), but it never causes preceding voiceless consonants to become voiced.

## How to Pronounce V

Lightly place your upper front teeth against your lower lip, just as you do for English **v**. Gently blow air through the narrow gap between your teeth and lip while vibrating your vocal cords. Ensure your lips do not round or protrude, avoiding an English **w** sound.

## Spelling and Usage

The letter **V** is written as **V** uppercase and **v** lowercase. It appears freely at the beginning, middle, and end of words. Double **vv** indicates a lengthened consonant, as seen in words like *orvosi* versus *hívva* (`/ˈhiːvvɒ/`).

## Comparisons and Pitfalls

Native speakers of languages like German must remember that Hungarian **v** is always voiced `/v/`, never unvoiced `/f/` like German *Vogel*. Slavic or Spanish speakers must take care not to confuse `/v/` with a bilabial approximant or `/b/`. Always maintain clear contact between your upper teeth and lower lip to keep the sound crisp.

articles.title: W
articles.body:
## Sound of the Letter

The letter **W** is not part of the traditional native Hungarian alphabet and appears strictly in foreign loanwords, acronyms, and historical family names. In almost every case, it is pronounced identically to the Hungarian letter **V**, sounding like the voiced labiodental fricative `/v/`. Unlike in English, where it produces a smooth glide `/w/`, Hungarian speakers naturally replace this with a standard English 'v' sound.

## Pronunciation Guide

Place your upper teeth gently against the inner edge of your lower lip, just as you do for the English 'v'. Exhale steadily while activating your vocal cords to produce a continuous vibration. Do not round your lips into a circle as you would for an English 'w'; keep the dental-to-lip contact firm and buzzy.

## Spelling and Usage

In contemporary Hungarian, **W** is treated as an 'extended' alphabet letter and alphabetised alongside **V**. Fully assimilated everyday borrowings typically swap it out for standard **v**, as seen in *vattacukor*. However, it is preserved in international terms like **WC**, SI units like *watt*, and aristocratic historic surnames such as *Wesselényi*.

## Nuances and Pitfalls

The most frequent error for English speakers is pronouncing **W** as a rounded glide `/w/`. Even in English borrowings like *whisky* or *western*, Hungarians predominantly say `/ˈviski/` and `/ˈvɛstɛrn/`. Remember that the letter's Hungarian name is *dupla vé* (double V), which directly reinforces its standard `/v/` pronunciation.

articles.title: X
articles.body:
## The Sound of the Letter X

The letter **X** is not native to Hungarian and is used exclusively in loanwords, representing the consonant cluster `/ks/`. Unlike in English, where an initial *x* often softens to `/z/` (as in *xylophone*), Hungarian pronounces an initial **x** crisply as `/ks/` (sounding like *ksilofon*). In intervocalic positions or through voice assimilation, it occasionally surfaces as `/gz/`.

## How to Pronounce It

To articulate this letter, produce a sharp, voiceless velar stop `/k/` by pressing the back of the tongue against the soft palate, then immediately release the air into an unvoiced alveolar sibilant `/s/`. Keep your lips relaxed and slightly spread. Do not let vocal fold vibration sneak in at the beginning of words, even if your native tongue normally voices initial *x*.

## Spelling and Usage

The letter **X** appears primarily in classical Greco-Latin borrowings and modern internationalisms such as **taxi** or **oxigén**. In purely integrated or assimilated vocabulary, Hungarian often spells out the cluster phonetically as **ksz** or **gz** (for example, *szex* vs. *egzotikus*). Both lowercase **x** and uppercase **X** follow standard Latin script forms.

## Variants and Common Mistakes

English speakers often make the error of pronouncing words like *xilofon* with an English `/z/` sound; in Hungarian, it must start with a distinct `/ks/`. Additionally, ensure you do not replace the crisp alveolar `/s/` with the postalveolar Hungarian *sz* vs *s* sound; it should always be the whistling `/s/` (as in English *sit*), never Hungarian *s* (`/ʃ/`). In voiced contexts, as in loanwords related to *egzakt*, native assimilation may shift the sound naturally to `/gz/`.

articles.title: Y
articles.body:
## Sound of Y

The letter **Y** (*ipszilon*) is not traditionally used on its own for native vocabulary, appearing mainly in foreign loanwords and historical family names. In loanwords like *yacht*, it represents the palatal glide `/j/`, identical to the English **y** in *yes*. In historical surnames, it typically represents the vowel sound `/i/`.

## How to say it

To produce the `/j/` sound heard in modern loanwords, raise the middle body of your tongue close to the hard palate. Keep your vocal cords vibrating while allowing air to glide smoothly over the tongue without friction. Your lips should be relaxed and spread, matching the vowel that follows immediately.

## Spelling and usage

In modern Hungarian orthography, **Y** is used almost exclusively in foreign borrowings, brand names, and traditional aristocratic family names. It also serves as a crucial component of native digraphs like **gy**, **ly**, **ny**, and **ty**, where it historically indicated palatalization rather than a distinct independent letter sound. When standing alone in an old surname such as *Báthory*, it is pronounced as a simple short Hungarian *i*.

## Pronunciation nuances

Learners often confuse whether to pronounce a lone **Y** as a consonant or a vowel. Treat it as `/j/` in loanwords like *yoga* or *yacht*, but switch to the vowel `/i/` at the end of traditional Hungarian surnames like *Vörösmarty*. Avoid pronouncing it as a rounded vowel like French *u* or German *ü*, which does not occur for this letter in Hungarian.

articles.title: Z
articles.body:
## The Sound of Z

The letter **Z** in Hungarian represents the voiced alveolar fricative `/z/`, which is identical to the English 'z' in *zebra* or *buzz*. Unlike in German or Italian, where this letter often represents an affricate like `ts`, Hungarian **Z** is always a continuous, smooth buzzing sound. However, when it stands immediately before a voiceless consonant, it undergoes regressive voicing assimilation and becomes a voiceless `/s/`.

## How to Pronounce Z

Place the tip of your tongue very close to the alveolar ridge just behind your upper front teeth, leaving a tiny gap for air to pass. Keep your teeth close together and blow air through the channel while vibrating your vocal cords. If your throat does not vibrate, you are producing an 's' sound instead of a proper voiced **Z**.

## Spelling and Positions

**Z** can appear in all word positions: word-initially as in *zene* (music), medially as in *búza* (wheat), and word-finally as in *méz* (honey). It can be doubled as **ZZ** to represent a geminate long consonant `/zː/`, as heard in *izzad* (to sweat). It also forms digraphs such as **SZ** (`/s/`) and **ZS** (`/ʒ/`), which must be treated as completely separate single letters.

## Variants and Pitfalls

The primary variant occurs before voiceless consonants like *t*, *k*, or *h*, where `/z/` turns into `/s/`, such as in *húzta* (`/ˈhuːstɒ/`). German speakers must be especially careful not to pronounce **Z** as `/ts/`, which is written as **C** in Hungarian. Additionally, take care never to confuse single **Z** (`/z/`) with the digraph **SZ** (`/s/`), as swapping them changes word meanings entirely.

articles.title: A
articles.body:
## The Sound of the Letter A

In European Portuguese, the letter **A** has two primary oral sounds: an open `[a]` like the vowel in British English *bath*, and a closed, reduced `[ɐ]` similar to the *u* in *cut* or the final *a* in *sofa*. When stressed, it is usually open, but in unstressed positions, it automatically reduces to the much centraler `[ɐ]`. Additionally, before nasal consonants or under a tilde, it acquires a distinct nasal quality `[ɐ̃]`.

## How to Produce the Sound

For the open `[a]`, drop your lower jaw wide, keep your tongue low and flat on the floor of your mouth, and relax your lips completely. To make the reduced `[ɐ]`, keep your jaw slightly higher, retract the tongue toward the center of your mouth, and make a relaxed, neutral vocalisation. Avoid rounding your lips for either sound.

## Spelling and Patterns

The letter **A** can appear with various diacritics that indicate stress, openness, or nasality. An acute accent (**á**) marks a stressed open `[a]`, a circumflex (**â**) denotes a stressed closed or nasal `[ɐ]`, and a tilde (**ã**) marks the nasal vowel `[ɐ̃]`. In unstressed word-final positions, plain **a** is almost always pronounced as the reduced `[ɐ]`.

## Contrasts and Common Mistakes

Do not pronounce every **a** with a bright, open quality as in Spanish or Italian. For instance, in the word *casa* (`/ˈka.zɐ/`), the first vowel is open, but the final vowel must be reduced to `[ɐ]`. A frequent mistake for English speakers is to lengthen the unstressed final syllable instead of clipping it short and central.

articles.title: B
articles.body:
## The Sound of the Letter B

The letter **B** in European Portuguese usually represents the voiced bilabial plosive `[b]`, just like the English *b* in "boat". However, between vowels in natural connected speech, it softens into a voiced bilabial fricative `[β]`, where the lips do not fully seal. Unlike English, it is pronounced with less aspiration and tension.

## How to Pronounce B

To make the standard `[b]` sound, bring both lips completely together to stop the airflow, vibrate your vocal cords, and release the air cleanly. When it softens to `[β]` between vowels, simply bring your lips close enough to create slight friction without letting them snap completely shut. Keep your tongue relaxed and neutral at the bottom of your mouth.

## Spelling and Distribution

The letter **B** is written identically in uppercase (*B*) and lowercase (*b*) as in English. It appears frequently at the beginning of words (*bom*, *boca*) and internally before vowels or liquids (*branco*, *abrir*). Double *bb* never occurs in native Portuguese vocabulary, appearing only in foreign loanwords.

## Accents and Pitfalls

In careful speech and at the start of words, **B** sounds firmly like `[b]`, but between vowels it softens to `[β]` (as in *saber* `[sɐˈβeɾ]`). English speakers often make the mistake of aspirating it or failing to soften it in running speech. In northern Portugal, some speakers merge **B** and **V** into `[b]` or `[β]`, but standard European Portuguese keeps them strictly separate.

articles.title: C
articles.body:
## The Sounds of C

In European Portuguese, the letter **C** represents two entirely distinct sounds depending on what letter follows it. Before the vowels **a**, **o**, or **u**, or before a consonant, it sounds like `/k/` as in *cat*, but unlike in English, it is pronounced with almost no aspiration (a puff of air). Before the front vowels **e** and **i**, it softens to a voiceless sibilant `/s/`, exactly like the *s* in *sun*.

## How to Pronounce C

For the hard sound `/k/`, press the back of your tongue against the soft palate at the roof of your mouth, build up slight air pressure, and release it crisply without an extra breath. For the soft sound `/s/`, bring the tip or blade of your tongue very close to the alveolar ridge behind your upper front teeth. Blow a continuous, narrow stream of air across the ridge without vibrating your vocal cords.

## Spelling and Context

The hard variant occurs before **a**, **o**, and **u** (e.g., *carro*, *curto*) or before consonants (e.g., *claro*, *acto*). Before **e** or **i**, it consistently shifts to the soft sound (e.g., *centro*, *cinema*). If Portuguese requires a `/s/` sound before **a**, **o**, or **u**, the cedilla letter **Ç** is used instead, as in *coração*.

## Variants and Pitfalls

Notice the difference between the hard `/k/` in **casa** (`/ˈka.zɐ/`) and the soft `/s/` in **cedo** (`/ˈse.du/`). English speakers often make the mistake of heavily aspirating the `/k/`, which sounds foreign in Portuguese; keep it tight and clean. Another frequent error is pronouncing soft **C** before **e** or **i** as an English *ch* (`/tʃ/`), which never happens in standard European Portuguese.

articles.title: D
articles.body:
## Sound of the Letter

The letter **D** in European Portuguese represents a voiced dental plosive `/d/` or its soft approximant counterpart `[ð]`. Unlike English, where 'd' is alveolar and pronounced against the gum ridge behind your teeth, the Portuguese **D** is strictly dental, with the tongue tip touching the back of the upper front teeth. Notably, it never turns into an English 'j' sound `[dʒ]` before the vowel 'i', remaining crisp and purely dental.

## How to Say It

Place the tip or blade of your tongue firmly against the back of your upper front incisors to block the airflow. Build up a small amount of air pressure behind the closure, engage your vocal cords to create voicing, and release the contact cleanly. In casual speech between two vowels, soften the contact slightly without completely stopping the airflow, creating a smooth friction similar to the 'th' in 'this'.

## Spelling Patterns

The letter **D** appears in uppercase as **D** and lowercase as **d**, commonly found at the beginning of words and between vowels. It rarely appears at the very end of native Portuguese words, with the exception of a few recent loanwords. Double 'dd' does not exist in standard Portuguese spelling.

## Accents and Pitfalls

The most frequent error for learners familiar with Brazilian Portuguese or English is affricating **D** before 'i' or unstressed 'e', pronouncing *dia* as 'jee-ah'. In European Portuguese, *dia* must always start with a clean `/d/`. Additionally, ensure you soften **d** into a voiced dental approximant `[ð]` between vowels in words like *vida* or *nada* to achieve an authentic, natural cadence.

articles.title: E
articles.body:
## The Sounds of Letter E

The letter **E** is one of the most versatile vowels in European Portuguese. In unstressed positions, it frequently reduces to a unique close central vowel `[ɨ]`—akin to a very short, muffled murmur—or to `[i]` at the start of words like in **escola**. Under stress, it splits into a closed `[e]` (like in "hey" without the glide) or an open `[ɛ]` (like in "bed").

## Pronunciation Guide

To produce the typical unstressed European Portuguese sound `[ɨ]`, place your tongue halfway between `[i]` and `[u]` with completely relaxed, unrounded lips, almost muttering behind clenched teeth. For the closed `[e]`, lift the tongue body high and keep the lips unrounded, forming a clean, pure sound without drifting into an English 'y' glide. For the open `[ɛ]`, drop your lower jaw slightly lower, keeping the tongue flat and tension low.

## Spelling and Written Accents

Written **E** is accented to resolve ambiguity: the circumflex (**ê**) forces the closed sound `[e]`, while the acute accent (**é**) indicates the open sound `[ɛ]`. Unaccented **E** adapts dramatically depending on its rhythm within the word, often becoming so reduced in speech that native speakers nearly drop it entirely.

## Key Contrasts and Mistakes to Avoid

Learners often mistakenly pronounce unstressed **E** as an open `[e]` or `[ɛ]` as they would in Spanish or Brazilian Portuguese; this immediately gives away a foreign accent. Make sure not to turn unstressed final **-e** (as in **noite**) into an English "ee" sound—keep it muffled as `[ɨ]` or let it fade into near silence.

articles.title: F
articles.body:
## The Sound of F

The Portuguese letter **F** represents the voiceless labiodental fricative `/f/`. It sounds exactly like the English 'f' in **father** or **leaf**. It is entirely consistent and does not alter its sound based on adjacent vowels or stress.

## How to Produce /f/

Gently rest your upper front teeth against the inner edge of your lower lip. Blow air steadily through the narrow gap between your teeth and lip without activating your vocal cords. Keep the airflow continuous and friction-like.

## Spelling Patterns

The letter **F** is written as uppercase **F** and lowercase **f**. It appears initially in words like **fogo** and medially in words like **café**, but it never doubles in native Portuguese spelling (unlike English). It never occurs at the very end of native Portuguese words.

## Nuances and Common Mistakes

Because `/f/` is identical across English and Portuguese, it poses almost no pronunciation challenge for learners. The main pitfall is not the consonant itself, but forgetting European Portuguese vowel reduction in surrounding syllables, such as pronouncing unstressed **e** or **o** too clearly. Always focus on keeping the consonant crisp while reducing the unstressed vowels correctly.

articles.title: G
articles.body:
## Sound of the Letter G

The Portuguese letter **G** has two main sounds depending on the vowel that follows. Before **a**, **o**, or **u**, it represents a hard voiced velar plosive `/ɡ/`, just like the English 'g' in 'gate'. When placed before **e** or **i**, it softens into a voiced postalveolar fricative `/ʒ/`, identical to the 's' in English 'measure'.

## How to Pronounce It

For the hard sound `/ɡ/`, press the back of your tongue against the soft palate at the back of your mouth, build up slight air pressure, and release it while vibrating your vocal cords. For the soft sound `/ʒ/`, gently arch the front of your tongue toward the roof of your mouth behind the upper teeth and let voiced air flow smoothly through the narrow channel with relaxed lips.

## Spelling Rules

To maintain the hard `/ɡ/` sound before **e** or **i**, Portuguese spelling requires inserting a silent **u**, forming the digraph **gu** as in *guerra* (`/ˈɡɛ.ʁɐ/`). Conversely, if a `/ʒ/` sound appears before **a**, **o**, or **u**, the letter **J** must be used instead, as in *janela*.

## Comparing Variants and Common Mistakes

Compare the hard `/ɡ/` in *gato* (`/ˈɡa.tu/`) with the soft `/ʒ/` in *gente* (`/ˈʒẽ.tɨ/`). A frequent mistake for English speakers is pronouncing the soft **G** with an affricate `/dʒ/` (as in 'judge'); be sure to produce a smooth, continuous friction sound without any initial 'd' stop.

articles.title: H
articles.body:
## Sound of the Letter H

In European Portuguese, standalone **H** is completely silent and produces no sound whatsoever. Unlike English, where 'h' often represents an aspirated breath like `[h]`, Portuguese words beginning with **H** start directly on the vowel. It only modifies pronunciation when combined into digraphs like **ch** (`/ʃ/`), **lh** (`/ʎ/`), and **nh** (`/ɲ/`).

## How to Pronounce H

When you encounter an isolated **H** at the beginning of a word, simply do not produce any breath or friction. Relax your vocal tract entirely and prepare your mouth directly for the following vowel. Do not attempt to exhale or add an English-style aspiration.

## Spelling and Rules

Isolated **H** appears primarily at the start of words for etymological reasons inherited from Latin or Greek, as in **homem** or **hora**. It never appears alone at the end of native words. Crucially, it forms the bedrock of three essential Portuguese digraphs: **ch**, **lh**, and **nh**.

## Usage and Common Mistakes

The most frequent error for English speakers is aspirating initial **H** in words like **hotel** (`/ɔˈtɛɫ/`) or **hoje** (`/ˈo.ʒɨ/`). Always treat the letter as completely invisible unless it is paired behind **c**, **l**, or **n**. Pronouncing an audible breath can sound unnatural and distort the natural vowel linking between words.

articles.title: I
articles.body:
## The Sound of the Letter I

In European Portuguese, the letter **I** most commonly represents the close front unrounded vowel `/i/`, much like the 'ee' in English *see* or *machine*, but articulated with slightly greater tension. Unlike some English varieties that relax this sound into a loose `/ɪ/` (as in *sit*), Portuguese keeps it crisp and bright. It can also function as the glide `/j/` when forming diphthongs alongside other vowels.

## How to Produce the Sound

Spread your lips into a gentle smile and raise the front of your tongue high towards the hard palate, keeping it tense without quite touching. The edges of your tongue should rest gently against your upper side teeth while your vocal cords vibrate freely. Ensure you do not slacken your jaw into an English short 'i' sound; hold the position firmly.

## Spelling Patterns

The letter **I** appears across all word positions, whether initial (*ilha*), medial (*vida*), or final (*quase* sometimes sounds similar, though spelled with 'e'). An acute accent (**í**) marks an irregular stress on this sound (*país*, *saúde*), particularly to break an otherwise natural diphthong via hiatus. When followed or preceded by another vowel in the same syllable, it acts as a glide without requiring a dedicated spelling change.

## Variants and Common Pitfalls

While usually pronounced `/i/` in words like *fita*, it transforms smoothly into `/j/` in diphthongs such as *foi* or *noite*. English speakers often make the mistake of reducing unstressed Portuguese **i** to a lax `/ɪ/` as in *bit*, which sounds unnatural. Remember to keep the vowel clean, bright, and tense across all syllables.

articles.title: J
articles.body:
## The Sound of J

The letter **J** in European Portuguese always represents the voiced postalveolar fricative `/ʒ/`. It sounds exactly like the 's' in English **measure** or **vision**, or the 'g' in **genre**. Unlike English, it is never pronounced as an affricate `/dʒ/` like the 'j' in **jump**.

## Mouth and Tongue Placement

Gently round your lips and push them slightly outward. Place the blade of your tongue close to the alveolar ridge just behind your upper teeth, allowing air to squeeze through continuously. Simultaneously vibrate your vocal cords to make the sound voiced and smooth.

## Spelling Rules and Context

The letter **J** appears before all vowels (**a**, **e**, **i**, **o**, **u**) and consistently keeps the `/ʒ/` sound regardless of its position. Before **e** and **i**, it shares the exact same sound with the letter **G** (as in **gente**). Unlike some languages, Portuguese never doubles this consonant as 'jj'.

## Avoiding Mistakes

English speakers often default to an explosive `/dʒ/` sound, which should be strictly avoided in standard European Portuguese. Spanish speakers must also take care not to pronounce it as a harsh guttural `/x/` or `/h/`. Always ensure the airflow is smooth, buzzing, and continuous in words like **jogo** and **jardim**.

articles.title: K
articles.body:
## The Sound of K

In European Portuguese, the letter **K** represents the voiceless velar plosive `/k/`, identical to the 'c' in *cat* or 'k' in *skate*. Unlike in English, this sound is pronounced with almost no aspiration (no strong puff of air) following the burst. Because the letter is not native to Portuguese vocabulary, it appears strictly in loanwords, international acronyms, and metric abbreviations.

## How to Produce the Sound

Raise the back of your tongue firmly against your soft palate (velum) to stop the airflow completely. Build up gentle air pressure behind the closure without voicing. Release the seal crisply into the following vowel without adding an extra breathy 'h' sound.

## Spelling Rules & Position

Officially integrated into the Portuguese alphabet via the 1990 Orthographic Agreement, **K** remains restricted to loanwords, brand names, and derived forms like *kantiano*. Native Portuguese words exclusively use **C** (before *a*, *o*, *u*) or the digraph **QU** (before *e*, *i*) to represent the sound `/k/`. Capitalization follows international standards, such as **km** for kilometre or **K** for potassium.

## Variants and Pitfalls

The letter **K** has only one pronunciation in Portuguese: `/k/`. English speakers should avoid heavy aspiration, especially before front vowels like `/i/` in words like *kilo*. Additionally, take care not to confuse spelling habits; standard Portuguese terms use *quilo* or *quilómetro*, while **kilo** and **km** are maintained as metric symbols or foreign borrowings.

articles.title: L
articles.body:
## The Sound of L

In European Portuguese, the letter **L** has two main sounds depending on its position. Before a vowel, it is a clear `[l]` like the English 'l' in 'light'. Syllable-finally, it becomes a prominent velarised or **dark L** `[ɫ]`, similar to the 'l' in English 'ball' or 'milk', but even more resonant.

## How to Pronounce It

For the clear `[l]`, place the tip of your tongue against the upper gum ridge and let voice flow around the sides. For the dark `[ɫ]` at the end of a syllable, keep the tongue tip near or on the gums while simultaneously arching the back of your tongue toward the soft palate. Avoid turning the final **L** into a 'w' sound.

## Spelling and Patterns

The letter **L** is written as uppercase **L** and lowercase **l**. It regularly appears alone or doubled (**ll**, mostly found in loanwords), and combines with other consonants in clusters like **bl**, **cl**, or **fl**. Note that the digraph **lh** represents a completely different palatal sound `[ʎ]`.

## Variants and Common Pitfalls

Notice the difference between the initial clear sound in **lua** `[ˈlu.ɐ]` and the dark sound in **sol** `[sɔɫ]`. Brazilian Portuguese speakers often turn final **L** into `[w]` (pronouncing **sol** like 'sou'), but European Portuguese maintains a distinct velarised consonant `[ɫ]`. English speakers should be careful not to drop the tongue-tip contact when producing this syllable-final sound.

articles.title: M
articles.body:
## Sound of the letter

At the beginning of a syllable, the letter **M** represents the bilabial nasal consonant `/m/`, exactly like the English 'm' in *mother*. However, when it appears at the end of a syllable or word, it is not pronounced as a physical consonant; instead, it nasalises the preceding vowel and often generates a nasal glide, as in `bem` (`/ˈbɐ̃j̃/`).

## How to say it

To pronounce `/m/` before a vowel, close your lips firmly together and vibrate your vocal cords while letting the air escape freely through your nose. When **M** closes a syllable, do not close your lips to articulate an 'm' sound; simply keep your mouth in the position of the vowel and lower your soft palate to redirect the airstream through the nasal cavity.

## Spelling conventions

The letter **M** appears initially, medially, and word-finally in European Portuguese. Before the consonants **b** and **p**, the nasal marker is always written with **m** rather than **n** (as in *campo* or *lembrar*). At the end of words, it commonly marks nasal diphthongs, such as the third-person plural verb ending *-em* or *-am*.

## Variants and common mistakes

Contrast the clear bilabial `/m/` in *mar* with the syllable-closing nasalisation in *bom* (`/ˈbõ/`). A very common mistake among English speakers is pressing their lips together at the end of words like *falam* or *viagem*; ensure your lips stay open and let only the nasal vowel or diphthong carry through.

articles.title: N
articles.body:
## The Sound of the Letter

The letter **N** in European Portuguese usually sounds like the English `n` in *net* when it appears before a vowel, represented as `/n/`. However, at the end of a syllable or before another consonant, it is not pronounced as a distinct consonant; instead, it nasalises the preceding vowel, as in *canto* (`/ˈkɐ̃.tu/`). This nasalisation is softer and does not end with a full tongue contact on the alveolar ridge.

## How to Produce the Sound

To pronounce the initial sound `/n/`, place the tip of your tongue against the alveolar ridge behind your upper teeth while letting air flow through your nose and vibrating your vocal cords. When **N** closes a syllable, keep your tongue resting in the mouth rather than touching the roof, letting the air escape simultaneously through your nose and mouth to produce a pure nasal vowel. Do not press the tongue up at the end of nasal vowels.

## Spelling and Positions

**N** can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of syllables. When combined with **H** as the digraph **NH**, it represents the palatal nasal `/ɲ/`, similar to the sound in *canyon*. At the end of words, true **N** is rare in native Portuguese words, with final nasal sounds usually represented by **M** instead.

## Variants and Pitfalls

The main variation is between the clear alveolar consonant `/n/` before vowels (such as *noite*) and the vowel-nasalising function inside syllables (such as *ponte*). English speakers frequently make the mistake of pronouncing a hard English `/n/` or `/ŋ/` before consonants in words like *canto*. Remember to simply nasalise the vowel without completing a dental or velar closure.

articles.title: O
articles.body:
## The Sound of O

The letter **O** in European Portuguese represents several distinct vowels, but when stressed and open, it produces `[ɔ]`, exactly like the vowel in the British English word "thought" or "cloth". Unlike Brazilian Portuguese or English, unstressed **O** in European Portuguese nearly always reduces to an unstressed `[u]` sound (like in "put"). It can also represent a close `[o]` or a nasal `[õ]` depending on accent marks and neighbouring consonants.

## How to Pronounce It

To produce the open sound `[ɔ]`, drop your lower jaw moderately low while keeping your lips loosely rounded into an oval shape. Position your tongue low in the back of your mouth, ensuring the throat stays open and relaxed. Do not let the sound glide into an "ow" or "oh-oo" diphthong; keep the vowel pure and steady throughout.

## Spelling Rules

When stressed, **O** can be written with an acute accent (**ó**) to explicitly signal the open sound `[ɔ]`, as in **avó** (grandmother). A circumflex (**ô**) marks the closed quality `[o]`, as in **avô** (grandfather). Without accents, spelling alone does not always reveal whether a stressed **O** is open or closed, so vocabulary must be learned individually. At the end of unstressed words or before non-nasal consonants without stress, it is consistently pronounced as `[u]`.

## Comparing Variations and Common Pitfalls

The most common mistake English speakers make is pronouncing unstressed final **O** as a rounded diphthong `/oʊ/` instead of a short, muted `[u]`. For instance, in **olho** (`/ˈɔ.ʎu/`), the first vowel is open `[ɔ]`, but the final vowel reduces completely to `[u]`. Another crucial distinction is between open `[ɔ]` in **avó** and closed `[o]` in **avô**, where confusing the vowel changes the meaning from "grandmother" to "grandfather".

articles.title: P
articles.body:
## The Sound of European Portuguese P

The letter **P** in European Portuguese represents an unaspirated voiceless bilabial plosive `/p/`. Unlike English `p` at the beginning of words, which is accompanied by a puff of air, the Portuguese sound is produced crisply without any aspiration. It sounds very close to the `p` in the English word *spin* rather than *pin*.

## How to Pronounce P

Bring both lips completely together to block the airflow from your lungs momentarily. Build up slight air pressure behind the lips without vibrating your vocal cords. Then, release the lips cleanly and sharply into the following vowel without letting out an extra puff of breath.

## Spelling and Rules for P

The letter **P** occurs at the beginning of words like **pão** and between vowels as in **copo**. In older orthographies, silent consonants were common, but under the current Orthographic Agreement, silent **p** has been eliminated in words where it was unpronounced (such as *ação* instead of *acção*). However, it remains fully pronounced when written in learned clusters like **apto** (`/ˈa.ptu/`) or **psicologia** (`/psi.ku.lu.ˈʒi.ɐ/`).

## Accent Tips and Common Mistakes

English speakers must avoid aspirating this sound, as producing a breathy `[pʰ]` will instantly reveal an accent. Compare **pão** (`/ˈpɐ̃w̃/`) with the English word *pound*; keep the lips tight and the release dry. In consonant sequences such as **captar** or **pneu**, ensure the `/p/` is audibly articulated rather than dropped.

articles.title: Q
articles.body:
## The Sound of Q

In European Portuguese, the letter **Q** always appears combined with **U**. Depending on the vowel that follows, the combination is either pronounced as a single voiceless velar stop `/k/` or as the cluster `/kw/`. Unlike in English, it never produces a standalone sound without this pairing.

## Pronouncing Q

To produce the base sound, press the back of your tongue against the soft palate and release a sharp burst of unvoiced air without vibrating your vocal cords. When followed by **a** or **o**, round your lips tightly immediately upon release to produce the glide `/w/`. When followed by **e** or **i**, keep your lips neutral and articulate only the clean `/k/`.

## Spelling Patterns

The letter **Q** is never written without an accompanying **u** in native Portuguese vocabulary. Before the vowels **e** and **i**, the digraph `qu` serves purely as an orthographic device to keep the hard `/k/` sound intact. Before **a** and **o**, the **u** is fully vocalised as a glide.

## Sounds and Pitfalls

The primary challenge for learners is knowing when the **u** is voiced. In words like **quatro** `/ˈkwa.tɾu/`, you must articulate the `/w/`, whereas in **quero** `/ˈkɛ.ɾu/` or **quem** `/kɐ̃j̃/`, the **u** is completely silent. Avoid pronouncing the English 'kw' sound before front vowels like **e** and **i**.

articles.title: R
articles.body:
## The Sounds of R

In European Portuguese, the letter **R** represents two distinct phonemes depending on its position: a strong guttural sound `/ʁ/` and a soft alveolar tap `/ɾ/`. The strong **R** at the start of words or spelled **rr** is articulated deep in the throat, much like the French or modern German **r**. The weak single **R** between vowels is a quick flick of the tongue against the gum ridge, identical to the tapped sound in Spanish **caro** or American English **water**.

## How to Pronounce R

To make the strong sound `/ʁ/`, raise the back of your tongue toward the uvula at the rear of the soft palate and let the air friction pass without engaging the tongue tip. For the soft tap `/ɾ/`, keep the back of your tongue relaxed and quickly strike the alveolar ridge behind your upper front teeth with the tip of your tongue once. Never curl your tongue backward into the retroflex American or English 'r'.

## Spelling Patterns

A single initial **R** (as in **rua**) or an internal double **rr** (as in **carro**) always triggers the strong guttural `/ʁ/`. A single internal **R** between vowels (as in **caro**) or after an initial consonant (like **prato**) is always the tapped `/ɾ/`. At the end of syllables or words like **falar**, the tap `/ɾ/` is standard, though it is articulated very lightly and often almost silenced in casual rapid speech.

## Contrasting Sounds and Common Mistakes
