The most critical distinction in Portuguese is between the tap in **caro** (`/ˈka.ɾu/`, expensive) and the guttural roll in **carro** (`/ˈka.ʁu/`, car), as swapping them alters the meaning entirely. English speakers frequently substitute their native postalveolar approximant `/ɹ/`, which makes words sound heavily accented or unintelligible. Pay careful attention to whether **R** is single or doubled, and articulate the correct mouth position accordingly.

articles.title: S
articles.body:
## Sound Overview

The letter **S** is one of the most versatile consonants in European Portuguese, changing its sound depending on its surrounding letters. At the start of a word, as in `sol`, it sounds just like the crisp English voiceless `s` in *sun*. However, in other positions it regularly transforms into a voiced `z`, a soft `ʃ` (like English *sh*), or a voiced `ʒ` (like the *s* in *measure*).

## Mouth & Tongue Positioning

To pronounce the initial sound in `sol` (`/s/`), keep your tongue tip close to the alveolar ridge just behind your upper teeth without touching it. Allow a steady, voiceless stream of air to hiss through the narrow central groove of your tongue. Your vocal cords should remain completely still and relaxed.

## Spelling Patterns

At the beginning of a word, a single **S** is always pronounced `/s/`. Between two vowels, a single **S** sounds like `/z/`, which is why words needing a voiceless sound in that position are spelled with double **SS**, such as *passo*. At the end of syllables or words, it automatically turns into a palatal fricative (`/ʃ/` or `/ʒ/`).

## Pronunciation Variations & Pitfalls

Notice how the sound shifts across environments: compare **sol** (`/s/`), **casa** (`/z/`), and **festa** (`/ʃ/`). A frequent mistake for English speakers is pronouncing the coda **S** as a flat `s` or `z` instead of European Portuguese's signature palatal `sh` sound. Pay careful attention when linking words in connected speech, where a final **S** before a vowel becomes `/z/`.

articles.title: T
articles.body:
## The Sound of T

The Portuguese letter **T** represents a voiceless dental plosive, written as `/t/`. Unlike English /t/, which is pronounced behind the teeth on the alveolar ridge and accompanied by a puff of air, European Portuguese `/t/` is entirely dental and completely unaspirated. Moreover, unlike Brazilian Portuguese, it never softens into a "ch" sound before `i` or unstressed `e`.

## How to Pronounce T

Touch the tip of your tongue firmly against the back of your upper front teeth rather than the gum ridge behind them. Build up slight air pressure behind the seal and release it cleanly without letting out a burst of breath (aspiration). Keep the tongue firm and avoid turning the sound into an affricate.

## Spelling and Distribution

The letter **T** appears at the beginning of syllables across all word positions, as in **tempo** (`/ˈtẽ.pu/`) and **noite** (`/ˈnoj.tɨ/`). It also occurs in learned consonant clusters such as **ct** (e.g. **facto**), where it remains clearly articulated. In native vocabulary, double **tt** is not used in modern Portuguese spelling.

## Regional Comparisons and Common Pitfalls

English speakers must avoid releasing a breathy puff of air, as well as placing the tongue too far back on the alveolar ridge. The most crucial contrast to bear in mind is with Brazilian Portuguese: in Portugal, **noite** is pronounced `/ˈnoj.tɨ/` with a crisp dental `/t/`, never with an affricate like `[tʃ]`. Keep the articulation forward, sharp, and dry in every environment.

articles.title: U
articles.body:
## The Sound of U

In European Portuguese, the letter **U** normally sounds like the close back vowel `/u/`, similar to the 'oo' in English 'boot' but noticeably tighter and shorter. In unstressed syllables, it keeps this pure round quality without drifting into the lax vowel found in English 'foot'. When followed by **m** or **n** in the same syllable, as in **um**, it becomes fully nasalized as `/ũ/`.

## How to Pronounce It

Round your lips firmly into a tight, small circle and pull your tongue body high up toward the soft palate at the back of your mouth. Keep the vocal cords vibrating while holding the tongue steady, avoiding any glide into a diphthong. For nasal variants like **um**, lower your soft palate so air escapes through your nose simultaneously.

## Spelling Patterns

The letter **U** appears in stressed and unstressed roots alike, such as **uva** or **luta**. It also acts as a glide in diphthongs like **mau** and follows consonants in combinations like **qu-** and **gu-**, where it is sometimes silent before **e** or **i** (as in **querer**) but pronounced before **a** (as in **quase**). When written with an acute accent (**ú**), it signals an irregular stressed syllable.

## Variants and Pitfalls

The standard vowel `/u/` contrasts with the semivowel `/w/` found in rapid diphthongs (**água**) and the nasal vowel `/ũ/` (**fundo**). English speakers often make the mistake of pronouncing **u** as `/juː/` (like in 'music' or 'cute') after consonants like **d**, **t**, or **n**. Remember that Portuguese **U** is always a pure monophthong unless explicitly written with an accompanying vowel.

articles.title: V
articles.body:
## The Sound of V

In European Portuguese, the letter **V** represents the voiced labiodental fricative `/v/`. It sounds exactly like the English 'v' in 'vine' or 'voice'. Unlike Spanish, standard European Portuguese maintains a sharp, clear distinction between the sounds of **b** and **v**.

## How to Produce /v/

Rest your upper front teeth lightly against your lower lip, just as you would for an English 'v' or 'f'. Push air through the narrow contact while vibrating your vocal cords. Ensure the sound remains a sustained friction rather than an explosive stop like **b**.

## Spelling and Distribution

The letter **V** appears at the beginning of words and between vowels, as in **vinho** (wine) and **ouvir** (to hear). It never combines with other letters to form silent digraphs and retains its voiced fricative value consistently across standard European Portuguese orthography.

## Regional Accents and Common Pitfalls

Standard Portuguese keeps `/v/` and `/b/` strictly separated, contrasting words like **vale** (valley) and **bale** (dance). However, learners should be aware that in certain northern dialects of Portugal, **v** is frequently merged with **b** (producing `/b/`). Avoid this northern merger unless aiming for a specific regional dialect.

articles.title: W
articles.body:
## The Sound of W

In European Portuguese, the letter **W** is not native and appears almost exclusively in foreign loanwords, international acronyms, and names. In English borrowings like **web**, it represents the labio-velar glide `[w]`, sounding exactly like the English 'w'. In German loanwords or proper names, it is pronounced as the voiced labiodental fricative `[v]`, matching the sound of native Portuguese **v**.

## How to Produce It

For English loanwords, round your lips tightly into a small circle while pulling the back of your tongue toward your soft palate, producing a smooth glide `[w]`. For German borrowings, rest your upper front teeth lightly on your lower lip and engage your vocal cords to create the buzzing friction of `[v]`. Avoid adding an extra vowel sound before the glide.

## Spelling Rules and Usage

The letter **W** was officially integrated into the Portuguese alphabet under the 1990 Orthographic Agreement. It is exclusively used for foreign words, scientific symbols such as **W** for watt, and proper nouns like **Washington**. Outside of these loan contexts, the sound `[w]` is naturally represented in native words by the vowel letter **u**.

## Variants and Potential Pitfalls

The main variation depends entirely on the language of origin: it yields `[w]` in terms like **whisky** and `[v]` in Germanic terms like **wagneriano**. A frequent mistake for learners is attempting to pronounce English borrowings with a `[v]` sound out of an overgeneralized assumption that all European languages do so. Always adapt the pronunciation according to the origin of the loanword.

articles.title: X
articles.body:
## The Sound of X

In European Portuguese, the letter **X** is famous for having multiple phonetic values, though its primary and most iconic sound is the voiceless postalveolar fricative `/ʃ/`. This default sound is virtually identical to the English **sh** in *shoe* or *crush*. However, depending on etymology and position, **X** can also sound like `/z/`, `/s/`, or `/ks/`.

## How to Pronounce It

To produce the default `/ʃ/` sound, round your lips slightly and raise the blade of your tongue toward the hard palate just behind your alveolar ridge. Expel air smoothly through this narrow channel without vibrating your vocal cords. For the voiced `/z/` variant (as in *exame*), simply place your tongue tip near the upper teeth and vibrate your vocal cords like a buzzing bee.

## Spelling and Patterns

At the start of native words like *xadrez* or *xícara*, and following diphthongs like in *caixa*, **X** is invariably pronounced `/ʃ/`. When the prefix **ex-** is followed by a vowel, it systematically shifts to `/z/`, as in *exercício*. Learned or international words usually preserve `/ks/` (e.g., *táxi*), while a handful of historic exceptions use `/s/` (e.g., *máximo*).

## Variants and Common Traps

Learners commonly make the mistake of pronouncing every **X** as `/ks/` due to English or Spanish habits. Remember that native Portuguese words almost never use the `/ks/` cluster; words like *peixe* or *baixo* must strictly have the soft `/ʃ/` sound. Be cautious with words like *próximo* (`/ˈpɾɔ.si.mu/`), where pronouncing `/ks/` sounds overly foreign to native ears.

articles.title: Y
articles.body:
## The Sound of Y

The letter **Y** (*ípsilon*) is not historically native to European Portuguese and appears strictly in foreign loanwords, symbols, and proper names. It is pronounced either as the palatal glide `[j]`, like the **y** in English *yes*, or as the pure vowel `[i]`, identical to the **ee** in *feet*. Unlike the German *ü* or French *u*, it never produces a rounded front vowel.

## Pronouncing the Letter

To articulate the semivowel `[j]`, spread your lips into a smile and raise the front of your tongue close to the hard palate. Allow air to pass through continuously while immediately transitioning into the following vowel sound. If it serves as a pure vowel, keep the tongue blade high and fronted without letting the mouth glide.

## Spelling and Usage

Following the 1990 Orthographic Agreement, **Y** is formally part of the 26-letter Portuguese alphabet, though its role is restricted. You will encounter it primarily in international terminology such as **yoga** or scientific symbols like **yd** (yard). In traditional Portuguese vocabulary, this sound is almost universally spelled with **I**.

## Nuances and Common Pitfalls

Notice the difference between the glide `[j]` in **yoga** (`/ˈjɔ.ɡɐ/`) and the full vowel `[i]` in names like **Sydney** (`/ˈsid.nej/`). A common mistake for learners from Germanic backgrounds is attempting to pronounce **Y** with rounded lips as `[y]`. In European Portuguese, always keep your lips completely unrounded as you would for a standard *i*.

articles.title: Z
articles.body:
## The Sound of Z

In European Portuguese, the letter **Z** represents a voiced alveolar fricative `/z/` when it begins a word or sits between vowels, exactly like the English 'z' in *zoo*. However, at the end of a word or syllable, it undergoes European Portuguese sibilant assimilation. In final position, it sounds like `/ʃ/` (English 'sh') before a pause or voiceless sound, or `/ʒ/` (the 's' in *measure*) before a voiced consonant.

## How to Pronounce Z

To make the standard `/z/` sound, place the tip of your tongue near your upper tooth ridge without completely stopping the airflow. Push air through the narrow channel while vibrating your vocal cords. For the syllable-final variants, simply retract your tongue slightly toward the palate into an 'sh' or 'zh' posture.

## Spelling and Patterns

The letter **Z** commonly appears at the beginning of words (*zona*), between vowels (*beleza*), and as a feminine or abstract noun ending (*rapaz*, *timidez*). Across word boundaries, final **-z** links to a following vowel sound, seamlessly turning back into a voiced `/z/` as in *paz e amor* (`/pa.z‿i.ɐˈmoɾ/`).

## Variants and Common Pitfalls

Learners often make the mistake of pronouncing word-final **Z** as an English `/z/`. In European Portuguese, *paz* is never pronounced with a buzzing 'z', but rather with a soft 'sh' sound (`/paʃ/`). Remember to listen carefully to the consonant that follows: final **-z** adjusts continuously between `/ʃ/`, `/ʒ/`, and `/z/` depending on the environment.

articles.title: A
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter A is /eɪ/. It sounds like the word 'day' without the D. The letter has three main sounds. The short sound is /æ/ in (cat) /kæt/. The long sound is /eɪ/ in (make) /meɪk/. The weak sound is /ə/ in (about) /əˈbaʊt/.

## How to say it

For the name, open your mouth a little. Start with your tongue in the middle. Then slide it up and forward. For the short sound, open your mouth wide and keep your tongue low and forward.

## Reading rules

A is short when the syllable ends with a consonant, as in (map) /mæp/. A is long when a silent E follows, as in (cake) /keɪk/. In a syllable with no stress, A is weak, as in (sofa) /ˈsoʊ.fə/. Each of these sounds has its own article.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the name as a short sound. The name has a glide. Do not say the short A like the A in 'father'. Say (cat) /kæt/ with your mouth wide and your tongue forward.
articles.summary: A is called /eɪ/. It has a short sound, a long sound and a weak sound.

articles.title: B
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter B is /bi/. It sounds like the word 'bee'. The letter makes the sound /b/ in most words. Listen to it in (bed) /bɛd/ and in (cab) /kæb/.

## How to say it

Close your lips. Let the air build up. Open your lips and use your voice. Put your hand on your throat. You will feel it vibrate.

## Reading rules

B is silent after M at the end of a word. Listen to (climb) /klaɪm/ and (lamb) /læm/. B is also silent before T in some words. Listen to (doubt) /daʊt/ and (debt) /dɛt/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the B in (climb) /klaɪm/ or (doubt) /daʊt/. Do not turn B into /p/ at the end of a word. Keep your voice on.
articles.summary: B is called /bi/. It makes the sound /b/, and it is sometimes silent.

articles.title: C
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter C is /si/. It sounds like the word 'sea'. The letter makes two main sounds. It is /k/ in (cat) /kæt/. It is /s/ in (city) /ˈsɪ.ti/.

## How to say it

For /k/, press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth. Then release it with a small puff of air. For /s/, put your tongue behind your upper teeth. Push air through the small space.

## Reading rules

C is /k/ before A, O, U and before most consonants. C is /s/ before E, I and Y. Listen to (cent) /sɛnt/ and (cycle) /ˈsaɪ.kəl/. C can also be /ʃ/ in words like (ocean) /ˈoʊ.ʃən/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /k/ in (city) /ˈsɪ.ti/. Do not say /s/ in (cat) /kæt/. Look at the letter after C. It tells you the sound.
articles.summary: C is called /si/. It sounds like /k/ or /s/, depending on the next letter.

articles.title: D
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter D is /di/. It sounds like the word 'Dee'. The letter makes the sound /d/ in most words. Listen to it in (dog) /dɔɡ/ and in (bed) /bɛd/.

## How to say it

Touch the tip of your tongue to the ridge behind your upper teeth. Hold the air for a moment. Release it and use your voice.

## Reading rules

The ending -ED changes its sound. After a quiet sound, it is /t/, as in (hoped) /hoʊpt/. After T or D, it is /ɪd/, as in (wanted) /ˈwɑn.tɪd/. After a voiced sound, it is /d/, as in (played) /pleɪd/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say -ED as a full syllable in (hoped) /hoʊpt/. Say /t/. Do not drop the D at the end of (bed) /bɛd/. Use your voice.
articles.summary: D is called /di/. It makes the sound /d/. At the end of a past verb it can be /t/.

articles.title: E
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter E is /i/. It sounds like the word 'we' without the W. The short sound is /ɛ/ in (bed) /bɛd/. The long sound is /i/ in (me) /mi/. The weak sound is /ə/ in (open) /ˈoʊ.pən/.

## How to say it

For the short sound, open your mouth a little and keep your tongue forward. For the long sound, smile and raise your tongue high and forward. Keep the long sound steady.

## Reading rules

E is short in a syllable that ends with a consonant, as in (egg) /ɛɡ/. E is long at the end of a short word, as in (be) /bi/. A final E is usually silent. It makes the vowel before it long, as in (make) /meɪk/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the silent E at the end of a word. Do not say the short E like /i/. Say (bed) /bɛd/ with your mouth a little open.
articles.summary: E is called /i/. It has a short sound, a long sound and it is often silent.

articles.title: F
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter F is /ɛf/. It sounds like the word 'eff'. The letter makes the sound /f/. Listen to it in (fast) /fæst/ and in (leaf) /lif/.

## How to say it

Put your upper teeth on your lower lip. Push air through the small space. Do not use your voice. The sound is a soft, steady hiss.

## Reading rules

F is almost always /f/. One very common word is different. The word (of) /əv/ is said with a final /v/, not /f/. The letters PH and GH also make /f/ in some words. They have their own articles.

## Common mistakes

Do not use your voice on F. If you do, it becomes /v/. Do not say the word (of) /əv/ with /f/ at the end.
articles.summary: F is called /ɛf/. It makes the sound /f/.

articles.title: G
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter G is /dʒi/. It sounds like the word 'gee'. The letter makes two main sounds. It is /ɡ/ in (go) /ɡoʊ/. It is /dʒ/ in (gem) /dʒɛm/.

## How to say it

For /ɡ/, press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth. Release it with your voice on. For /dʒ/, press your tongue to the ridge behind your upper teeth. Release it slowly with a buzz.

## Reading rules

G is often /ɡ/ before A, O, U and consonants. G is often /dʒ/ before E, I and Y, as in (giant) /ˈdʒaɪ.ənt/. There are exceptions. Listen to (get) /ɡɛt/ and (give) /ɡɪv/. In some French words, G is /ʒ/, as in (genre) /ˈʒɑn.rə/.

## Common mistakes

Do not use one rule for every word. Learn the exceptions, like (get) /ɡɛt/ and (give) /ɡɪv/. Do not say /dʒ/ in (go) /ɡoʊ/.
articles.summary: G is called /dʒi/. It sounds like hard /ɡ/ or soft /dʒ/.

articles.title: H
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter H is /eɪtʃ/. The letter makes the sound /h/ at the start of most words. Listen to it in (hat) /hæt/ and in (help) /hɛlp/.

## How to say it

Open your mouth. Push air out from your throat. Do not use your voice. The sound is a soft breath.

## Reading rules

H is silent in a few words. Listen to (hour) /aʊr/ and (honest) /ˈɑ.nɪst/. After a vowel, H is usually silent, as in (oh) /oʊ/. H joins other letters to make new sounds, in CH, SH, TH and PH.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the H in (hour) /aʊr/ or (honest) /ˈɑ.nɪst/. Do not drop the H in (hat) /hæt/. Say it with a soft breath.
articles.summary: H is called /eɪtʃ/. It makes a breath sound, and it is sometimes silent.

articles.title: I
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter I is /aɪ/. It sounds like the word 'eye'. The short sound is /ɪ/ in (pin) /pɪn/. The long sound is /aɪ/ in (time) /taɪm/.

## How to say it

For the short sound, open your mouth a little. Keep your tongue high and forward. The sound is quick and relaxed. For the long sound, start with your mouth open and slide your tongue up toward Y.

## Reading rules

I is short when the syllable ends with a consonant, as in (sit) /sɪt/. I is long when a silent E follows, as in (ice) /aɪs/ and (time) /taɪm/. In some words from other languages, I is /i/, as in (police) /pəˈlis/ and (ski) /ski/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the short I like a long 'ee'. (Sit) /sɪt/ and (seat) /sit/ are different words. Do not say a silent E at the end of (time) /taɪm/.
articles.summary: I is called /aɪ/. It has a short sound and a long sound.

articles.title: J
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter J is /dʒeɪ/. It sounds like the word 'jay'. The letter makes the sound /dʒ/. Listen to it in (job) /dʒɑb/ and in (jump) /dʒʌmp/.

## How to say it

Put your tongue behind your upper teeth, near the ridge. Hold the air for a moment. Release it slowly with a buzz. Use your voice.

## Reading rules

J is /dʒ/ in all normal English words. In some words from other languages, J is different. In (jalapeño) /ˌhɑ.ləˈpeɪ.noʊ/ it is /h/. In (hallelujah) /ˌhæ.ləˈlu.jə/ it is /j/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /ʒ/, the sound in 'vision'. Do not say /j/, the sound in 'yes'. Start with a short /d/ and then slide into the buzz.
articles.summary: J is called /dʒeɪ/. It makes the sound /dʒ/.

articles.title: K
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter K is /keɪ/. It sounds like the word 'Kay'. The letter makes the sound /k/. Listen to it in (kite) /kaɪt/ and in (milk) /mɪlk/.

## How to say it

Press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth. Release it with a small puff of air. Do not use your voice.

## Reading rules

K is silent before N at the start of a word. Listen to (knee) /ni/ and (knot) /nɑt/. K and C often make the same sound. We use K before E, I and Y, as in (key) /ki/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the K in (knee) /ni/. Say only the N. Do not use your voice, or K becomes /ɡ/.
articles.summary: K is called /keɪ/. It makes the sound /k/. It is silent before N.

articles.title: L
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter L is /ɛl/. The letter makes the sound /l/. Listen to it at the start of (lamp) /læmp/. Listen to it at the end of (milk) /mɪlk/. The sound at the end is darker.

## How to say it

Touch the tip of your tongue to the ridge behind your upper teeth. Let the air flow around the sides of your tongue. Use your voice.

## Reading rules

L is silent in some words. Listen to (calm) /kɑm/, (talk) /tɔk/ and (half) /hæf/. L is clear at the start of a word. It is dark at the end of a word, as in (ball) /bɔl/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the L in (calm) /kɑm/ or (talk) /tɔk/. Do not put your tongue between your teeth. Keep it on the ridge.
articles.summary: L is called /ɛl/. It makes the sound /l/. It is silent in a few words.

articles.title: M
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter M is /ɛm/. The letter makes the sound /m/. Listen to it in (map) /mæp/ and in (milk) /mɪlk/.

## How to say it

Close your lips. Let the air come out through your nose. Use your voice. You can feel your lips vibrate.

## Reading rules

M is /m/ in almost every word. It is silent only in very rare words, like (mnemonic) /nəˈmɑ.nɪk/. At the end of a word, keep your lips closed until the sound ends, as in (swim) /swɪm/.

## Common mistakes

Do not open your lips too early at the end of a word. Do not say the M in (mnemonic) /nəˈmɑ.nɪk/. Start with N.
articles.summary: M is called /ɛm/. It makes the sound /m/.

articles.title: N
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter N is /ɛn/. The letter makes the sound /n/. Listen to it in (net) /nɛt/ and in (sun) /sʌn/. Before K or G, it makes the sound /ŋ/, as in (sink) /sɪŋk/.

## How to say it

For /n/, touch the tip of your tongue to the ridge behind your upper teeth. Let the air come out through your nose. For /ŋ/, press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth.

## Reading rules

N is /ŋ/ before K, as in (bank) /bæŋk/. N is silent after M at the end of a word. Listen to (autumn) /ˈɔ.təm/ and (hymn) /hɪm/. The letters NG have their own article.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the N in (autumn) /ˈɔ.təm/. Do not say a hard /k/ after /ŋ/ in a word like (sink) /sɪŋk/. The sound is /ŋ/, and then /k/.
articles.summary: N is called /ɛn/. It makes the sound /n/. Before K or G it sounds like /ŋ/.

articles.title: O
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter O is /oʊ/. It sounds like the word 'owe'. The short sound is /ɑ/ in (hot) /hɑt/. The long sound is /oʊ/ in (go) /ɡoʊ/. The weak sound is /ə/ in (lemon) /ˈlɛ.mən/.

## How to say it

For the long sound, round your lips and slide them to a tighter shape. For the short sound, open your mouth wide. Keep your lips relaxed and not round.

## Reading rules

O is short in a syllable that ends with a consonant, as in (ox) /ɑks/. O is long when a silent E follows, as in (home) /hoʊm/. O has other sounds. Listen to (love) /lʌv/ and (do) /du/. Learn these words one by one.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the short O with round lips. Do not say the long O without the glide. Do not say (hot) /hɑt/ with the long sound /oʊ/.
articles.summary: O is called /oʊ/. It has a short sound, a long sound and a weak sound.

articles.title: P
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter P is /pi/. It sounds like the word 'pea'. The letter makes the sound /p/. Listen to it in (pen) /pɛn/ and in (cup) /kʌp/.

## How to say it

Close your lips. Let the air build up. Open your lips with a small puff of air. Do not use your voice. At the start of a word, the puff is strong.

## Reading rules

P is silent before N, S and T at the start of some words. Listen to (psychology) /saɪˈkɑ.lə.dʒi/. P is also silent in (cupboard) /ˈkʌ.bɚd/. P and H together make /f/, as in (phone) /foʊn/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the P in (cupboard) /ˈkʌ.bɚd/. Do not use your voice, or P becomes /b/. Hold a paper in front of your mouth. It should move on (pen) /pɛn/.
articles.summary: P is called /pi/. It makes the sound /p/. It is silent in a few words.

articles.title: Q
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter Q is /kju/. It sounds like the word 'cue'. The letter Q is almost always followed by U. Together, QU sounds like /kw/. Listen to it in (queen) /kwin/ and in (quick) /kwɪk/.

## How to say it

Say /k/ first. Press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth. Then round your lips quickly for /w/. Slide into the next vowel.

## Reading rules

QU is /kw/ in most words. In some words from French, QU is just /k/. Listen to (unique) /juˈnik/ and (bouquet) /buˈkeɪ/. A few words from other languages have Q alone, as in (qi) /tʃi/.

## Common mistakes

Do not leave out the /w/ in (queen) /kwin/. Do not say the U as a full vowel. Say /kw/ in one quick move.
articles.summary: Q is called /kju/. It almost always appears with U and sounds like /kw/.

articles.title: R
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter R is /ɑr/. It sounds like the word 'are'. The letter makes the sound /r/. Listen to it in (red) /rɛd/ and in (run) /rʌn/.

## How to say it

Pull your tongue back. Raise the sides of your tongue. Do not let the tip touch the roof of your mouth. Round your lips a little. Use your voice.

## Reading rules

In American English, R is said after a vowel too. Listen to (car) /kɑr/ and (hard) /hɑrd/. R changes the vowel before it. The groups AR, ER, IR, OR and UR have their own articles.

## Common mistakes

Do not tap or roll the R. Do not drop the R in (car) /kɑr/. Keep your tongue back and do not touch the roof of your mouth.
articles.summary: R is called /ɑr/. It makes the American /r/ sound. You say it in every position.

articles.title: S
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter S is /ɛs/. The letter makes four sounds. It is /s/ in (sun) /sʌn/. It is /z/ in (rose) /roʊz/. It is /ʃ/ in (sugar) /ˈʃʊ.ɡɚ/. It is /ʒ/ in (vision) /ˈvɪ.ʒən/.

## How to say it

For /s/ and /z/, put your tongue behind your upper teeth. Push air through the small space. Use your voice for /z/ only. For /ʃ/ and /ʒ/, pull your tongue back a little and round your lips.

## Reading rules

S is /s/ at the start of a word and after quiet sounds, as in (cats) /kæts/. S is /z/ between vowels and after voiced sounds, as in (dogs) /dɔɡz/. Each of the four sounds has its own article.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /s/ in (rose) /roʊz/. Say /z/. Do not say /s/ in (vision) /ˈvɪ.ʒən/. Say /ʒ/.
articles.summary: S is called /ɛs/. It makes four sounds: /s/, /z/, /ʃ/ and /ʒ/.

articles.title: T
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter T is /ti/. It sounds like the word 'tea'. The letter makes the sound /t/ in most words. Listen to it in (ten) /tɛn/ and in (top) /tɑp/.

## How to say it

Touch the tip of your tongue to the ridge behind your upper teeth. Let the air build up. Release it with a small puff. Do not use your voice.

## Reading rules

In American English, T between vowels is a quick tap /ɾ/, as in (water) /ˈwɔ.ɾɚ/. T is silent in (listen) /ˈlɪ.sən/. T can be /tʃ/ in (nature) /ˈneɪ.tʃɚ/, and /ʃ/ in (nation) /ˈneɪ.ʃən/. Each of these has its own article.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the T in (listen) /ˈlɪ.sən/. Do not use your voice, or T becomes /d/. Say the tap quickly in (water) /ˈwɔ.ɾɚ/.
articles.summary: T is called /ti/. It makes the sound /t/. It can also sound like /ɾ/, /tʃ/ or /ʃ/, or be silent.

articles.title: U
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter U is /ju/. It sounds like the word 'you'. The short sound is /ʌ/ in (cup) /kʌp/. The long sound is /ju/ in (music) /ˈmju.zɪk/. After some letters, it is /u/, as in (rule) /rul/.

## How to say it

For the short sound, open your mouth a little. Keep your tongue in the middle and your lips relaxed. For the long sound, say /j/ and then round your lips tightly.

## Reading rules

U is short in a syllable that ends with a consonant, as in (up) /ʌp/. U is long when a silent E follows, as in (cube) /kjub/. After R, L and J, it is /u/ without the /j/, as in (flute) /flut/. In (put) /pʊt/, it is a short rounded sound.

## Common mistakes

Do not say (cup) /kʌp/ with a rounded /ʊ/. Do not say /ju/ in (rule) /rul/. Do not mix (cut) /kʌt/ and (put) /pʊt/. They are different.
articles.summary: U is called /ju/. It has a short sound and a long sound.

articles.title: V
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter V is /vi/. It sounds like the word 'vee'. The letter makes the sound /v/. Listen to it in (van) /væn/ and in (river) /ˈrɪ.vɚ/.

## How to say it

Put your upper teeth on your lower lip. Push air through the small space. Use your voice. You will feel a buzz on your lip.

## Reading rules

V is /v/ in almost every word. It is never silent. Words in English do not end in V. They add a silent E, as in (have) /hæv/ and (give) /ɡɪv/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /b/ or /w/ for V. Do not turn V into /f/ at the end of a word. Keep your voice on.
articles.summary: V is called /vi/. It makes the sound /v/.

articles.title: W
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter W is /ˈdʌ.bəl.ju/. The letter makes the sound /w/. Listen to it in (wet) /wɛt/ and in (win) /wɪn/.

## How to say it

Round your lips tightly. Pull your tongue back. Then open your lips quickly into the next vowel. Use your voice.

## Reading rules

W is silent before R at the start of a word. Listen to (write) /raɪt/ and (wrong) /rɔŋ/. W is also silent in a few common words. Listen to (two) /tu/, (who) /hu/ and (answer) /ˈæn.sɚ/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the W in (write) /raɪt/. Do not say /v/ for W. Round your lips, and do not touch your teeth.
articles.summary: W is called 'double-u'. It makes the sound /w/. It is silent in a few words.

articles.title: X
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter X is /ɛks/. The letter often makes the sound /ks/. Listen to it in (box) /bɑks/ and in (six) /sɪks/. In some words, it is /ɡz/, as in (exam) /ɪɡˈzæm/.

## How to say it

For /ks/, say /k/ and then /s/ with no pause. For /ɡz/, say /ɡ/ and then /z/, and use your voice. Say both sounds in one smooth move.

## Reading rules

X is /ks/ at the end of a word and before a consonant. X is /ɡz/ between vowels before a stressed syllable. X is /z/ at the start of a word, as in (xylophone) /ˈzaɪ.lə.foʊn/. Each sound has its own article.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /ɡz/ in (box) /bɑks/. Do not say /ks/ in (exam) /ɪɡˈzæm/. Do not say 'ex' at the start of (xylophone) /ˈzaɪ.lə.foʊn/. Say /z/.
articles.summary: X is called /ɛks/. It sounds like /ks/, /ɡz/ or /z/.

articles.title: Y
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter Y is /waɪ/. It sounds like the word 'why'. At the start of a word, Y is /j/, as in (yes) /jɛs/. At the end of a long word, Y is /i/, as in (happy) /ˈhæ.pi/.

## How to say it

For /j/, raise the middle of your tongue toward the roof of your mouth. Then slide into the next vowel. For /i/, smile and keep your tongue high and forward.

## Reading rules

Y is a consonant at the start of a syllable. Y is a vowel in other places. At the end of a short word, it is /aɪ/, as in (fly) /flaɪ/. In the middle of a word, it can be /ɪ/, as in (gym) /dʒɪm/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /dʒ/ for the Y in (yes) /jɛs/. Do not say a long 'eye' sound at the end of (happy) /ˈhæ.pi/. Say /i/.
articles.summary: Y is called /waɪ/. It sounds like /j/, /i/, /ɪ/ or /aɪ/.

articles.title: Z
articles.body:
## The sound

The name of the letter Z is /zi/. It sounds like the word 'zee'. The letter makes the sound /z/. Listen to it in (zoo) /zu/ and in (zebra) /ˈzi.brə/.

## How to say it

Put your tongue behind your upper teeth. Push air through the small space. Use your voice. You will feel a buzz.

## Reading rules

Z is /z/ in almost every word. In some words, it is /ts/, as in (pizza) /ˈpit.sə/. Before an unstressed vowel, it can be /ʒ/, as in (azure) /ˈæ.ʒɚ/. A double Z is usually /z/, as in (buzz) /bʌz/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /s/ for Z. Keep your voice on. Do not say /dz/. The sound is a clean buzz.
articles.summary: Z is called /zi/. It makes the sound /z/.

articles.title: A
articles.body:
## The sound

The short sound of the letter A is /æ/. Listen to it in (cat) /kæt/. Listen again in (map) /mæp/ and in (apple) /ˈæ.pəl/.

## How to say it

Open your mouth wide. Drop your jaw. Keep your tongue low and forward. Keep your lips relaxed. Make the sound short.

## Reading rules

A is short when the syllable ends with a consonant. Listen to (hat) /hæt/, (hand) /hænd/ and (bag) /bæɡ/. This is the most common sound for A in short words.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /ɛ/, the sound in 'bed'. Do not say /ɑ/, the sound in 'father'. Say (cat) /kæt/ with your mouth wide and your tongue forward.
articles.summary: Short A makes the sound /æ/, as in 'cat'.

articles.title: A
articles.body:
## The sound

The long sound of the letter A is /eɪ/. It sounds like the name of the letter. Listen to it in (make) /meɪk/. Listen again in (cake) /keɪk/ and in (baby) /ˈbeɪ.bi/.

## How to say it

Open your mouth a little. Start with your tongue in the middle. Then slide it up and forward. The sound has two parts, but it is one beat.

## Reading rules

A is long when a silent E follows, as in (name) /neɪm/. A is also long at the end of a syllable, as in (table) /ˈteɪ.bəl/. The letters AI and AY also make this sound, as in (rain) /reɪn/ and (day) /deɪ/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say a short, flat /e/. Slide up to the end of the sound. Do not say the silent E in (make) /meɪk/.
articles.summary: Long A makes the sound /eɪ/, as in 'make'.

articles.title: A
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter A can make the open sound /ɑ/. Listen to it in (father) /ˈfɑ.ðɚ/. Listen again in (spa) /spɑ/ and in (palm) /pɑm/.

## How to say it

Open your mouth wide. Keep your tongue low and in the back of your mouth. Keep your lips relaxed and not round. Hold the sound steady.

## Reading rules

This sound is less common. It appears in a few words. Learn them one by one. Listen to (drama) /ˈdrɑ.mə/ and (calm) /kɑm/. Before R, the sound is similar, as in (car) /kɑr/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the short /æ/ of (cat) /kæt/. The mouth is wider and the tongue is further back. Do not say the L in (calm) /kɑm/.
articles.summary: A can make the open sound /ɑ/, as in 'father'.

articles.title: A
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter A can make the weak sound /ə/. It is called the schwa. Listen to it in (about) /əˈbaʊt/. Listen again in (sofa) /ˈsoʊ.fə/ and in (banana) /bəˈnæ.nə/.

## How to say it

Relax your mouth. Keep your tongue in the middle. Do not round your lips. Make the sound very short and quiet.

## Reading rules

A is weak in a syllable that has no stress. It sounds /ə/ at the start of (again) /əˈɡɛn/. It sounds /ə/ at the end of (sofa) /ˈsoʊ.fə/. Many English words have this sound. The stressed syllable is louder and longer.

## Common mistakes

Do not say a full vowel in a weak syllable. Do not say (about) /əˈbaʊt/ like 'a-bout' with two strong parts. Make the first part weak.
articles.summary: A can be weak, and then it makes the sound /ə/.

articles.title: C
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter C makes the sound /k/ before A, O and U. Listen to it in (cat) /kæt/. Listen again in (cup) /kʌp/ and in (cold) /koʊld/.

## How to say it

Press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth. Release it with a small puff of air. Do not use your voice.

## Reading rules

C is also /k/ before most consonants, as in (clap) /klæp/ and (cry) /kraɪ/. At the end of a word, we often write CK, as in (back) /bæk/. The sound is the same.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /s/ in (cat) /kæt/. Do not use your voice, or C becomes /ɡ/. Say a small puff of air at the start.
articles.summary: Hard C makes the sound /k/, as in 'cat'.

articles.title: C
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter C makes the sound /s/ before E, I and Y. Listen to it in (city) /ˈsɪ.ti/. Listen again in (cent) /sɛnt/ and in (cycle) /ˈsaɪ.kəl/.

## How to say it

Put your tongue behind your upper teeth. Push air through the small space. Do not use your voice. The sound is a steady hiss.

## Reading rules

C before E, I or Y is soft. Listen to (face) /feɪs/ and (nice) /naɪs/. This rule is very reliable. Words like (circle) /ˈsɜr.kəl/ show both sounds. The first C is /s/ and the last C is /k/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /k/ before E or I. Do not say /ʃ/ for this C. Say a clean /s/.
articles.summary: Soft C makes the sound /s/, as in 'city'.

articles.title: C
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter C can make the sound /ʃ/. It is the 'sh' sound. Listen to it in (ocean) /ˈoʊ.ʃən/. Listen again in (special) /ˈspɛ.ʃəl/ and in (social) /ˈsoʊ.ʃəl/.

## How to say it

Pull your tongue back a little. Round your lips slightly. Push air through the space. Do not use your voice. The sound is a soft, long hiss.

## Reading rules

This happens with CI and CE before another vowel, after a stressed syllable. Listen to (delicious) /dɪˈlɪ.ʃəs/ and (musician) /mjuˈzɪ.ʃən/. The spelling does not show the sound clearly. Learn these words one by one.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /s/ in (special) /ˈspɛ.ʃəl/. Do not say /k/. Say /ʃ/.
articles.summary: C can make the sound /ʃ/, as in 'ocean'.

articles.title: G
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter G makes the sound /ɡ/ before A, O and U. Listen to it in (go) /ɡoʊ/. Listen again in (gas) /ɡæs/ and in (dog) /dɔɡ/.

## How to say it

Press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth. Release it with your voice on. Put your hand on your throat. You will feel it vibrate.

## Reading rules

G is also /ɡ/ before most consonants, as in (glad) /ɡlæd/ and (green) /ɡrin/. To keep a hard G before E or I, we add U or H. Listen to (guess) /ɡɛs/ and (ghost) /ɡoʊst/. A few words keep a hard G before E or I. Listen to (get) /ɡɛt/, (give) /ɡɪv/ and (girl) /ɡɜrl/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /dʒ/ in (go) /ɡoʊ/. Do not whisper the G. Keep your voice on. Do not say the U in (guess) /ɡɛs/ as a vowel.
articles.summary: Hard G makes the sound /ɡ/, as in 'go'.

articles.title: G
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter G can make the sound /dʒ/. It sounds like the 'j' in 'jam'. Listen to it in (gem) /dʒɛm/. Listen again in (giant) /ˈdʒaɪ.ənt/ and in (gentle) /ˈdʒɛn.təl/.

## How to say it

Put your tongue behind your upper teeth, near the ridge. Hold the air for a moment. Release it slowly with a buzz. Use your voice.

## Reading rules

G is often soft before E, I and Y. Listen to (giraffe) /dʒəˈræf/ and (ginger) /ˈdʒɪn.dʒɚ/. This rule is less reliable than the rule for C. Words like (get) /ɡɛt/ and (give) /ɡɪv/ are exceptions.

## Common mistakes

Do not say hard /ɡ/ in (gem) /dʒɛm/. Do not say /ʒ/, the sound in 'vision'. Do not drop the first small /d/ in the sound.
articles.summary: Soft G makes the sound /dʒ/, as in 'gem'.

articles.title: G
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter G makes the sound /dʒ/ in some word endings. Listen to it in (gym) /dʒɪm/. Listen again in (age) /eɪdʒ/ and in (energy) /ˈɛ.nɚ.dʒi/.

## How to say it

Put your tongue behind your upper teeth, near the ridge. Hold the air for a moment. Release it slowly with a buzz. Use your voice. Keep the sound short at the end of a word.

## Reading rules

A final -GE is /dʒ/, as in (page) /peɪdʒ/. The ending -GY is /dʒi/, as in (biology) /baɪˈɑ.lə.dʒi/. The ending -DGE is also /dʒ/, as in (bridge) /brɪdʒ/. The E at the end of -GE is silent.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the silent E at the end of (age) /eɪdʒ/. Do not say hard /ɡ/ in (gym) /dʒɪm/. Do not say /ʒ/.
articles.summary: G also makes /dʒ/ in the endings -ge, -gy and -dge.

articles.title: S
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter S makes the sound /s/. Listen to it at the start of (sun) /sʌn/ and (sit) /sɪt/. Listen to it at the end of (cats) /kæts/.

## How to say it

Put your tongue behind your upper teeth. Push air through the small space. Do not use your voice. The sound is a steady hiss.

## Reading rules

S is /s/ at the start of a word. S is /s/ in clusters, as in (stop) /stɑp/. After a quiet sound like /t/, /k/ or /p/, the plural S is /s/. Listen to (books) /bʊks/ and (maps) /mæps/.

## Common mistakes

Do not use your voice on this S. If you do, it becomes /z/. Do not say /ʃ/. Keep your tongue forward.
articles.summary: S makes the sound /s/ at the start of a word and after quiet sounds.

articles.title: S
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter S can make the sound /z/. It is a buzzing sound. Listen to it in (rose) /roʊz/. Listen again in (busy) /ˈbɪ.zi/ and in (dogs) /dɔɡz/.

## How to say it

Put your tongue behind your upper teeth. Push air through the small space. Use your voice. Put your hand on your throat. You will feel it vibrate.

## Reading rules

S is often /z/ between two vowels, as in (easy) /ˈi.zi/. After a voiced sound like /g/, /b/ or a vowel, the plural S is /z/, as in (beds) /bɛdz/ and (toys) /tɔɪz/. Very common words like (is) /ɪz/ and (as) /æz/ use /z/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /s/ in (rose) /roʊz/ or (is) /ɪz/. Keep your voice on. Do not say /dz/. The sound is a clean buzz.
articles.summary: S makes the sound /z/ between vowels and after voiced sounds.

articles.title: S
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter S can make the sound /ʃ/. It is the 'sh' sound. Listen to it in (sugar) /ˈʃʊ.ɡɚ/. Listen again in (sure) /ʃʊr/ and in (mission) /ˈmɪ.ʃən/.

## How to say it

Pull your tongue back a little. Round your lips slightly. Push air through the space. Do not use your voice. The sound is a soft, long hiss.

## Reading rules

S is /ʃ/ at the start of only two common words, (sugar) /ˈʃʊ.ɡɚ/ and (sure) /ʃʊr/. S is also /ʃ/ in the ending -SSION, as in (session) /ˈsɛ.ʃən/. After a consonant, -SION is also /ʃ/, as in (tension) /ˈtɛn.ʃən/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /s/ in (sugar) /ˈʃʊ.ɡɚ/. Do not say /tʃ/, the sound in 'chair'. Say a smooth /ʃ/.
articles.summary: S can make the sound /ʃ/, as in 'sugar'.

articles.title: S
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter S can make the sound /ʒ/. It is the buzzing sound in the middle of 'measure'. Listen to it in (vision) /ˈvɪ.ʒən/. Listen again in (measure) /ˈmɛ.ʒɚ/ and in (usual) /ˈju.ʒu.əl/.

## How to say it

Pull your tongue back a little. Round your lips slightly. Push air through the space. Use your voice. You will feel a soft buzz.

## Reading rules

S is /ʒ/ between vowels before -ION, -URE and -UAL. Listen to (television) /ˈtɛ.lə.vɪ.ʒən/ and (treasure) /ˈtrɛ.ʒɚ/. The sound is rare at the start of a word. It appears in loan words like (genre) /ˈʒɑn.rə/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /ʃ/ in (vision) /ˈvɪ.ʒən/. Use your voice. Do not say /dʒ/, the sound in 'jam'.
articles.summary: S can make the sound /ʒ/, as in 'vision'.

articles.title: T
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter T makes the sound /t/. Listen to it in (ten) /tɛn/ and in (top) /tɑp/. Listen again at the end of (cat) /kæt/.

## How to say it

Touch the tip of your tongue to the ridge behind your upper teeth. Let the air build up. Release it with a small puff. Do not use your voice.

## Reading rules

T has a puff of air at the start of a word and at the start of a stressed syllable, as in (table) /ˈteɪ.bəl/. After S, the puff is small, as in (stop) /stɑp/. In American English, T between vowels is a quick tap /ɾ/, as in (butter) /ˈbʌ.ɾɚ/.

## Common mistakes

Do not use your voice, or T becomes /d/. Do not skip the T at the end of (cat) /kæt/. Hold a paper in front of your mouth. It should move on (ten) /tɛn/.
articles.summary: T makes the sound /t/. At the start of a word, it has a small puff of air.

articles.title: T
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter T can make the sound /ʃ/. It is the 'sh' sound. Listen to it in (nation) /ˈneɪ.ʃən/. Listen again in (station) /ˈsteɪ.ʃən/ and in (action) /ˈæk.ʃən/.

## How to say it

Pull your tongue back a little. Round your lips slightly. Push air through the space. Do not use your voice. The sound is a soft, long hiss.

## Reading rules

T is /ʃ/ in the endings -TION, -TIAL and -TIENT. Listen to (partial) /ˈpɑr.ʃəl/ and (patient) /ˈpeɪ.ʃənt/. The stress falls on the syllable before the ending. After S, the ending is different. It is /tʃ/, as in (question) /ˈkwɛs.tʃən/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /t/ in (nation) /ˈneɪ.ʃən/. Do not say 'tee-on'. Say /ʃən/ as one weak syllable.
articles.summary: T can make the sound /ʃ/ in the ending -tion.

articles.title: T
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter T can make the sound /tʃ/. It sounds like the 'ch' in 'chair'. Listen to it in (nature) /ˈneɪ.tʃɚ/. Listen again in (future) /ˈfju.tʃɚ/ and in (picture) /ˈpɪk.tʃɚ/.

## How to say it

Put your tongue behind your upper teeth, near the ridge. Hold the air for a moment. Release it with a hissing sound. Do not use your voice.

## Reading rules

T is /tʃ/ in the ending -TURE. T is also /tʃ/ after S in the ending -STION, as in (question) /ˈkwɛs.tʃən/. The letters TCH make the same sound, as in (catch) /kætʃ/. The stress falls before the ending.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /t/ in (nature) /ˈneɪ.tʃɚ/. Do not say 'na-ture' with a strong U. Say a weak /ɚ/ at the end.
articles.summary: T can make the sound /tʃ/ in the ending -ture.

articles.title: -t- (silent)
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter T is silent in some words. Listen to (listen) /ˈlɪ.sən/. Listen again to (castle) /ˈkæ.səl/ and to (often) /ˈɔ.fən/. You write the T, but you do not say it.

## How to say it

Say the words without a T sound. Your tongue stays down. After the S, move straight to the next vowel. Keep the word smooth.

## Reading rules

T is silent in the groups STEN and STLE, as in (fasten) /ˈfæ.sən/ and (whistle) /ˈwɪ.səl/. T is also silent in (Christmas) /ˈkrɪs.məs/. In (often) /ˈɔ.fən/, many people say the T, and many do not.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the T in (listen) /ˈlɪ.sən/ or (castle) /ˈkæ.səl/. Do not say the word with a hard stop. Keep it smooth.
articles.summary: T is silent in some words, as in 'listen'.

articles.title: X
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter X most often makes the sound /ks/. Listen to it in (box) /bɑks/. Listen again in (six) /sɪks/ and in (fox) /fɑks/.

## How to say it

Say /k/ first. Press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth. Then move your tongue forward and say /s/. Do not stop between the two sounds.

## Reading rules

X is /ks/ at the end of a word. X is also /ks/ before a consonant, as in (next) /nɛkst/. X is /ks/ in words like (mix) /mɪks/ and (tax) /tæks/. This is the most common sound for X.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /ɡz/ in (box) /bɑks/. Do not split X into two slow sounds. Say it in one quick move.
articles.summary: X sounds like /ks/ at the end of a word and before a consonant.

articles.title: X
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter X can make the sound /ɡz/. Listen to it in (exam) /ɪɡˈzæm/. Listen again in (exist) /ɪɡˈzɪst/ and in (example) /ɪɡˈzæm.pəl/.

## How to say it

Say /ɡ/ first. Press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth and use your voice. Then move your tongue forward and say /z/. Do not stop between the two sounds.

## Reading rules

X is /ɡz/ when it comes between two vowels, and the stress falls on the next syllable. Listen to (exact) /ɪɡˈzækt/ and (examine) /ɪɡˈzæ.mɪn/. If the stress is before X, it is /ks/, as in (exercise) /ˈɛk.sɚ.saɪz/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /ks/ in (exam) /ɪɡˈzæm/. Use your voice. Do not say the first E as a full vowel. It is weak, /ɪ/.
articles.summary: X sounds like /ɡz/ between vowels before a stressed syllable.

articles.title: X
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter X can make the sound /kʃ/. Listen to it in (luxury) /ˈlʌk.ʃɚ.i/. Listen again in (anxious) /ˈæŋk.ʃəs/ and in (complexion) /kəmˈplɛk.ʃən/.

## How to say it

Say /k/ first. Press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth. Then pull your tongue forward and round your lips for /ʃ/. Do not stop between the two sounds.

## Reading rules

X is /kʃ/ before the ending -ION, -IOUS and -URY, when the stress falls before X. Listen to (obnoxious) /ɑbˈnɑk.ʃəs/. This sound is rare. Learn these words one by one.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /ks/ in (luxury) /ˈlʌk.ʃɚ.i/. Do not say /ɡz/. Say /kʃ/, with a 'sh' after the /k/.
articles.summary: X can make the sound /kʃ/, as in 'luxury'.

articles.title: Y
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter Y makes the sound /j/ at the start of a word. Listen to it in (yes) /jɛs/. Listen again in (yellow) /ˈjɛ.loʊ/ and in (yard) /jɑrd/.

## How to say it

Raise the middle of your tongue toward the roof of your mouth. Do not touch it. Then slide quickly into the next vowel. Use your voice.

## Reading rules

Y is /j/ before a vowel at the start of a syllable. Listen to (you) /ju/ and (beyond) /biˈjɑnd/. At the end of a word, Y is a vowel, not /j/. Y is also a vowel in the middle of some words.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /dʒ/ for Y. Do not say a full 'ee' before the next vowel. Keep the glide quick.
articles.summary: Y makes the sound /j/ at the start of a word or syllable.

articles.title: Y
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter Y can make the short vowel sound /ɪ/. Listen to it in (gym) /dʒɪm/. Listen again in (myth) /mɪθ/ and in (symbol) /ˈsɪm.bəl/.

## How to say it

Open your mouth a little. Keep your tongue high and forward. Keep your lips relaxed. Make the sound quick.

## Reading rules

Y is /ɪ/ in the middle of some words, often words from Greek. Listen to (system) /ˈsɪ.stəm/ and (rhythm) /ˈrɪ.ðəm/. These words follow the same rule as a short I. The syllable ends with a consonant.

## Common mistakes

Do not say a long 'eye' sound in (gym) /dʒɪm/. Do not say a long 'ee'. Say a short, relaxed /ɪ/.
articles.summary: Y can make the short vowel /ɪ/, as in 'gym'.

articles.title: Y
articles.body:
## The sound

The letter Y can make the long vowel sound /aɪ/. Listen to it in (my) /maɪ/. Listen again in (cry) /kraɪ/ and in (fly) /flaɪ/.

## How to say it

Start with your mouth open and your tongue low. Then slide your tongue up and forward. The sound has two parts, but it is one beat.

## Reading rules

Y is /aɪ/ at the end of a short word, as in (try) /traɪ/. Y is also /aɪ/ before a silent E, as in (type) /taɪp/ and (style) /staɪl/. At the end of a longer word, Y is usually /i/, as in (happy) /ˈhæ.pi/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /i/ at the end of (my) /maɪ/. Slide up to the end of the sound. Do not say the silent E in (type) /taɪp/.
articles.summary: Y can make the long sound /aɪ/, as in 'my'.

articles.title: kn-
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters KN at the start of a word make the sound /n/. The K is silent. Listen to (knee) /ni/. Listen again in (knot) /nɑt/ and in (knock) /nɑk/.

## How to say it

Say the N only. Touch the tip of your tongue to the ridge behind your upper teeth. Let the air come out through your nose. Use your voice.

## Reading rules

KN is always /n/ at the start of a word. Listen to (knit) /nɪt/ and (kneel) /nil/. Long ago, people said both sounds. Today we write the K, but we do not say it.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /k/ before the N. Do not say 'kuh-nee'. Say (knee) /ni/ as 'nee'.
articles.summary: KN at the start of a word sounds like /n/. The K is silent.

articles.title: kn-
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters KN make the sound /n/ in many words with a long vowel or a glide. Listen to (know) /noʊ/. Listen again in (knife) /naɪf/ and in (knew) /nu/.

## How to say it

Say the N only. Then say the vowel. Keep the word smooth. Do not stop between the N and the vowel.

## Reading rules

Words with KN are often common words. Listen to (knight) /naɪt/ and (known) /noʊn/. Many of them are related. (Know) /noʊ/, (known) /noʊn/ and (knowledge) /ˈnɑ.lɪdʒ/ all start with /n/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /k/ at the start. Do not say the GH in (knight) /naɪt/. Say /naɪt/.
articles.summary: KN stays silent in words with long vowels, such as 'know' and 'knife'.

articles.title: wr-
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters WR at the start of a word make the sound /r/. The W is silent. Listen to (write) /raɪt/. Listen again in (wrong) /rɔŋ/ and in (wrap) /ræp/.

## How to say it

Say the R only. Pull your tongue back and raise the sides of it. Round your lips a little. Use your voice.

## Reading rules

WR is always /r/ at the start of a word. Listen to (wrist) /rɪst/ and (wreck) /rɛk/. The word (answer) /ˈæn.sɚ/ has a silent W too, but it is spelled differently.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /w/ before the R. Do not say 'wuh-rite'. Say (write) /raɪt/ as 'rite'.
articles.summary: WR at the start of a word sounds like /r/. The W is silent.

articles.title: gn-
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters GN make the sound /n/. The G is silent. Listen to (gnat) /næt/. Listen again in (gnaw) /nɔ/ and in (sign) /saɪn/.

## How to say it

Say the N only. Touch the tip of your tongue to the ridge behind your upper teeth. Let the air come out through your nose. Use your voice.

## Reading rules

GN is /n/ at the start of a word, as in (gnome) /noʊm/. GN is also /n/ at the end of a word, as in (design) /dɪˈzaɪn/. In longer related words, the G can be heard. Compare (sign) /saɪn/ and (signal) /ˈsɪɡ.nəl/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /ɡ/ in (sign) /saɪn/. Do not say /ɡ/ in (gnat) /næt/. Say only /n/.
articles.summary: GN at the start of a word, or at the end, sounds like /n/. The G is silent.

articles.title: -mb
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters MB at the end of a word make the sound /m/. The B is silent. Listen to (lamb) /læm/. Listen again in (comb) /koʊm/ and in (climb) /klaɪm/.

## How to say it

Close your lips and say /m/. Let the air come out through your nose. Use your voice. Do not open your lips for a B sound.

## Reading rules

MB is /m/ at the end of a word or before a suffix, as in (thumb) /θʌm/ and (bomb) /bɑm/. In the middle of some words, B is said. Listen to (number) /ˈnʌm.bɚ/ and (December) /dɪˈsɛm.bɚ/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the B in (lamb) /læm/. Do not stop the air after M. Close your lips once, and finish with /m/.
articles.summary: MB at the end of a word sounds like /m/. The B is silent.

articles.title: -lk
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters ALK make the sound /ɔk/. The L is silent. Listen to (walk) /wɔk/. Listen again in (talk) /tɔk/ and in (chalk) /tʃɔk/.

## How to say it

Open your mouth a little and round your lips. Say a steady /ɔ/. Then press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth for /k/. Do not touch the ridge with your tongue.

## Reading rules

In ALK, the L is silent. In ILK and ELK, the L is said. Listen to (milk) /mɪlk/, (silk) /sɪlk/ and (elk) /ɛlk/. Check each word. The spelling tells you the sound.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the L in (walk) /wɔk/ or (talk) /tɔk/. Do say the L in (milk) /mɪlk/. Keep your tongue away from the ridge in (walk) /wɔk/.
articles.summary: ALK sounds like /ɔk/. The L is silent. In ILK, the L is said.

articles.title: -lf
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters ALF make the sound /æf/ in American English. The L is silent. Listen to (calf) /kæf/. Listen again in (half) /hæf/ and in (calves) /kævz/.

## How to say it

Open your mouth wide for A. Keep your tongue forward and low. Then put your upper teeth on your lower lip for /f/. Do not touch the ridge with your tongue.

## Reading rules

In ALF, the L is silent. In ULF, OLF and ELF, the L is said. Listen to (gulf) /ɡʌlf/, (wolf) /wʊlf/ and (self) /sɛlf/. A few words can be said both ways. Check each word.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the L in (half) /hæf/. Do say the L in (self) /sɛlf/. Do not say the A like /ɑ/ in (father) /ˈfɑ.ðɚ/.
articles.summary: ALF sounds like /æf/. The L is silent. In ULF and ELF, the L is said.

articles.title: -stle
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters STLE at the end of a word make the sound /səl/. The T is silent. Listen to (castle) /ˈkæ.səl/. Listen again in (whistle) /ˈwɪ.səl/ and in (rustle) /ˈrʌ.səl/.

## How to say it

Say the S and then a weak /əl/. Do not stop between them. Do not touch the ridge with your tongue for a T. Keep the ending short and quiet.

## Reading rules

STLE is a common ending. Listen to (bustle) /ˈbʌ.səl/ and (hustle) /ˈhʌ.səl/. The stress falls on the first syllable. The ending has no stress. The same silent T appears in (listen) /ˈlɪ.sən/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the T in (castle) /ˈkæ.səl/. Do not say 'cas-tul' with a strong ending. Make the last syllable weak.
articles.summary: STLE sounds like /səl/. The T is silent.

articles.title: -gh(t)
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters GHT make the sound /t/. The GH is silent. Listen to (light) /laɪt/. Listen again in (night) /naɪt/ and in (eight) /eɪt/.

## How to say it

Say the vowel and then close with /t/. Touch the tip of your tongue to the ridge behind your upper teeth. Do not say any sound for GH.

## Reading rules

GHT usually follows a long vowel or a glide. Listen to (right) /raɪt/ and (weight) /weɪt/. After the letters OU, the sound is /ɔ/, as in (thought) /θɔt/ and (bought) /bɔt/. The word (laugh) /læf/ is different. There, GH is /f/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /ɡ/ or /h/ for GH. Do not say 'lig-ht'. Say (light) /laɪt/ as 'lite'.
articles.summary: GHT sounds like /t/. The GH is silent. The vowel before it is long.

articles.title: -bt
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters BT make the sound /t/. The B is silent. Listen to (debt) /dɛt/. Listen again in (doubt) /daʊt/ and in (subtle) /ˈsʌ.təl/.

## How to say it

Say the vowel and then close with /t/. Touch the tip of your tongue to the ridge behind your upper teeth. Do not close your lips for a B.

## Reading rules

BT is a rare pattern. It appears in a few common words. Listen to (doubtful) /ˈdaʊt.fəl/ and (debtor) /ˈdɛ.tɚ/. The B comes from the old Latin word. We write it, but we do not say it.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the B in (debt) /dɛt/. Do not say 'deb-t'. Say (debt) /dɛt/ as 'det'.
articles.summary: BT sounds like /t/. The B is silent.

articles.title: -sland
articles.body:
## The sound

In the word (island) /ˈaɪ.lənd/, the S is silent. The ending sounds like /lənd/. Listen to the word (isle) /aɪl/. The S is silent in (aisle) /aɪl/ too.

## How to say it

Say the long vowel /aɪ/ first. Slide your tongue up. Then say a clear /l/ and a weak /ənd/. Do not say any sound for S.

## Reading rules

The S in (island) /ˈaɪ.lənd/ is a spelling mistake from long ago. Writers thought it came from a Latin word. It did not. Learn the word as a whole. The stress falls on the first syllable.

## Common mistakes

Do not say 'iz-land' or 'is-land'. Do not say the S. Say (island) /ˈaɪ.lənd/ as 'eye-lund'.
articles.summary: In 'island', the S is silent. The word sounds like /ˈaɪ.lənd/.

articles.title: th
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters TH can make the sound /θ/. It is a soft hiss with your tongue between your teeth. Listen to it in (think) /θɪŋk/. Listen again in (bath) /bæθ/ and in (three) /θri/.

## How to say it

Put the tip of your tongue between your teeth. Push air through the small space. Do not use your voice. The sound is soft and light.

## Reading rules

TH is /θ/ in most words that carry meaning, such as (thing) /θɪŋ/ and (month) /mʌnθ/. TH is /θ/ at the start and at the end of words. A few words use TH as /t/. Listen to (Thomas) /ˈtɑ.məs/ and (thyme) /taɪm/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /s/ or /t/ for TH. Put your tongue between your teeth. Do not use your voice, or the sound becomes /ð/.
articles.summary: TH makes the sound /θ/ in most nouns, verbs and adjectives.

articles.title: th
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters TH can make the sound /ð/. It is a buzzing sound with your tongue between your teeth. Listen to it in (this) /ðɪs/. Listen again in (that) /ðæt/ and in (mother) /ˈmʌ.ðɚ/.

## How to say it

Put the tip of your tongue between your teeth. Push air through the small space. Use your voice. You will feel a buzz on your tongue.

## Reading rules

TH is /ð/ in short function words, such as (the) /ðə/, (them) /ðɛm/ and (with) /wɪð/. TH is /ð/ between vowels, as in (father) /ˈfɑ.ðɚ/. A final TH after a long vowel and a silent E is also /ð/, as in (breathe) /brið/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /d/ or /z/ for TH. Put your tongue between your teeth. Keep your voice on.
articles.summary: TH makes the sound /ð/ in function words and in the middle of some words.

articles.title: sh
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters SH make the sound /ʃ/. Listen to it in (ship) /ʃɪp/. Listen again in (fish) /fɪʃ/ and in (shoe) /ʃu/.

## How to say it

Pull your tongue back a little. Round your lips. Push air through the space. Do not use your voice. The sound is a soft, long hiss.

## Reading rules

SH is always /ʃ/. It can come at the start, in the middle and at the end of a word. Listen to (wash) /wɑʃ/ and (fashion) /ˈfæ.ʃən/. The sound /ʃ/ can also be written with other letters, such as TI, CI and SS.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /s/ for SH. Do not say /tʃ/, the sound in 'chair'. Do not say two separate sounds, S and H. Say one smooth sound.
articles.summary: SH makes the sound /ʃ/, the quiet 'shh' sound.

articles.title: ch
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters CH usually make the sound /tʃ/. Listen to it in (chin) /tʃɪn/. Listen again in (chair) /tʃɛr/ and in (rich) /rɪtʃ/.

## How to say it

Put your tongue behind your upper teeth, near the ridge. Hold the air for a moment. Release it with a hissing sound. Do not use your voice.

## Reading rules

CH is /tʃ/ in most common English words. Listen to (lunch) /lʌntʃ/ and (much) /mʌtʃ/. The letters TCH make the same sound, as in (watch) /wɑtʃ/. A few words use CH differently. Those have their own articles.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /ʃ/ in (chin) /tʃɪn/. Do not say /k/. Start with a short /t/, and release it into the hiss.
articles.summary: CH usually makes the sound /tʃ/, as in 'chair'.

articles.title: ch
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters CH can make the sound /k/. Listen to it in (school) /skul/. Listen again in (echo) /ˈɛ.koʊ/ and in (chemist) /ˈkɛ.mɪst/.

## How to say it

Press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth. Release it with a small puff of air. Do not use your voice. Do not say any sound for H.

## Reading rules

CH is /k/ in many words that come from Greek. Listen to (character) /ˈkɛ.rɪk.tɚ/ and (Christmas) /ˈkrɪs.məs/. Many of them are about science or learning, such as (chemistry) /ˈkɛ.mɪ.stri/. The word (ache) /eɪk/ is also /k/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /tʃ/ in (school) /skul/. Do not say /ʃ/. Say /k/ and do not say the H.
articles.summary: CH makes the sound /k/ in words from Greek, as in 'school'.

articles.title: ch
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters CH can make the sound /ʃ/. It is the 'sh' sound. Listen to it in (chef) /ʃɛf/. Listen again in (machine) /məˈʃin/ and in (chic) /ʃik/.

## How to say it

Pull your tongue back a little. Round your lips. Push air through the space. Do not use your voice. The sound is a soft, long hiss.

## Reading rules

CH is /ʃ/ in words that came from French in modern times. Listen to (brochure) /broʊˈʃʊr/ and (Chicago) /ʃɪˈkɑ.ɡoʊ/. These words are not many. The spelling does not show the sound. Learn them one by one.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /tʃ/ in (chef) /ʃɛf/. Do not say /k/. Say a smooth /ʃ/.
articles.summary: CH makes the sound /ʃ/ in words from French, as in 'chef'.

articles.title: ph
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters PH make the sound /f/. Listen to it in (phone) /foʊn/. Listen again in (photo) /ˈfoʊ.toʊ/ and in (elephant) /ˈɛ.lə.fənt/.

## How to say it

Put your upper teeth on your lower lip. Push air through the small space. Do not use your voice. The sound is a soft, steady hiss.

## Reading rules

PH is /f/ in words that come from Greek. Listen to (dolphin) /ˈdɑl.fɪn/ and (graph) /ɡræf/. A few names use PH as /v/. Listen to (Stephen) /ˈsti.vən/. Do not say a P sound before the F.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /p/ and then /h/. Say /f/ only. Do not say 'puh-hone'. Say (phone) /foʊn/ as 'fone'.
articles.summary: PH makes the sound /f/, as in 'phone'.

articles.title: ng
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters NG make the sound /ŋ/ at the end of a word. It is one sound, made in the nose. Listen to it in (sing) /sɪŋ/. Listen again in (long) /lɔŋ/ and in (ring) /rɪŋ/.

## How to say it

Press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth. Let the air come out through your nose. Use your voice. Do not touch the roof with the tip of your tongue.

## Reading rules

At the end of a word, NG is just /ŋ/. There is no /ɡ/. In the middle of some words, you also say /ɡ/. Listen to (finger) /ˈfɪŋ.ɡɚ/ and (angry) /ˈæŋ.ɡri/. Compare (singer) /ˈsɪ.ŋɚ/, where there is no /ɡ/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /ɡ/ at the end of (sing) /sɪŋ/. Do not say /n/ and /g/ as two sounds. Keep the back of your tongue up.
articles.summary: NG makes the sound /ŋ/, as in 'sing'.

articles.title: -tion
articles.body:
## The sound

The ending -TION usually makes the sound /ʃən/. It is one weak syllable. Listen to it in (nation) /ˈneɪ.ʃən/. Listen again in (station) /ˈsteɪ.ʃən/ and in (information) /ˌɪn.fɚˈmeɪ.ʃən/.

## How to say it

Pull your tongue back a little for /ʃ/. Round your lips slightly. Then say a weak /ən/. Do not stress the ending.

## Reading rules

The stress falls on the syllable before -TION. Listen to (action) /ˈæk.ʃən/ and (creation) /kriˈeɪ.ʃən/. After the letter S, the ending is /tʃən/. Listen to (question) /ˈkwɛs.tʃən/ and (suggestion) /səɡˈdʒɛs.tʃən/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say 'tee-on'. Do not stress the ending. Say /ʃən/ quickly and quietly.
articles.summary: TION usually sounds like /ʃən/. After S, it sounds like /tʃən/.

articles.title: -eigh
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters EIGH usually make the sound /eɪ/. The GH is silent. Listen to (weigh) /weɪ/. Listen again in (sleigh) /sleɪ/ and in (eight) /eɪt/.

## How to say it

Open your mouth a little. Start with your tongue in the middle. Then slide it up and forward. The sound has two parts, but it is one beat.

## Reading rules

EIGH is /eɪ/ in most words. Listen to (neighbor) /ˈneɪ.bɚ/ and (freight) /freɪt/. One common word is different. Listen to (height) /haɪt/. Here the sound is /aɪ/, and the ending is /t/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the GH. Do not say (height) /haɪt/ with /eɪ/. Say /haɪt/, like 'hite'.
articles.summary: EIGH usually sounds like /eɪ/, as in 'weigh'. In 'height' it sounds like /aɪ/.

articles.title: -ough
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters OUGH have several sounds. In (through) /θru/, the sound is /u/. It sounds like the word 'two'. Listen to the word again. It rhymes with (blue) /blu/.

## How to say it

Round your lips tightly. Raise the back of your tongue. Keep the sound long and steady. Do not move your lips while you say it.

## Reading rules

OUGH is /u/ in only a few words. Listen to (through) /θru/ and (throughout) /θruˈaʊt/. The same letters sound different in other words. Compare (though) /ðoʊ/ and (thought) /θɔt/. Each of them has its own article.

## Common mistakes

Do not say OUGH the same way in every word. Do not say the GH. Learn each word by itself.
articles.summary: OUGH can sound like /u/, as in 'through'.

articles.title: -ough
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters OUGH can make the sound /oʊ/. The GH is silent. Listen to (though) /ðoʊ/. Listen again in (although) /ɔlˈðoʊ/ and in (dough) /doʊ/.

## How to say it

Round your lips and slide them to a tighter shape. Keep your tongue in the back of your mouth. The sound has two parts, but it is one beat.

## Reading rules

OUGH is /oʊ/ at the end of a word. Listen to (thorough) /ˈθɜ.roʊ/ and (borough) /ˈbɜ.roʊ/. The same letters sound different in other words. Compare (through) /θru/ and (thought) /θɔt/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the GH. Do not say (though) /ðoʊ/ with /u/. Say /ðoʊ/, like 'tho'.
articles.summary: OUGH can sound like /oʊ/, as in 'though'.

articles.title: -ough
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters OUGHT make the sound /ɔt/. The GH is silent. Listen to (thought) /θɔt/. Listen again in (bought) /bɔt/ and in (brought) /brɔt/.

## How to say it

Open your mouth a little and round your lips. Keep your tongue low in the back of your mouth. Hold the vowel steady. Then close with /t/.

## Reading rules

OUGHT after most consonants is /ɔt/. Listen to (fought) /fɔt/ and (ought) /ɔt/. Many of these words are the past tense of a verb. Other OUGH words are different. Listen to (enough) /ɪˈnʌf/, (cough) /kɔf/ and (bough) /baʊ/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the GH. Do not say (thought) /θɔt/ with /oʊ/. Say /θɔt/. Learn each OUGH word by itself.
articles.summary: OUGH sounds like /ɔ/ before T, as in 'thought' and 'bought'.

articles.title: ea in seară (evening)
articles.body:
## The sound

The group EA makes the sound /e̯a/. It is one beat. Say a very short E, and slide into A. Listen to it in (seară) /ˈse̯a.rə/, which means evening. Listen again in (cafea) /kaˈfe̯a/, which means coffee.

## How to say it

Start with your mouth almost closed, as for E. Open your jaw quickly toward A. Do not stop between the two sounds. The whole group takes the time of one vowel.

## Reading rules

EA is usually one syllable. Listen to (mea) /me̯a/, which means my. In some words the E and A are two separate beats. Listen to (ideal) /i.deˈal/, which means ideal. At the start of a word, EA sounds like /ja/, as in (ea) /ja/, which means she.

## Common mistakes

Do not say two full vowels with a pause between them. Do not say /ia/ with a strong 'y'. Keep the E very short, and move straight into A.
articles.summary: EA is one quick beat. It starts with a short E and glides into A.

articles.title: oa in noapte (night)
articles.body:
## The sound

The group OA makes the sound /o̯a/. It is one beat. Say a very short O, and slide into A. It sounds close to 'wa' in 'water'. Listen to it in (noapte) /ˈno̯ap.te/, which means night. Listen again in (soare) /ˈso̯a.re/, which means sun.

## How to say it

Round your lips for O. Then open your mouth and let your lips relax for A. Do this in one smooth move. The lip change is quick.

## Reading rules

OA is usually one syllable. Listen to (floare) /ˈflo̯a.re/, which means flower, and (școală) /ˈʃko̯a.lə/, which means school. A few words use two beats. Listen to (oază) /oˈa.zə/, which means oasis.

## Common mistakes

Do not say a long 'oh' and then a long 'ah'. Do not drop the O. The lip shape starts round and ends open. Keep it as one beat.
articles.summary: OA is one quick beat. It sounds like the 'wa' in 'water'.

articles.title: ia in iarnă (winter)
articles.body:
## The sound

The group IA makes the sound /ja/. It is one beat. It sounds like 'ya' in 'yard'. Listen to it in (iarnă) /ˈjar.nə/, which means winter. Listen again in (băiat) /bəˈjat/, which means boy.

## How to say it

Say a quick 'y'. Slide at once into A. Keep your tongue high at the start and low at the end. Do not pause between the two parts.

## Reading rules

IA is usually /ja/. Listen to (piatră) /ˈpja.trə/, which means stone, and (iar) /jar/, which means again. In some words I and A are separate beats. Listen to (pian) /piˈan/, which means piano.

## Common mistakes

Do not say a full 'ee' before A. The I is only a quick glide. Do not add a third sound in the middle.
articles.summary: IA is one quick beat. It sounds like 'ya' in 'yard'.

articles.title: ie in ieri (yesterday)
articles.body:
## The sound

The group IE makes the sound /je/. It is one beat. It sounds like 'ye' in 'yes'. Listen to it in (ieri) /jer/, which means yesterday. Listen again in (miere) /ˈmje.re/, which means honey.

## How to say it

Say a quick 'y'. Slide at once into E. Keep your lips relaxed and slightly spread. Do not pause between the two parts.

## Reading rules

IE is usually /je/. Listen to (fier) /fjer/, which means iron, and (piept) /pjept/, which means chest. At the end of some words, I and E are two beats. Listen to (familie) /faˈmi.li.e/, which means family.

## Common mistakes

Do not say a full 'ee' before E. The I is only a quick glide. Do not turn the sound into English 'ee-eh' with a pause.
articles.summary: IE is one quick beat. It sounds like 'ye' in 'yes'.

articles.title: io in iod (iodine)
articles.body:
## The sound

The group IO makes the sound /jo/. It is one beat. It sounds like 'yo' in 'yoga'. Listen to it in (iod) /jod/, which means iodine. Listen again in (ghiozdan) /ɡjozˈdan/, which means school bag.

## How to say it

Say a quick 'y'. Round your lips at once and move into O. Keep the O pure. Do not pause between the two parts.

## Reading rules

IO is usually /jo/ when it is one syllable. Some words use two beats. Listen to (avion) /a.viˈon/, which means airplane, and (biologie) /bi.o.loˈdʒi.e/, which means biology. Check the stress in each word.

## Common mistakes

Do not say 'ee-oh' with two full beats in a word like (iod) /jod/. The I is only a glide. Do not end with an 'oo' glide.
articles.summary: IO is one quick beat. It sounds like 'yo' in 'yoga'.

articles.title: iu in iubit (beloved)
articles.body:
## The sound

The group IU makes the sound /ju/. It is one beat. It sounds like 'you' in 'youth', but shorter. Listen to it in (iubit) /juˈbit/, which means beloved. Listen again in (iute) /ˈju.te/, which means fast.

## How to say it

Say a quick 'y'. Round your lips tightly for U. Keep the lips round until the sound ends. Do not pause between the two parts.

## Reading rules

IU is /ju/ when it is one beat. Listen to (iubire) /juˈbi.re/, which means love. Some words use two beats. Listen to (fiul) /ˈfi.ul/, which means the son, and (triumf) /triˈumf/, which means triumph.

## Common mistakes

Do not say a full 'ee' before U. The I is only a quick glide. Do not unround your lips for U.
articles.summary: IU is one quick beat. It sounds like 'you' in 'youth'.

articles.title: ua in ziua (the day)
articles.body:
## The sound

The group UA makes the sound /wa/. It is one beat. Say a very short U, and slide into A. Listen to it in (ziua) /ˈzi.wa/, which means the day. Listen again in (roua) /ˈro.wa/, which means the dew.

## How to say it

Round your lips tightly for U. Open them quickly for A. Do this in one smooth move. The U is very short.

## Reading rules

UA is /wa/ in words like (ziua) /ˈzi.wa/ and (roua) /ˈro.wa/. In other words, U and A are two beats. Listen to (lua) /ˈlu.a/, which means to take, and (grua) /ˈɡru.a/, which means crane.

## Common mistakes

Do not say a full 'oo' and then a full 'ah'. Do not drop the U in (ziua) /ˈzi.wa/. Keep the glide short and light.
articles.summary: UA is one quick beat. It sounds like 'wa' in 'water'.

articles.title: ue in înșeuează (saddles)
articles.body:
## The sound

The group UE is rare in Romanian words. U and E usually make two beats: /u.e/. Listen to it in (duet) /duˈet/, which means duet. Listen again in (continuează) /kon.ti.nu.eˈa.zə/, which means it continues.

## How to say it

Round your lips tightly for U. Then open them and move your tongue forward for E. Make a small break between the two sounds. Each sound is clear.

## Reading rules

UE is mostly found in words from Latin and from other languages. Both letters keep their own sound. Stress usually falls on the E, as in (duet) /duˈet/. Check the stress in each word, because it can change.

## Common mistakes

Do not blend U and E into one sound. Do not drop the U. Say both sounds clearly.
articles.summary: UE is rare. U and E usually make two separate beats.

articles.title: ai in mai (May / more)
articles.body:
## The sound

The group AI makes the sound /aj/. It is one beat. It sounds like 'eye', but shorter. Listen to it in (mai) /maj/, which means more. Listen again in (hai) /haj/, which means come on.

## How to say it

Open your mouth for A. Then slide your tongue forward and up toward I. Keep it quick. The sound ends with a short 'y'.

## Reading rules

AI is /aj/ in most words. Listen to (cai) /kaj/, which means horses. In some words, A and I are two beats. Listen to (aici) /aˈitʃ/, which means here. Check the stress in each word.

## Common mistakes

Do not say a long 'ay' as in 'day'. Do not stop at A. Move to the short I at the end. Do not make the I a full vowel.
articles.summary: AI is one quick beat. It sounds like 'eye', but shorter.

articles.title: ei in trei (three)
articles.body:
## The sound

The group EI makes the sound /ej/. It is one beat. It sounds like the 'ay' in 'day', but shorter. Listen to it in (trei) /trej/, which means three. Listen again in (lei) /lej/, which means lions.

## How to say it

Open your mouth a little for E. Then slide your tongue slightly higher toward I. Keep your lips relaxed. The sound ends with a short 'y'.

## Reading rules

EI is /ej/ when it is one beat. Listen to (ei) /ej/, which means they. In some words, E and I are two beats. Listen to (atei) /aˈte.i/, which means atheists.

## Common mistakes

Do not draw the sound out into a long 'ay'. Keep the first part short. Do not make the I a full vowel.
articles.summary: EI is one quick beat. It sounds like 'ay' in 'day', but shorter.

articles.title: oi in doi (two)
articles.body:
## The sound

The group OI makes the sound /oj/. It is one beat. It sounds like 'oy' in 'boy'. Listen to it in (doi) /doj/, which means two. Listen again in (noi) /noj/, which means we.

## How to say it

Round your lips for O. Then slide your tongue forward and up toward I, and let your lips relax. Do it in one smooth move.

## Reading rules

OI is /oj/ in most words. Listen to (foi) /foj/, which means sheets. In some words, O and I are two beats. Listen to (oi) /oj/, which means sheep, and (eroi) /eˈroj/, which means heroes.

## Common mistakes

Do not say a long 'oh' and then 'ee'. Keep one smooth beat. Keep the first part short. Do not make the I a full vowel.
articles.summary: OI is one quick beat. It sounds like 'oy' in 'boy'.

articles.title: ui in pui (chicken / you put)
articles.body:
## The sound
