The group UI makes the sound /uj/. It is one beat. It sounds like 'ooey', but very short. Listen to it in (pui) /puj/, which means chick. Listen again in (cui) /kuj/, which means nail.

## How to say it

Round your lips tightly for U. Then slide your tongue forward and spread your lips for I. Do it in one smooth move.

## Reading rules

UI is /uj/ when it is one beat. Listen to (lui) /luj/, which means his. In some words, U and I are two beats. Listen to (ruină) /ruˈi.nə/, which means ruin, and (construit) /kon.struˈit/, which means built.

## Common mistakes

Do not say a full 'oo' and then a full 'ee' in (pui) /puj/. Keep the second part very short. Do not drop the U.
articles.summary: UI is one quick beat. It sounds like 'ooey', but very short.

articles.title: au in sau (or)
articles.body:
## The sound

The group AU makes the sound /aw/. It is one beat. It sounds like 'ow' in 'cow'. Listen to it in (sau) /saw/, which means or. Listen again in (au) /aw/, which means they have.

## How to say it

Open your mouth wide for A. Then round your lips and move your tongue back toward U. Do it in one smooth move. The sound ends with a short 'w'.

## Reading rules

AU is /aw/ at the end of many words. In some words, A and U are two beats. Listen to (aur) /ˈa.ur/, which means gold, and (aurit) /a.uˈrit/, which means gilded.

## Common mistakes

Do not say 'ah-oo' with a break. Do not stop at A. Move toward U and keep it short.
articles.summary: AU is one quick beat. It sounds like 'ow' in 'cow'.

articles.title: eu in greu (heavy / hard)
articles.body:
## The sound

The group EU makes the sound /ew/. It is one beat. Say E, and move your lips toward U. Listen to it in (greu) /ɡrew/, which means heavy or hard. Listen again in (leu) /lew/, which means lion.

## How to say it

Start with your tongue forward, as for E. Round your lips as you finish. Do it in one smooth move. The sound ends with a short 'w'.

## Reading rules

EU is /ew/ in most words. Listen to (mereu) /meˈrew/, which means always. In two very common words, EU starts with a 'y'. Listen to (eu) /jew/, which means I, and (ești) /jeʃtʲ/, which means you are.

## Common mistakes

Do not say a long 'eh' and a long 'oo'. Keep one beat. Do not say the English 'you' sound. Keep it short.
articles.summary: EU is one quick beat. It starts with E and ends with a short 'w'.

articles.title: eai in vedeai (you used to see)
articles.body:
## The sound

The group EAI makes the sound /e̯aj/. It is one beat. Say a very short E, glide into A, and finish with a short 'y'. Listen to it in (vedeai) /veˈde̯aj/, which means you used to see. Listen again in (spuneai) /spuˈne̯aj/, which means you used to say.

## How to say it

Start with your mouth almost closed, as for E. Open your jaw toward A. Then raise your tongue toward I at the end. Do all three in one smooth move.

## Reading rules

EAI is a common ending in the past tense, for the word 'you'. Listen to (mergeai) /merˈdʒe̯aj/, which means you used to go. The stress usually falls on the syllable before this ending.

## Common mistakes

Do not say three full beats. Keep it as one beat. Do not make the I a full vowel.
articles.summary: EAI is one beat. It is common in verb endings.

articles.title: iai in tăiai (you were cutting)
articles.body:
## The sound

The group IAI makes the sound /jaj/. It is one beat. Say a quick 'y', open to A, and finish with a short 'y'. Listen to it in (tăiai) /təˈjaj/, which means you used to cut. Listen again in (copiai) /koˈpjaj/, which means you used to copy.

## How to say it

Start with your tongue high, as for 'y'. Drop your jaw for A. Then raise your tongue toward I. Do it in one smooth move.

## Reading rules

IAI appears in the past tense, for the word 'you'. Listen to (apropiai) /a.proˈpjaj/, which means you approached. The stress falls on the syllable before this ending.

## Common mistakes

Do not say two full vowels. The first and last sounds are only glides. Do not say three beats.
articles.summary: IAI is one beat. It starts and ends with a quick 'y'.

articles.title: eau in beau (I drink / they drink)
articles.body:
## The sound

The group EAU makes the sound /e̯aw/. It is one beat. Say a very short E, glide into A, and finish with a short 'w'. Listen to it in (beau) /be̯aw/, which means they drink. Listen again in (vedeau) /veˈde̯aw/, which means they used to see.

## How to say it

Start with your mouth almost closed, as for E. Open your jaw toward A. Then round your lips toward U at the end. Do all three in one smooth move.

## Reading rules

EAU is a common ending in the past tense, for the word 'they'. Listen to (mergeau) /merˈdʒe̯aw/, which means they used to go. The stress usually falls on the syllable before this ending.

## Common mistakes

Do not say three full beats. Keep it as one beat. Do not make the U a full vowel.
articles.summary: EAU is one beat. It is common in verb endings.

articles.title: iau in iau (I take / they take)
articles.body:
## The sound

The group IAU makes the sound /jaw/. It is one beat. Say a quick 'y', open to A, and finish with a short 'w'. Listen to it in (iau) /jaw/, which means I take. Listen again in (tăiau) /təˈjaw/, which means they used to cut.

## How to say it

Start with your tongue high, as for 'y'. Drop your jaw for A. Then round your lips toward U. Do it in one smooth move.

## Reading rules

IAU appears in the past tense, for the word 'they'. Listen to (copiau) /koˈpjaw/, which means they used to copy. It also appears in the verb (a lua) /a ˈlu.a/, as in (iau) /jaw/, which means I take.

## Common mistakes

Do not say two full vowels. The first sound is only a glide. Do not say three beats.
articles.summary: IAU is one beat. It starts with a quick 'y' and ends with a short 'w'.

articles.title: ioa in creioane (pencils)
articles.body:
## The sound

The group IOA makes the sound /jo̯a/. It is one beat. Say a quick 'y', then a short O, and slide into A. Listen to it in (creioane) /kreˈjo̯a.ne/, which means pencils. Listen again in (mioare) /ˈmjo̯a.re/, which means lambs.

## How to say it

Start with your tongue high, as for 'y'. Round your lips for a short O. Then open your mouth for A. Do all three in one smooth move.

## Reading rules

IOA is usually one beat, and the stress falls on it. Listen to (aripioară) /a.riˈpjo̯a.rə/, which means little wing. It appears in many plural nouns. Compare (creion) /kreˈjon/, which means pencil, with (creioane) /kreˈjo̯a.ne/, which means pencils.

## Common mistakes

Do not say three full beats. The first two sounds are only glides. Keep it as one smooth beat.
articles.summary: IOA is one beat. It starts with a quick 'y' and ends with a quick 'wa'.

articles.title: ch in cherry (/tʃ/)
articles.body:
## The sound

The groups CE and CI make the sound /tʃ/. It is like 'ch' in 'church'. Listen to it in (ceai) /tʃaj/, which means tea. Listen again in (cine) /ˈtʃi.ne/, which means who.

## How to say it

Put your tongue behind your upper teeth, near the ridge. Hold the air for a moment. Release it with a hissing sound. Do not use your voice.

## Reading rules

C before E or I is always /tʃ/. Listen to (zece) /ˈze.tʃe/, which means ten, and (cinci) /tʃintʃ/, which means five. Sometimes E or I is silent. It only shows the soft sound. Listen to (ceas) /tʃas/, which means clock, and (ciorbă) /ˈtʃor.bə/, which means soup.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /s/ for C before E or I. Do not say /k/. Say /tʃ/. Do not say the I fully at the end of (cinci) /tʃintʃ/. It is a soft whisper.
articles.summary: CE and CI make the sound /tʃ/. It sounds like 'ch' in 'church'.

articles.title: j in jam (/dʒ/)
articles.body:
## The sound

The groups GE and GI make the sound /dʒ/. It is like 'j' in 'jam'. Listen to it in (ger) /dʒer/, which means frost. Listen again in (girafă) /dʒiˈra.fə/, which means giraffe.

## How to say it

Put your tongue behind your upper teeth, near the ridge. Hold the air for a moment. Release it with a buzzing sound. Use your voice.

## Reading rules

G before E or I is always /dʒ/. Listen to (gem) /dʒem/, which means jam. Sometimes E or I is silent. It only shows the soft sound. Listen to (geam) /dʒam/, which means window, and (dragi) /dradʒʲ/, which means dear.

## Common mistakes

Do not say hard /ɡ/ before E or I. Do not say /ʒ/, the sound in 'measure'. Say /dʒ/. Keep your voice on.
articles.summary: GE and GI make the sound /dʒ/. It sounds like 'j' in 'jam'.

articles.title: k in key (/k/)
articles.body:
## The sound

The groups CHE and CHI make the sound /k/. Romanian uses CH to keep a hard K before E or I. Listen to it in (cheie) /ˈke.je/, which means key. Listen again in (chibrit) /kiˈbrit/, which means match.

## How to say it

Press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth. Release it with only a little air. Do not use your voice. The H is silent.

## Reading rules

CH is only written before E or I. Listen to (chei) /kej/, which means keys, and (ureche) /uˈre.ke/, which means ear. At the end of a word, a final I is whispered. Listen to (vechi) /vekʲ/, which means old.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /tʃ/, the sound in 'church'. In Romanian, CH is /k/. Do not say the H as a breath. It is silent.
articles.summary: CHE and CHI make a hard /k/ sound before E or I.

articles.title: g in get / give (/g/)
articles.body:
## The sound

The groups GHE and GHI make the sound /ɡ/. Romanian uses GH to keep a hard G before E or I. Listen to it in (ghid) /ɡid/, which means guide. Listen again in (ghete) /ˈɡe.te/, which means boots.

## How to say it

Press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth. Release it with your voice on. The H is silent.

## Reading rules

GH is only written before E or I. Listen to (gheață) /ˈɡja.tsə/, which means ice, and (unghie) /ˈun.ɡje/, which means nail. At the end of a word, a final I is whispered.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /dʒ/, the sound in 'jam'. In Romanian, GH is /ɡ/. Do not say the H as a breath. It is silent.
articles.summary: GHE and GHI make a hard /ɡ/ sound before E or I.

articles.title: ea
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters EA usually make the long sound /i/. Listen to it in (eat) /it/. Listen again in (meat) /mit/ and in (sea) /si/.

## How to say it

Smile. Raise your tongue high and forward. Keep the sound steady. Do not move your tongue while you say it.

## Reading rules

EA is sometimes /ɛ/. Listen to (bread) /brɛd/ and (head) /hɛd/. EA is /eɪ/ in a few words. Listen to (great) /ɡreɪt/ and (steak) /steɪk/. Learn these words one by one.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the same sound in every EA word. Do not say (bread) /brɛd/ like (read) /rid/. Check each word.
articles.summary: EA usually sounds like /i/, as in 'eat'. Sometimes it sounds like /ɛ/ or /eɪ/.

articles.title: ee
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters EE make the long sound /i/. Listen to it in (see) /si/. Listen again in (feed) /fid/ and in (tree) /tri/.

## How to say it

Smile. Raise your tongue high and forward. Keep the sound steady. Hold it a little longer than a short vowel.

## Reading rules

EE is /i/ in almost every word. Listen to (week) /wik/ and (green) /ɡrin/. There are almost no exceptions. This is one of the most reliable patterns in English.

## Common mistakes

Do not shorten the sound to /ɪ/. (Feed) /fid/ and (fit) /fɪt/ are different. Do not move your tongue during the sound.
articles.summary: EE makes the long sound /i/, as in 'see'.

articles.title: ai
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters AI make the long sound /eɪ/. Listen to it in (rain) /reɪn/. Listen again in (wait) /weɪt/ and in (mail) /meɪl/.

## How to say it

Open your mouth a little. Start with your tongue in the middle. Then slide it up and forward. The sound has two parts, but it is one beat.

## Reading rules

AI is /eɪ/ in most words. It is a stressed sound. In a few words, AI is different. Listen to (said) /sɛd/ and (again) /əˈɡɛn/. In an unstressed syllable, AI is weak, as in (captain) /ˈkæp.tɪn/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say two vowels, 'ah-ee'. Say one smooth sound. Do not say (said) /sɛd/ like (paid) /peɪd/.
articles.summary: AI makes the long sound /eɪ/, as in 'rain'.

articles.title: oa
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters OA make the long sound /oʊ/. Listen to it in (boat) /boʊt/. Listen again in (road) /roʊd/ and in (coat) /koʊt/.

## How to say it

Round your lips and slide them to a tighter shape. Keep your tongue in the back of your mouth. The sound has two parts, but it is one beat.

## Reading rules

OA is /oʊ/ in most words. Before R, it is /ɔ/, as in (roar) /rɔr/ and (board) /bɔrd/. One word is different. Listen to (broad) /brɔd/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /ɔ/ in (boat) /boʊt/. Do not say two vowels, 'oh-ah'. Say one smooth sound.
articles.summary: OA makes the long sound /oʊ/, as in 'boat'.

articles.title: oo
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters OO usually make the long sound /u/. Listen to it in (moon) /mun/. Listen again in (cool) /kul/ and in (food) /fud/. OO can also make the short sound /ʊ/. Listen to (book) /bʊk/.

## How to say it

For the long sound, round your lips tightly and raise the back of your tongue. For the short sound, round your lips less and relax. Keep both sounds steady.

## Reading rules

OO is short /ʊ/ before K and in a few words. Listen to (good) /ɡʊd/ and (foot) /fʊt/. In two common words, OO is /ʌ/. Listen to (blood) /blʌd/ and (flood) /flʌd/. Most other OO words use the long sound.

## Common mistakes

Do not say (book) /bʊk/ with the long /u/. Do not say (food) /fud/ with the short /ʊ/. Listen to the vowel length.
articles.summary: OO makes the long sound /u/, as in 'moon', or the short sound /ʊ/, as in 'book'.

articles.title: ou
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters OU usually make the sound /aʊ/. Listen to it in (out) /aʊt/. Listen again in (loud) /laʊd/ and in (house) /haʊs/.

## How to say it

Open your mouth wide. Then round your lips and move your tongue back. The sound has two parts, but it is one beat.

## Reading rules

OU has other sounds in some words. Listen to (soup) /sup/ and (group) /ɡrup/. Listen to (touch) /tʌtʃ/ and (young) /jʌŋ/. In (could) /kʊd/, the sound is short. Learn these words one by one.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the same sound in every OU word. Do not say (soup) /sup/ like (south) /saʊθ/. Check each word.
articles.summary: OU usually sounds like /aʊ/, as in 'out'.

articles.title: ow
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters OW can make two sounds. One is /aʊ/. Listen to it in (cow) /kaʊ/. Listen again in (owl) /aʊl/ and in (down) /daʊn/. The other is /oʊ/. Listen to (snow) /snoʊ/.

## How to say it

For /aʊ/, open your mouth wide. Then round your lips and move your tongue back. For /oʊ/, round your lips and slide them to a tighter shape. Both sounds are one beat.

## Reading rules

OW at the end of a word is often /oʊ/. Listen to (show) /ʃoʊ/ and (yellow) /ˈjɛ.loʊ/. OW before L or N is often /aʊ/ in (town) /taʊn/. But (bowl) /boʊl/ and (own) /oʊn/ use /oʊ/. Learn each word.

## Common mistakes

Do not use one sound for every OW word. Do not say (cow) /kaʊ/ with /oʊ/. Do not say (snow) /snoʊ/ with /aʊ/.
articles.summary: OW can sound like /aʊ/, as in 'cow', or like /oʊ/, as in 'snow'.

articles.title: ie
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters IE can make two sounds. One is /aɪ/. Listen to it in (pie) /paɪ/. Listen again in (tie) /taɪ/. The other is /i/. Listen to (chief) /tʃif/ and (brief) /brif/.

## How to say it

For /aɪ/, start with your mouth open and slide your tongue up and forward. For /i/, smile and raise your tongue high and forward. Keep the sound steady.

## Reading rules

IE at the end of a short word is /aɪ/. Listen to (die) /daɪ/ and (lie) /laɪ/. IE in the middle of a word is often /i/. Listen to (field) /fild/ and (piece) /pis/. A few words are different. Listen to (friend) /frɛnd/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say (friend) /frɛnd/ with /i/. Say /ɛ/. Do not mix (pie) /paɪ/ and (piece) /pis/. The sounds are different.
articles.summary: IE can sound like /aɪ/, as in 'pie', or like /i/, as in 'chief'.

articles.title: au
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters AU usually make the sound /ɔ/. Listen to it in (author) /ˈɔ.θɚ/. Listen again in (pause) /pɔz/ and in (caught) /kɔt/.

## How to say it

Open your mouth a little and round your lips. Keep your tongue low in the back of your mouth. Hold the vowel steady.

## Reading rules

AU is /ɔ/ in most words. Listen to (August) /ˈɔ.ɡəst/ and (because) /bɪˈkɔz/. In a few words, AU is /æ/. Listen to (laugh) /læf/ and (aunt) /ænt/. Learn these words one by one.

## Common mistakes

Do not say (author) /ˈɔ.θɚ/ with /a/. Do not say the U as a separate sound. Do not say (laugh) /læf/ with /ɔ/.
articles.summary: AU usually sounds like /ɔ/, as in 'author'.

articles.title: oi
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters OI make the sound /ɔɪ/. Listen to it in (oil) /ɔɪl/. Listen again in (coin) /kɔɪn/ and in (noise) /nɔɪz/.

## How to say it

Round your lips and open your mouth a little. Then slide your tongue up and forward, and relax your lips. The sound has two parts, but it is one beat.

## Reading rules

OI is used in the middle of a word. At the end of a word, we write OY. Listen to (point) /pɔɪnt/ and (voice) /vɔɪs/. OI is /ɔɪ/ in almost every word. A few words from French are different. Listen to (memoir) /ˈmɛm.wɑr/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say two separate vowels, 'oh-ee'. Say one smooth sound. Do not say /ɔ/ only.
articles.summary: OI makes the sound /ɔɪ/, as in 'oil'.

articles.title: oy
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters OY make the sound /ɔɪ/. Listen to it in (boy) /bɔɪ/. Listen again in (toy) /tɔɪ/ and in (enjoy) /ɪnˈdʒɔɪ/.

## How to say it

Round your lips and open your mouth a little. Then slide your tongue up and forward, and relax your lips. The sound has two parts, but it is one beat.

## Reading rules

OY is used at the end of a word and before a vowel. Listen to (royal) /ˈrɔɪ.əl/ and (loyal) /ˈlɔɪ.əl/. OY always makes the same sound as OI. It never changes.

## Common mistakes

Do not say two separate vowels, 'oh-ee'. Say one smooth sound. Do not say /ɔ/ only.
articles.summary: OY makes the sound /ɔɪ/, as in 'boy'.

articles.title: ar
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters AR usually make the sound /ɑr/. Listen to it in (car) /kɑr/. Listen again in (arm) /ɑrm/ and in (star) /stɑr/.

## How to say it

Open your mouth wide for /ɑ/. Then pull your tongue back and raise the sides of it for /r/. Do not touch the roof of your mouth.

## Reading rules

After the letter W, AR is /ɔr/, as in (warm) /wɔrm/. In a syllable with no stress, AR is weak /ɚ/. Listen to (sugar) /ˈʃʊ.ɡɚ/ and (dollar) /ˈdɑ.lɚ/.

## Common mistakes

Do not drop the R. Do not say (car) /kɑr/ with /æ/. Do not tap the R.
articles.summary: AR usually sounds like /ɑr/, as in 'car'.

articles.title: er
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters ER make the sound /ɜr/ in a stressed syllable. Listen to it in (her) /hɜr/. Listen again in (fern) /fɜrn/ and in (term) /tɜrm/.

## How to say it

Keep your mouth open a little. Pull your tongue back and raise the sides of it. Round your lips slightly. Do not touch the roof of your mouth. Hold the sound steady.

## Reading rules

In a syllable with no stress, ER is weak /ɚ/. Listen to (water) /ˈwɔ.ɾɚ/ and (butter) /ˈbʌ.ɾɚ/. Before a vowel, ER is /ɛr/, as in (very) /ˈvɛ.ri/ and (period) /ˈpɪ.ri.əd/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say the vowel and the R as two separate sounds. Do not drop the R. Do not say (her) /hɜr/ like 'hair'.
articles.summary: ER usually sounds like /ɜr/ in a stressed syllable and /ɚ/ in a weak one.

articles.title: ir
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters IR make the sound /ɜr/. It is the same sound as ER. Listen to it in (bird) /bɜrd/. Listen again in (shirt) /ʃɜrt/ and in (girl) /ɡɜrl/.

## How to say it

Keep your mouth open a little. Pull your tongue back and raise the sides of it. Round your lips slightly. Do not touch the roof of your mouth. Hold the sound steady.

## Reading rules

IR is /ɜr/ in almost every word. Listen to (first) /fɜrst/ and (third) /θɜrd/. IR with a silent E is different. Listen to (fire) /faɪr/ and (wire) /waɪr/. Here the vowel is long.

## Common mistakes

Do not say a short /ɪ/ and then /r/. Say one sound. Do not say (bird) /bɜrd/ like 'beer'.
articles.summary: IR sounds like /ɜr/, as in 'bird'.

articles.title: or
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters OR usually make the sound /ɔr/. Listen to it in (corn) /kɔrn/. Listen again in (storm) /stɔrm/ and in (for) /fɔr/.

## How to say it

Round your lips. Open your mouth a little. Then pull your tongue back and raise the sides of it for /r/. Do not touch the roof of your mouth.

## Reading rules

After the letter W, OR is /ɜr/, as in (word) /wɜrd/ and (worm) /wɜrm/. In a syllable with no stress, OR is weak /ɚ/. Listen to (doctor) /ˈdɑk.tɚ/ and (actor) /ˈæk.tɚ/.

## Common mistakes

Do not drop the R. Do not say (word) /wɜrd/ with /ɔr/. Do not say (doctor) /ˈdɑk.tɚ/ with a strong ending.
articles.summary: OR usually sounds like /ɔr/, as in 'corn'.

articles.title: ur
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters UR make the sound /ɜr/. It is the same sound as ER and IR. Listen to it in (fur) /fɜr/. Listen again in (burn) /bɜrn/ and in (nurse) /nɜrs/.

## How to say it

Keep your mouth open a little. Pull your tongue back and raise the sides of it. Round your lips slightly. Do not touch the roof of your mouth. Hold the sound steady.

## Reading rules

UR is /ɜr/ in most words. Listen to (turn) /tɜrn/ and (hurt) /hɜrt/. UR with a silent E is different. Listen to (cure) /kjʊr/ and (pure) /pjʊr/. In a syllable with no stress, UR is weak /ɚ/, as in (sulfur) /ˈsʌl.fɚ/.

## Common mistakes

Do not say /ʌ/ and then /r/. Say one sound. Do not say (turn) /tɜrn/ like 'torn'.
articles.summary: UR sounds like /ɜr/, as in 'fur'.

articles.title: bl
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters BL make two sounds that join together: /b/ and /l/. Listen to it in (blue) /blu/. Listen again in (black) /blæk/ and in (blow) /bloʊ/.

## How to say it

Close your lips for /b/. As you open them, move your tongue to the ridge behind your upper teeth for /l/. Do not add a vowel between the two sounds.

## Reading rules

BL is common at the start of a word. Listen to (blind) /blaɪnd/ and (blanket) /ˈblæŋ.kɪt/. It can also be in the middle of a word, as in (table) /ˈteɪ.bəl/. Say both sounds in one syllable.

## Common mistakes

Do not say 'buh-lue'. There is no vowel between B and L. Say (blue) /blu/ as one syllable.
articles.summary: BL is a blend. Say /b/ and /l/ together.

articles.title: br
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters BR make two sounds that join together: /b/ and /r/. Listen to it in (brown) /braʊn/. Listen again in (brick) /brɪk/ and in (bring) /brɪŋ/.

## How to say it

Close your lips for /b/. As you open them, pull your tongue back for /r/. Do not add a vowel between the two sounds.

## Reading rules

BR is common at the start of a word. Listen to (bread) /brɛd/ and (brother) /ˈbrʌ.ðɚ/. It can also be in the middle of a word, as in (umbrella) /ʌmˈbrɛ.lə/. Say both sounds in one syllable.

## Common mistakes

Do not say 'buh-rown'. There is no vowel between B and R. Do not tap the R.
articles.summary: BR is a blend. Say /b/ and /r/ together.

articles.title: cl
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters CL make two sounds that join together: /k/ and /l/. Listen to it in (clap) /klæp/. Listen again in (club) /klʌb/ and in (clean) /klin/.

## How to say it

Press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth for /k/. As you release it, move the tip of your tongue to the ridge behind your upper teeth for /l/. Do not add a vowel between the sounds.

## Reading rules

CL is common at the start of a word. Listen to (class) /klæs/ and (clock) /klɑk/. The C is always hard before L. It is /k/, never /s/. Say both sounds in one syllable.

## Common mistakes

Do not say 'kuh-lap'. There is no vowel between C and L. Do not say /s/ for C.
articles.summary: CL is a blend. Say /k/ and /l/ together.

articles.title: cr
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters CR make two sounds that join together: /k/ and /r/. Listen to it in (crab) /kræb/. Listen again in (cry) /kraɪ/ and in (cross) /krɔs/.

## How to say it

Press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth for /k/. As you release it, pull your tongue back for /r/. Do not add a vowel between the sounds.

## Reading rules

CR is common at the start of a word. Listen to (crown) /kraʊn/ and (cream) /krim/. The C is always hard before R. It is /k/, never /s/. Say both sounds in one syllable.

## Common mistakes

Do not say 'kuh-rab'. There is no vowel between C and R. Do not tap the R.
articles.summary: CR is a blend. Say /k/ and /r/ together.

articles.title: dr
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters DR make two sounds that join together: /d/ and /r/. Listen to it in (drop) /drɑp/. Listen again in (dress) /drɛs/ and in (drink) /drɪŋk/.

## How to say it

Touch your tongue to the ridge behind your upper teeth for /d/. As you release it, pull your tongue back for /r/. Do not add a vowel between the sounds.

## Reading rules

DR is common at the start of a word. Listen to (dream) /drim/ and (draw) /drɔ/. The two sounds are very close. The D can sound a little like /dʒ/. This is normal. Say both sounds in one syllable.

## Common mistakes

Do not say 'duh-rop'. There is no vowel between D and R. Do not tap the R.
articles.summary: DR is a blend. Say /d/ and /r/ together.

articles.title: fl
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters FL make two sounds that join together: /f/ and /l/. Listen to it in (flag) /flæɡ/. Listen again in (fly) /flaɪ/ and in (flat) /flæt/.

## How to say it

Put your upper teeth on your lower lip for /f/. As you release it, move the tip of your tongue to the ridge behind your upper teeth for /l/. Do not add a vowel between the sounds.

## Reading rules

FL is common at the start of a word. Listen to (flower) /ˈflaʊ.ɚ/ and (floor) /flɔr/. It can also be in the middle of a word, as in (waffle) /ˈwɑ.fəl/. Say both sounds in one syllable.

## Common mistakes

Do not say 'fuh-lag'. There is no vowel between F and L. Say (flag) /flæɡ/ as one syllable.
articles.summary: FL is a blend. Say /f/ and /l/ together.

articles.title: gr
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters GR make two sounds that join together: /ɡ/ and /r/. Listen to it in (grow) /ɡroʊ/. Listen again in (green) /ɡrin/ and in (grass) /ɡræs/.

## How to say it

Press the back of your tongue to the roof of your mouth for /ɡ/. As you release it, pull your tongue back for /r/. Use your voice for both sounds. Do not add a vowel between them.

## Reading rules

GR is common at the start of a word. Listen to (great) /ɡreɪt/ and (group) /ɡrup/. The G is always hard before R. It is /ɡ/, never /dʒ/. Say both sounds in one syllable.

## Common mistakes

Do not say 'guh-row'. There is no vowel between G and R. Do not say /dʒ/ for G.
articles.summary: GR is a blend. Say /ɡ/ and /r/ together.

articles.title: st
articles.body:
## The sound

The letters ST make two sounds that join together: /s/ and /t/. Listen to it in (stop) /stɑp/. Listen again in (star) /stɑr/ and in (fast) /fæst/.

## How to say it

Put your tongue behind your upper teeth for /s/. Push air through the small space. Then stop the air with a quick /t/. Do not use your voice. There is no puff of air after the S.

## Reading rules

ST can be at the start, in the middle and at the end of a word. Listen to (nest) /nɛst/ and (mister) /ˈmɪ.stɚ/. In a few words, T is silent. Listen to (castle) /ˈkæ.səl/ and (listen) /ˈlɪ.sən/. These words have their own article.

## Common mistakes

Do not say 'suh-top'. There is no vowel between S and T. Do not say the T in (castle) /ˈkæ.səl/.
articles.summary: ST is a blend. Say /s/ and /t/ together.

articles.title: What a Syllable Is
articles.body:
## Every Syllable Has a Vowel
Think of a syllable like a single beat in music. In Romanian, every syllable must have exactly one vowel sound at its center. Vowels are open sounds like A, E, I, O, and U. You make them by opening your mouth and letting your voice flow freely. Without a vowel sound, you cannot have a syllable. Consonants can stand before or after, but the vowel is always the true boss.

## What Your Mouth and Voice Do
When you say a vowel, your mouth opens up wide and your vocal cords buzz gently. Your jaw drops a little, and your tongue stays relaxed. Consonants briefly close or squeeze your mouth, but the vowel opens it right back up. When a syllable is stressed, your voice pushes slightly harder, sounding louder and a little higher. On unstressed syllables, your voice stays soft and relaxed.

## Listening to the Word Mama
Look at this easy Romanian word: **mama** /ˈma.ma/, which means mother. Clap your hands as you say it out loud. You will clap two times because there are two syllables: *ma* and *ma*. Each beat has one vowel sound: the open sound /a/. The first beat is stressed, so your voice goes up a tiny bit: *MA-ma*. Your lips touch for M, then open wide for A.

## A Helpful Tip for English Speakers
In English, people often turn unstressed vowels into a lazy, quiet "uh" sound. In Romanian, you must never swallow your vowels! Keep every vowel crisp and clear, even when it is not the stressed one. In **mama** /ˈma.ma/, both syllables have a clear, bright /a/ sound. Open your mouth nicely for each beat, and let both vowels ring out.
articles.summary: Every syllable in Romanian has exactly one vowel sound right at its heart.

articles.title: Open Syllables in Romanian
articles.body:
## What is an open syllable?
A syllable is a small beat of a word. When a syllable ends with a vowel sound, we call it an open syllable. In Romanian, open syllables are very common. There is no consonant at the end to close the sound or cut it off. Because the end is free, your voice can flow smoothly into the air. This gives Romanian its singing and clear rhythm.

## How to say the sound
Open your mouth neatly when you reach the vowel. Keep your tongue relaxed and steady without moving it halfway through. Do not rush or clip the sound away. The vowel should ring out with a bright, steady tone. If the syllable has the main stress, push your voice a bit stronger and higher. If it has no stress, still make the vowel clean. Never swallow the sound at the end.

## Listening to the example
Let us listen to the word **casă** /ˈka.sə/, which means house. This word has two beats: **ca** and **să**. Both beats end with a vowel sound! The first beat ends in **a**, and the second ends in **ă**. Your mouth opens wide for the first beat with a strong breath. Then it relaxes slightly for the second beat, keeping both vowels distinct and clearly audible.

## Mistakes to avoid
English speakers often mumble vowels that do not have stress. In English, you might turn weak vowels into a tiny blur. In Romanian, you must keep every open vowel honest and clear. Do not slide between sounds or add a quiet consonant sound at the end. Keep your lips and tongue still until the vowel finishes ringing out into the room.
articles.summary: When a syllable ends in a vowel, it is open, and you speak the vowel clearly.

articles.title: Closed Syllables
articles.body:
## What is a closed syllable?
A syllable is like a little beat in a word. When a syllable ends with a vowel, the sound stays wide open. But when a syllable ends with a consonant letter, like n or t, we call it a closed syllable. In Romanian, closed syllables are everywhere. The consonant shuts the sound like a little door at the very end of the beat.

## How your mouth works
To say a closed syllable, first make the vowel sound with an open mouth. Then, quickly bring your tongue, teeth, or lips together to shut the air. Do not drop the final sound! Keep your voice steady. If this beat has the stress, say it slightly louder and hold the sound a moment longer so the consonant rings out crisply.

## Listen to the example
Look at the Romanian word **pământ** /pəˈmɨnt/, which means earth. This word has two beats: pă-mânt. The second beat ends with the consonants n and t. It is a closed syllable. The stress falls right on this second part. Your mouth opens for the vowel, then your tongue touches your upper teeth firmly to make a clear, sharp ending.

## Mistakes to avoid
English speakers often swallow sounds at the end of words or make a quiet pause in the throat instead of a real sound. In Romanian, you must never swallow the ending. Tap your tongue against your teeth and make sure the consonant sound pops out cleanly before you pause or say another word.
articles.summary: When a syllable ends with a consonant, say that consonant clearly so people can hear it.

articles.title: Stress Is Free
articles.body:
## The moving stress

In Romanian, stress is free. This means the loudest beat does not stay in one fixed spot. It can land on the first syllable, the middle syllable, or the very end of a word. Because there is no single rule for every word, you need to listen carefully to each new word. Treat the stress like a part of the word's spelling!

## How to make the stress

When you say a stressed syllable, give your voice extra energy. Push a little more air from your lungs. Open your mouth a bit wider and make the vowel slightly longer. Your pitch will also jump up a little, like singing a higher musical note. The unstressed syllables should be quieter, shorter, and softer.

## Listen to the word băiat

Look at the word for boy: **băiat** /bəˈjat/. This word has two syllables: bă-iat. The stress lands right on the second syllable. When you say **băiat**, keep the first part quick and soft. Then, open your mouth wide on "iat" with more volume and a higher tone: bă-IAT!

## Common mistakes to avoid

English speakers often push stress to the beginning of short words. If you say "BĂ-iat", it sounds strange to Romanian ears. Do not guess where the stress goes based on English habits. Always listen to the audio track and repeat the loud beat on the exact same syllable.
articles.summary: In Romanian, stress can land on any syllable, so you must learn it for each new word.

articles.title: Stress on the Last Syllable
articles.body:
## The last syllable rule
In Romanian, many words are stressed right at the end. A syllable is a beat of a word. When a word has two beats, the second beat is often the strongest. In the word **ajuns** /aˈʒuns/, which means arrived, the second part sounds stronger than the first part. It does not sound like *A-juns*. Instead, it sounds like *a-JUNS*. You can hear this pattern in many action words and describing words in Romanian.

## How to make the sound
Start with a quiet, relaxed sound for the first syllable. Keep your voice low and calm. Then, make your mouth open slightly wider for the last syllable. Push a little more air out from your chest. Make the vowel sound longer, louder, and slightly higher in tone. For **ajuns** /aˈʒuns/, say "a" quickly and softly. Then push your lips forward for "juns" with more power.

## Listen and practice
Try tapping your foot or clapping your hands. Clap softly on the first beat and clap loudly on the last beat. Say **ajuns** /aˈʒuns/ along with your claps: soft *a*, loud *JUNS*. Listen to the Romanian audio closely. Notice how the voice climbs a little bit on the last syllable before falling down gently. Practicing with a rhythm helps your mouth remember where the big push of air belongs.

## Mistakes to avoid
English speakers often like to stress the first syllable of two-syllable words. If you say *A-juns*, it sounds unusual to Romanian ears. Do not rush through the end of the word. Give the final syllable its full time and energy. Keep the first vowel short and smooth, but never drop the strong beat at the very end.
articles.summary: Many Romanian words put the strongest beat on the very last syllable when you speak.

articles.title: Stress on the Second-Last Syllable
articles.body:
## A very common beat pattern

Words are built from small beats called syllables. When you clap along with a Romanian word, one beat usually sounds stronger than the others. In Romanian, that strong beat very often lands on the second-last syllable. Linguists call this the penultimate syllable. Counting backwards from the end of a word helps you find it easily. You find the last beat, then take one step back.

## How your mouth and voice work

To make a stressed syllable, your voice must do three things at once. First, push a little extra air out from your lungs. Second, make your vocal cords vibrate with a slightly higher musical tone. Third, hold the vowel sound a tiny bit longer while opening your mouth clearly. The weak syllables around it stay softer, shorter, and lower. Do not drop the final vowel completely.

## Practicing with copilul

Listen closely to the word **copilul** /koˈpi.lul/, which means the child. It has three beats: co - pi - lul. The middle beat, pi, is the second-last one. When you say **copilul** /koˈpi.lul/, open your lips gently for co, push your voice up strongly on pi, and then drop down softly on lul. English speakers often rush the end, but you must keep the final beat clear and calm.
articles.summary: In many Romanian words, you say the second-to-last syllable louder, longer, and with more breath.

articles.title: Stress on the Third-Last Syllable
articles.body:
## The third-last syllable beat

In Romanian, words can have many parts called syllables. When a word grows long, the main vocal push often lands on the third-last syllable. This special spot is called the antepenultimate syllable. Placing the beat here gives Romanian speech its lively and bouncing melody. It keeps you from rushing through long words or dropping sounds at the finish line.

## How your mouth makes the sound

To pronounce a long Romanian word, keep your jaw loose and your mouth relaxed. Let your vocal cords push a little more air on the stressed part so the pitch rises gently. Listen closely to the long word **fotografie** /fo.to.ɡraˈfi.e/, meaning photograph. Round your lips neatly for the vowels, tap your tongue, and let the voice float smoothly to the final sound.

## Mistakes English speakers make

English speakers often want to squeeze unstressed vowels into tiny, unclear mumbles. In Romanian, every single vowel must stay bright and distinct. Do not swallow the ending of **fotografie** /fo.to.ɡraˈfi.e/. Give each vowel its own clean shape. Also, avoid hitting the stressed syllable too hard like an English thud. Instead, keep your tone musical, light, and floating like a bright bell.
articles.summary: Learn how long Romanian words use third-last syllable stress to create a clear and bouncing rhythm.

articles.title: Stress Is Not Written
articles.body:
## Stress is hidden in spelling
In Romanian, letters never wear little accent marks to show where the voice should be loud. When you read a word, the strong beat is a secret hidden inside the spelling. Because there are no visual clues on the page, you cannot simply guess which syllable to hit. To find the secret loud beat, you must listen to audio recordings or look up the word in a learner's dictionary. The dictionary uses a tiny mark before the strong sound to guide your voice.

## How to make the stressed beat
When your voice hits the strong syllable, push more air out from your belly and lungs. Open your mouth a little wider and let your jaw drop comfortably. Your vocal cords tighten just enough to raise the musical pitch of your voice, making it sound slightly higher. Make this sound longer and clearer than the sounds around it. The weak syllables do not need much work; keep your mouth relaxed, make the sound short, and let your voice drop softly to a lower, quieter tone.

## Saying the example limbă
Look at the word **limbă** /ˈlim.bə/, which means language. The dictionary places the stress mark right before the first part. Say "lim" with a strong push of breath, higher pitch, and a clear mouth shape. Then quickly finish with "bă", keeping your mouth soft and relaxed. English speakers often want to guess stress patterns or change vowels too much. In Romanian, always listen first so you do not stress the wrong beat, and keep each vowel shape clear even when soft.
articles.summary: Romanian letters do not show stress, so you must listen carefully and check dictionaries to learn it.

articles.title: Diphthongs in One Syllable
articles.body:
## Two Vowels, One Beat
Sometimes two vowels meet and decide to travel together. Instead of making two separate sounds, they slide smoothly into one quick flow. In Romanian, we call this special vowel team a diphthong. You do not stop the breath between them. They belong to the very same syllable. Think of them as musical notes that slide together without any pause. They create one single beat for your ear.

## How Your Mouth Moves
Your mouth needs to glide without stopping. For the sound pair *oa*, start with rounded lips like a small circle for *o*. Immediately open your mouth wider for *a*. The louder stress lands on *a*. Keep your voice steady and warm. Do not close your throat between the sounds. One vowel is soft and fast, while the partner vowel is strong and clear. Your mouth never pauses between them.

## Hearing the Word
Listen to the word for rain: **ploaie** /ˈplo̯a.je/. Clap your hands as you say it. You will clap only two times: *ploa-ie*. The first beat is **ploa**. The letters *o* and *a* glide together into one syllable. Then the voice finishes on *ie*. If you listen closely, the word sounds flowing and soft, like drops falling from the sky. The vowels stay joined like best friends.

## Common English Mistakes
English speakers often try to split the vowels into two separate beats. They might say *plo-a-ye* with three distinct syllables. That breaks the melody of the word. Do not put a tiny pause or a glottal stop between the *o* and the *a*. Keep the air moving continuously from your chest. Let the lips glide from round to open in one single motion.
articles.summary: When two vowels glide smoothly together, they share one breath and stay inside a single syllable.

articles.title: Hiatus Splits Neighbouring Vowels
articles.body:
## Two Vowels, Two Beats
Sometimes two vowels stand next to each other, but they do not merge into one sound. Instead, they live in separate syllables. In grammar, we call this a hiatus. When this happens, you must not slide them together. Each vowel gets its own turn to shine. You say the first vowel, and then you say the second vowel clearly. Think of it like taking two small steps instead of one big jump.

## How Your Mouth and Voice Work
To say a hiatus, watch your mouth closely. Say the first vowel, then change your mouth shape for the second vowel. Do not rush! Your voice makes two separate little pulses of air. Your pitch might rise or fall gently between them. One of the syllables might be stronger, but both vowels must stay pure and clear. Your lips and tongue move from one shape to the next without blending the sounds into a single glide.

## Listen to the Word România
A wonderful example is the name of the country: **România** /ro.mɨˈni.a/. Clap your hands as you say it: ro-mâ-ni-a! Notice the very end. The letter "i" and the letter "a" are side by side. But you do not say "nya". You say "ni", and then you say "a". The stress sits on the syllable "ni", and the last syllable "a" floats softly right after it.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid
English speakers often like to squish two vowels together into a glide. For instance, you might want to turn "i-a" into "ya" like in "onion". In Romanian, that changes the rhythm of the word. Keep the two sounds distinct. Give each vowel its own small push of breath. If you speak too fast, slow down and tap your finger for every single syllable!
articles.summary: When two vowels stand together in separate syllables, pronounce each one clearly with its own little beat.

articles.title: Final -ă stays clear
articles.body:
## A vowel that never hides
In Romanian, every vowel likes to be heard. The letter **ă** often sits right at the end of a word. In some other languages, you might swallow or drop the last sound when speaking quickly. But in Romanian, the final **ă** is always a full vowel. You must never skip it or turn it into silence. It stays in the word until the very end, keeping the word whole and easy to understand.

## How to use your mouth
To make the **ă** sound, keep your mouth slightly open. Do not stretch your lips wide like a smile, and do not round them into a circle. Relax your tongue flat in the middle of your mouth. It sounds like the "a" in "sofa". In words ending in **ă**, the stress usually lands on the syllable before it. Say that first part with more power, and then say the final **ă** softly, but keep your voice ringing clearly.

## Practicing with lampă
Let us practice with a simple word: **lampă** /ˈlam.pə/. This word means "lamp". Notice that it has two parts: **lam** and **pă**. When you say it, give strong energy to **lam**. Then, step down gently to pronounce **pă**. Do not cut the word short! Make sure your listener hears the sweet, clear **ă** at the finish line before you stop talking.

## Common mistakes to avoid
Many English speakers see a word like **lampă** and want to say "lamp". In English, we often stop talking after a hard consonant, or we turn ending vowels into tiny whispers. In Romanian, if you drop the **ă**, the word sounds broken or changes its meaning completely. Always finish the word completely. Keep your breath flowing until that final **ă** floats all the way out of your mouth.
articles.summary: In Romanian, never drop the letter -ă at the end of a word; say it softly and clearly every time.

articles.title: Stress Stays on the Root
articles.body:
## The beat stays in place

Words are made of small pieces called syllables. One syllable always gets the big punch. We call this the stressed beat. In Romanian nouns, this heavy beat loves its home. When you change a noun from one to many, the word grows longer. You might also glue tiny tags to the end, like the word for "the". Even when the word grows, the loud beat stays right on the main root syllable. It does not slide forward to the new ending.

## How to use your voice

When you say the stressed syllable, push more air from your belly. Your voice should sound a little louder, longer, and slightly higher in pitch. Your mouth opens wider and holds the sound with energy. When you attach new endings, do not punch them. Keep your tongue relaxed and let your voice drop lower and softer on those extra parts. Think of the root syllable as a strong drumbeat, while the added endings are tiny, quiet taps that follow softly.

## Practice with the word child

Let us practice with the Romanian word for child: **copil** /koˈpil/. In **copil** /koˈpil/, the strong punch lands on the second beat, "pil". Now let us add the tag "ul" to say "the child": **copilul**. Notice where your voice pushes. It still punches "pil"! You say co-PIL-ul, never co-pil-UL. When you talk about many children, you say **copii**. The beat still stays on that same root vowel. The root holds the power every time.

## Tips for English speakers

English words often like to jump their beat when words get longer. Think of how "photograph" shifts into "photography". Romanian nouns do not jump around like that. English speakers often want to push the very last sound of a word when adding little endings. Do not push the tail of the word! Keep the ending syllables quiet and short. Keep your mouth gentle at the end, and always remember to put the main punch right back on the familiar root syllable.
articles.summary: In Romanian nouns, the loud clapping beat stays on the root word even when new endings are added.

articles.title: Stress in Verb Endings
articles.body:
## The special beat pattern
In Romanian, action words can surprise your ears. Often, the strongest beat jumps all the way to the end of the word. Instead of stressing the beginning, your voice hits the last part. This happens very often when we speak to a group of friends or talk about doing things together. Listening for this final beat helps you know who is doing the action.

## How your mouth and voice work
Start smoothly and do not shout the first part. Make your voice climb higher, grow louder, and hold the sound a tiny bit longer on the final syllable. Your mouth opens clearly for the vowel sound at the end. For example, in **vorbiți** /vorˈbit͡s/, the voice taps *vor* softly, then lands firmly on *biți*. The sound at the end is short, crisp, and sharp like a little snake hiss.

## Listen to the example
Let us practice with the word **vorbiți** /vorˈbit͡s/, which means "you speak". Notice how the voice rests strongly on the second beat. If you tap your foot or clap your hands, your hand claps hard on the ending: vor-BIȚI! Other action words do this too, like *citiți* or *dormiți*. The ending always rings out loud and bright.

## Mistakes to avoid
English speakers often like to stress the start of a word. If you say *VOR-biți*, it sounds confusing to Romanian ears. Do not rush through the ending or make it weak. Instead, keep the first syllable light and let your voice save its biggest energy for the final syllable. Keep your tongue relaxed until the quick, neat finish!
articles.summary: Many Romanian action words push the loudest beat straight onto the very last syllable of their endings.

articles.title: Masculine and Feminine Adjectives
articles.body:
## The rhythm pattern
When you turn a Romanian adjective into its girl form, the rhythm changes completely. The whole word grows longer. You attach an extra ending to the word, which adds a brand new syllable. At the same time, the main musical beat jumps to a different spot. It does not stay where it was before. The sound steps forward with plenty of energy.

## How your mouth makes the sound
Start by rounding your lips into a small circle for the "o" sound. Next, quickly open your jaw wide for a bright "a". Push more air from your belly right here. This makes the vowel louder, longer, and higher in pitch. Finally, relax your lips and mouth completely for the ending "ă". Let your tongue rest flat and quiet in the center.

## Compare the two words
First, listen to the boy word: **frumos**. It has two beats, and the strong push comes at the end. Now listen to the girl word: **frumoasă** /fru.moˈa.sə/. It gains an extra syllable! The strong stress shifts right onto that wide, open "a" sound. Say them back to back. Notice how your voice climbs high in the middle and drops softly at the end.

## Common mistakes to avoid
English speakers often leave the stress on the old syllable. Do not say the word with a flat rhythm. The middle vowel must carry the big musical beat. Another mistake is turning the final soft "ă" into a sharp "ah". Keep that last sound very short, quiet, and lazy. Let the strong middle vowel do all the heavy work.
articles.summary: Making an adjective feminine adds a new syllable at the end and moves the strong stress forward.

articles.title: -a and -ă Endings
articles.body:
## Two Different Endings
In Romanian, word endings are very important. The letter **ă** sounds soft and relaxed, while the letter **a** sounds open and bright. When you add **-a** to the end of a word, it often means "the". For example, **casă** means "a house", but **casa** means "the house". Changing the final sound changes the whole meaning!

## How Your Mouth Moves
To say **-ă**, keep your mouth relaxed and only slightly open. Your tongue rests flat in the middle, like saying "uh". To say **-a**, open your mouth wider and drop your jaw. Make the sound clear and bright, like saying "ah" at the doctor. In **casa** /ˈka.sa/, the stress is on the first syllable, but the final **-a** still stays open and clean.

## Listen and Compare
Listen carefully to pairs of words. Notice how the sound shifts at the very end.
- **casă** /ˈka.sə/ means "a house".
- **casa** /ˈka.sa/ means "the house".
- **fată** /ˈfa.tə/ means "a girl".
- **fata** /ˈfa.ta/ means "the girl".
Hear how **casa** ends with a wide, open vowel!

## Common Mistakes
English speakers often turn final vowels into a sleepy "uh" sound. In English, the end of "sofa" sounds like **-ă**. If you do that in Romanian, you might say "a house" when you mean "the house"! Always remember to open your mouth wide when you see the final **-a**.
articles.summary: In Romanian, the endings -a and -ă sound different and change the whole meaning of the word.

articles.title: Unstressed Short Words
articles.body:
## Weak little words
Some Romanian words are very short and light. The reflexive word **mă** is a good example. When we talk, these tiny words do not take a strong beat. They do not like to stand alone. Instead, they act like a little helper that leans directly onto the next word. You say both words together as if they were one single word.

## Mouth and voice
Keep your mouth soft and relaxed when you start. The vowel in **mă** is quiet and short. Your voice stays low and gentle. Do not push extra air out of your lungs yet. Keep the breath flowing smoothly without stopping. Then, let your voice jump with more energy right onto the next word. That second word gets the big, strong beat.

## The example sound
Listen to the phrase **mă uit** /mə ˈu̯it/, which means "I look". Notice how your lips stay relaxed on the first part and then quickly round for the next sound. You do not hear two separate beats. It sounds like "mă-uit" spoken in one smooth breath. The voice rises and feels stronger on the main word.

## Mistakes to avoid
English speakers often pause between words or make every word equally loud. Do not stop your voice after **mă**. If you say "mă... uit" with a break, it sounds unnatural. Also, do not hit **mă** with a heavy accent. Treat it like a tiny, quiet step that leads straight into the main action.
articles.summary: Little words like mă have no stress and quickly join the very next word.

articles.title: Stress in Long Romanian Words
articles.body:
## The pattern of -itate

Long words can look scary, but Romanian has friendly patterns to help you. When a long word ends with the suffix **-itate**, the stress always stays in the same place. It does not matter how many syllables come before it. The voice always jumps onto the syllable **ta**. Think of this suffix like a musical tune that never changes. When you see **-itate**, you already know where your voice needs to land.

## How your voice and mouth work

Say the early syllables evenly and smoothly. Do not rush them, and do not make them loud. When you reach the **ta** in **-itate**, open your mouth wide. Push more air from your belly so this beat is louder and slightly higher in pitch. Then, let your voice drop down softly for the final **te**. Your lips stay relaxed for the final sound. Remember: quiet build-up, loud jump on **ta**, and a gentle finish.

## Listen and say: universitate

Let us practice with a great example: **universitate** /u.ni.ver.siˈta.te/. This word means "university". Tap your hand on your desk for each beat: u - ni - ver - si - **TA** - te. Hear how the voice climbs gently up to **ta**? Other words work the exact same way, like **capacitate** or **activitate**. Once you master **universitate** /u.ni.ver.siˈta.te/, you can pronounce dozens of long Romanian words perfectly.

## Common mistakes for English speakers

In English, we say "uni-VER-sity". We like to put the stress near the middle of the word. Because of this, English speakers often try to say "uni-VER-sitate" in Romanian. That sounds strange to Romanian ears! Another mistake is swallowing the vowels before the stress. In Romanian, every single vowel must stay clear and crisp. Do not blur the early sounds, and always put your energy right on **ta**.
articles.summary: Long Romanian words with suffixes like -itate always keep their stress on the syllable right before the end.

articles.title: Count the Syllables
articles.body:
## Clap each beat
Every word is built from small sound beats called syllables. Each time your mouth opens for a vowel, you hear one beat. To find how many beats a word has, speak slowly and clap your hands once for every beat. Keep your lips relaxed and feel your chin drop down with each vowel sound.

## Find the strong beat
In Romanian words, one beat is always special. We call this the stressed syllable. Your voice goes slightly higher, stays longer, and sounds louder on this beat. When you clap, make regular soft claps for normal beats. Then, clap extra firmly or stamp your foot when you hit the strong, stressed beat.

## Practice with dimineață
Let us practice with the Romanian word for morning: **dimineață** /di.mi.ˈɲa.tsə/. Say it slowly while clapping: di - mi - nea - ță. That makes four beats! The third beat, *nea*, is the loudest one. Open your mouth a bit wider and make *nea* ring out: di - mi - **NEA** - ță. The last sound stays quiet.

## Mistakes to avoid
English speakers often swallow unstressed vowels, turning them into a fast murmur. In Romanian, keep every beat clear and crisp. Do not rush over the first two beats *di* and *mi*. Give each syllable its own distinct clap, and make sure your loudest clap lands right on *nea*.
articles.summary: Clap for every beat in a word, then give the strongest syllable a louder, longer tap.

articles.title: Stress and Vowel Contrast
articles.body:
## Strong and soft vowels

In Romanian, vowels change their power depending on stress. When a vowel carries the stress, it sounds bright, loud, and very clear. When a vowel has no stress, your voice relaxes. The vowel becomes shorter and quieter. Word endings change a lot because of this rule. An ending with stress keeps its pure, open sound. An unstressed ending sounds much lighter. Listening for this difference helps you understand who is speaking and what they are doing.

## Shape your mouth and voice

Watch what your body does when you speak. For a stressed vowel, drop your jaw slightly more and push extra air from your belly. Your pitch goes up a little bit, like singing a higher musical note. For an unstressed vowel, keep your jaw closer together and your lips relaxed. Do not push extra air. Your voice stays flat and quiet. Move smoothly between the relaxed parts and the strong, energetic beat of the word.

## Practice with vorbesc

Listen closely to the word **vorbesc** /vorˈbesk/, which means "I speak". This word has two syllables: "vor" and "besc". The stress hits the ending on "besc". Start with a quiet, relaxed "vor". Then open your mouth wider and push more air on "besc". The vowel /e/ in **vorbesc** /vorˈbesk/ sounds bright and sharp. Notice how your tongue lifts toward the middle of your mouth. The strong ending makes the whole word bounce forward with energy.

## Mistakes to avoid

English speakers often turn unstressed vowels into an "uh" sound, like the word "about". Be careful not to swallow the first part of Romanian words. Even when a vowel is unstressed, you must still shape it properly with your lips. Another common mistake is stressing the beginning instead of the ending. If you say "VOR-besc", the vowel /e/ becomes weak and fuzzy. Always keep your stress on the ending so the vowel stays bright and clear.
articles.summary: Stressed vowels sound clear and strong, while unstressed vowels sound softer and shorter in Romanian word endings.

articles.title: Practice: Stress in Word Pairs
articles.body:
## Moving Stress in Pairs

In Romanian, words often come in matching pairs. A word can change from a boy word to a girl word, or from one thing to many things. When the ending of the word changes, the strong beat can move too! Stress is the loudest, strongest beat in a word. When you read pairs, you must train your ear to follow the beat. Watching how the accent shifts helps you sound like a native speaker.

## How to Use Your Voice

Say each pair aloud with plenty of air. For the stressed syllable, open your mouth wider and push your voice higher. The stressed vowel sounds longer and clearer. When you reach an unstressed ending, make your voice softer and drop your pitch slightly. Relax your jaw and lips on the quiet parts. Pretend your voice is bouncing like a rubber ball right onto the loudest beat.

## Listen to the Words

Look at the adjective **frumos** /fruˈmos/. The strong beat is right at the end on the syllable "mos". Your voice climbs up and punches that vowel. Now listen to its pair, the feminine form **frumoasă** /fruˈmo̯a.sə/. The ending changed, and the stress moved slightly to the middle syllable! Tap your desk with your finger on each strong beat to feel the voice jump between the two words.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

English speakers often keep the stress on the very first syllable of every word. In Romanian, that sounds strange because stress loves to travel toward the end. Another common slip is making all syllables the same volume. Romanian words need a clear rhythm with high peaks and low valleys. Do not rush through the pairs. Speak slowly and let the strong syllable ring out loud and bright.
articles.summary: Say the word pairs out loud and move your voice's stress when the word ending changes.

articles.title: Soft C before E and I
articles.body:
## The soft C rule
In Romanian, the letter C changes its sound depending on the vowel that follows it. When the letter C stands directly before the vowels E or I, it becomes soft. It sounds exactly like the ch sound in the English word "church". In phonetic writing, this sound is written as /tʃ/. It never makes a hard K sound in this position. Learning this simple rule will allow you to read many everyday Romanian words correctly.

## How to make the sound
To produce this sound, lift the tip and blade of your tongue to touch the roof of your mouth. Press firmly right behind your top front teeth. Then, gently release the tongue to let a short puff of air hiss through. Your vocal cords do not vibrate for this consonant. Keep your lips pushed slightly forward and relaxed. Direct the breath smoothly into the vowel that follows, keeping your voice steady and natural.

## Romanian examples
A great word to practice is **cer** /tʃer/, which means "sky". Notice how the word begins with the exact same sound as "cherry". Another common word with this pattern is **cine** /tʃine/, which means "who". In both words, the letter C is followed immediately by E or I. Keep your pitch clear and even as you speak. Say the word **cer** /tʃer/ out loud several times until it feels effortless.

## Common mistakes to avoid
English speakers often see a soft C and want to pronounce it like an S. In English words like "center" or "city", the letter C makes an S sound. In Romanian, C never makes an S sound on its own. Pronouncing **cer** /tʃer/ with an S creates a completely different word. Always remember to use the ch sound whenever you see C followed by E or I in Romanian.
articles.summary: In Romanian, the letter C before E and I is pronounced like the English sound ch in church.

articles.title: Hard C Before A, O, U
articles.body:
## The basic sound rule
In Romanian, the letter **c** changes its sound depending on the vowel that follows it. When you see **c** right before **a**, **o**, or **u**, it always makes a plain sound like the English letter *k*. It never sounds like *s* or *ch* in these positions. A classic vocabulary word is **casă** /ˈka.sə/, which means house. Notice how the first letter sounds crisp and sharp before the vowel **a**. Other examples work the exact same way before **o** and **u**.

## Mouth and tongue position
To make this sound properly, lift the back of your tongue toward the soft part of the roof of your mouth. Close off the airflow completely for a split second. Then, release the back of your tongue quickly so the trapped air bursts out. Keep your vocal cords completely still, because this is an unvoiced sound. In Romanian, do not blow out a huge puff of extra air. The burst should be tight, direct, dry, and immediately blend right into the next vowel.

## Stress and vocal tone
The consonant **c** itself does not take stress, but it starts the syllable with energy. In the word **casă** /ˈka.sə/, the stress falls strongly on the first syllable. Make that first syllable slightly louder and hold its pitch steady. As you move to the second syllable, drop your pitch slightly and relax your voice. The hard sound should never wobble or change tone. Give it a firm, steady start so the rhythm of the word stays clear and natural.

## Mistakes to avoid
Native English speakers often push out a small puff of air when saying a *k* sound at the start of a word. In Romanian, this extra puff makes your speech sound heavy and foreign. Try holding your hand before your mouth while saying **casă** /ˈka.sə/. You should feel almost no breath hitting your fingers. Another mistake is softening the consonant into a *ch* sound. Keep the tongue pressed firmly at the back of the mouth, not near the front teeth.
articles.summary: The letter C sounds like a clean K whenever it comes right before the vowels A, O, or U.

articles.title: Soft G Before E and I
articles.body:
## The soft G sound

In Romanian, the letter **g** changes its sound depending on the vowel that follows it. When **g** stands right before **e** or **i**, it becomes soft. It sounds like the English **j** in the word **jump**. You hear this exact sound in many common Romanian words. If **g** stands before **a**, **o**, or **u**, it stays hard like in **go**. Remembering the two vowels **e** and **i** will help you read every word correctly.

## How to make the sound

Place the tip of your tongue against the roof of your mouth, just behind your top front teeth. Press the tongue gently to block the airflow for a tiny moment. Push air forward and let your tongue pull back quickly. Your vocal cords must vibrate to create a buzzing voice sound. Keep your lips slightly rounded and relaxed. In the word **gene** /ˈdʒe.ne/, put more stress and a slightly higher pitch on the first syllable.

## Practice with words

Listen closely to the audio recordings and repeat each word clearly. A great example to practice is **gene** /ˈdʒe.ne/, which means eyelashes or genes. Notice how the sound starts cleanly without any delay. You can also hear this sound in the word **ger** /ˈdʒer/, which means severe cold. Another good word is **girafă** /dʒiˈra.fə/, which means giraffe. Say the words slowly at first so your tongue finds the right spot.

## Mistakes to avoid

English speakers sometimes forget to use the soft sound before these vowels. Never pronounce this letter as a hard **g** like in **garden** when reading **ge** or **gi**. Another common mistake is making a soft French **zh** sound without the tongue tap. Make sure your tongue touches the roof of your mouth first to create the **d** part of the sound. Keep the vowel right after the consonant crisp, clear, and steady.
articles.summary: In Romanian, the letter g sounds like the English j whenever it comes directly before e or i.

articles.title: Hard G Before A, O, U
articles.body:
## The Rule for Letter G

In Romanian, spelling is very regular and predictable. The letter **g** changes its sound based on the letter that follows it. When **g** stands right before the vowels **a**, **o**, or **u**, it always makes a hard sound. You hear this same basic consonant sound in English words like *game*, *gold*, or *guitar*. It never turns into a soft sound before these three vowels.

## How to Make the Sound

To make this sound, place the back of your tongue against your soft palate. The soft palate is the squishy roof at the very back of your mouth. Block the airflow for a tiny moment. Then drop your tongue quickly to let the air burst out. Turn your voice box on because this sound needs vibrating vocal cords. Keep your lips relaxed and ready for the next vowel.

## Example and Word Stress

A great example of this rule is the Romanian word **gară** /ˈɡa.rə/, which means station. The word starts with a clear, firm hard **g** sound right before the vowel **a**. The word has two syllables: **ga** and **ră**. You put stronger stress on the first syllable **ga**. Your voice stays steady, with a natural pitch drop on the final unstressed syllable **ră**.

## Mistakes to Avoid

English speakers sometimes try to soften this sound or add extra breath. Do not pronounce this letter like the soft **g** in *gem* or *giant*. Never blow extra air like an **h** sound when you release the tongue. Simply make a clean, crisp, voiced pop from the back of your throat. Keep the sound short and firm before you sing out the following vowel.
articles.summary: In Romanian, the letter g sounds like a hard g when it appears before the vowels a, o, and u.

articles.title: The Letters Ghe and Ghi
articles.body:
## The Rule for Ghe and Ghi
In Romanian, the letter **g** before **e** or **i** usually sounds soft like the English *j*. To keep the **g** hard, Romanian adds a silent letter **h**. The groups **ghe** and **ghi** always have a hard **g** sound, like in *guitar* or *game*. You never pronounce the **h** as a breath. It works only as a silent helper to protect the hard sound.

## How Your Mouth Makes the Sound
Push the back of your tongue against the soft roof of your mouth. Build up a small puff of air behind your tongue. Release the air suddenly while vibrating your vocal cords. Your tongue stays down in the front of your mouth. Do not push your tongue against the front ridge like you do for a *j* sound.

## Stress and Romanian Examples
Listen carefully to the word **ghici** /ˈɡi.tʃi/, which means to guess. The stress lands on the first syllable **ghi-**. Your voice starts a bit higher on the hard **g** and drops slightly on **-ci**. Another common word is **ghem** /ˈɡem/, which means ball of yarn. In both words, the sound is crisp and firm.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid
English speakers often want to pronounce the letter **h** as a puff of breath. In Romanian **ghe** and **ghi**, the **h** makes no sound at all. Another common mistake is turning the **g** into a soft *j* sound like in *giant*. Always remember that the silent **h** locks the hard sound in place.
articles.summary: The letter H keeps the G sound hard before the vowels E and I in Romanian.

articles.title: The letters che and chi
articles.body:
## The sound pattern

In Romanian, the letter c usually sounds like ch in cheese when it comes before e or i. When the letter h is added between them, the sound changes completely. The letters **che** and **chi** make a single soft k sound. The letter h is completely silent here. It only acts as a sign to keep the sound sharp and crisp. A great example of this is the word **chiar** /kjar/, which means even or really.

## How your mouth makes the sound

To make this sound, lift the middle of your tongue toward the roof of your mouth. Press the sides of your tongue against your upper molars. Build a tiny burst of air behind your tongue. Release the air quickly without letting your vocal cords vibrate right away. The sound feels lighter and sharper than the normal k in kangaroo. Keep your lips relaxed and ready for the next vowel sound. Your voice should stay steady and bright.

## Common mistakes to avoid

English speakers often see the letters ch and want to say the ch sound from chicken. Another common mistake is trying to breathe out an audible h sound after the k. Remember that both letters merge into one single stop. Treat **chiar** /kjar/ as starting with a sharp k followed smoothly by a quick y sound. Never make the buzzing or dragging sound of an English ch. Keep the release brief, clean, and light.
articles.summary: In Romanian, the letters che and chi make a single soft k sound before vowels.

articles.title: The Sounds ș and ț
articles.body:
## Two Special Romanian Letters

Romanian uses two special letters with a small comma underneath. The letter **ș** has a comma under s. The letter **ț** has a comma under t. You must never skip these little marks. They completely change how the letters sound. In Romanian, **ș** always sounds like the English *sh*. In Romanian, **ț** always sounds like the English *ts*. This rule has no exceptions at all. Whenever you see these letters, their sounds stay exactly the same.

## How Your Mouth Makes the Sounds

To say **ș**, push your lips out a little bit into a small circle. Put your tongue near the roof of your mouth, just behind your top teeth. Blow air smoothly over your tongue without using your voice. To say **ț**, place the tip of your tongue against the back of your top front teeth. Stop the air completely for a split second. Then, pull your tongue back quickly to release a sharp burst of air. Keep your voice box quiet for both sounds.

## Examples and Word Stress

A great example word is **școală** /ʃkoˈa.lə/, which means school. Notice how the first sound is a soft rushing whisper. The strong beat or stress lands on the syllable *a*. Another common word is **țară** /ˈt͡sa.rə/, which means country. Here, the sharp *ts* sound starts the word. The stress falls on the first syllable. Keep your pitch steady and natural as you move through the word. Do not let your voice rise too high.

## Common Mistakes for English Speakers

English speakers often mistake the letter **ș** for a regular *s*. Always remember that the comma gives it a *sh* sound. Never pronounce **ș** like the *s* in sun. Another mistake happens with **ț**. English speakers sometimes pronounce it like a normal *t*. Remember that **ț** is a combination sound like *ts* in cats. Never say just *t* when you see the comma. Practice switching smoothly between the soft *sh* and the sharp *ts*.
articles.summary: In Romanian, the letter ș always sounds like sh, and the letter ț always sounds like ts.

articles.title: Plural t Becomes ț
articles.body:
## The consonant change
In Romanian, many words change their root consonant when they become plural. A very common change happens with the letter **t**. When masculine nouns take the plural ending **-i**, the sound /t/ shifts to /t͡s/, which is spelled **ț**. This sound shift is called a consonant alternation. It happens because the plural marker softens the consonant before it. A clear example is the singular word *frate* (brother), which becomes the plural **frați** /frat͡sʲ/ (brothers).

## Mouth and tongue position
To pronounce **ț**, touch the tip of your tongue against the ridge behind your upper teeth. Stop the air for an instant, then release it with a sharp hiss. It sounds like the "ts" in the word "cats". The final letter **i** in **frați** is not a full vowel. It is a tiny puff of breath that raises the middle of your tongue toward the roof of your mouth. Keep your lips relaxed and do not add an extra syllable.

## Stress and tone
The stress does not jump to the plural ending. In the word **frați** /frat͡sʲ/, the stress stays firmly on the first syllable, **fra-**. Make this first syllable louder and slightly higher in pitch. The ending **-ți** is spoken softly and quickly with a falling pitch. Keep your voice natural and steady. Another common example is the singular noun *bărbat* (man), which follows the exact same pattern and becomes *bărbați* (men).

## Common mistakes to avoid
English speakers often make two simple mistakes with this plural form. First, do not keep the hard **t** sound from the singular. Saying *frati* instead of **frați** sounds unnatural in Romanian. Second, avoid pronouncing the final **-i** as a loud vowel like "ee". The word **frați** has only one syllable, not two. Make sure you stop the sound promptly after the crisp hissing burst.
articles.summary: In Romanian plurals, the letter t often turns into ț before the plural ending i.

articles.title: Plural Shift: T to Ț
articles.body:
## The Sound Shift Pattern

In Romanian, word endings often change the sounds inside the word. When a masculine noun ends with a T, that T usually changes in the plural form. The plural marker pulls the T forward into a sharp "ts" sound. Romanian writes this new sound with the letter Ț. For example, a single boy is a băiat. When you talk about more than one, the word changes to **băieți** /bəˈjet͡sʲ/. The vowel inside also changes from A to E. This sound change happens very frequently in masculine words.

## Mouth Position and Tone

To make this new sound, press the tip of your tongue against the back of your upper teeth. Stop the air for a tiny split second. Then, release the air quickly with a sharp hissing sound. It sounds just like the "ts" at the end of the English word "cats". The final I is not a full vowel. It is just a tiny whisper of air that softens the Ț. The stress lands strongly on the middle syllable: bă-IEȚI. Your voice should stay firm and level on that stressed middle part.

## Practicing the Example

Listen closely to the audio for **băieți** /bəˈjet͡sʲ/. You will hear three clear parts in this short word. First comes the short, neutral sound "bă". Next comes the loud, energetic syllable "ie". Finally, the word ends on the quick, crisp sound "ți". Do not stretch the word out at the end. The final sound should feel like a quick tap against your teeth. Keep your lips relaxed as you finish the word.

## Common English Mistakes

Many English speakers forget to change the consonant sound completely. They often try to say a regular T sound followed by a long "ee" vowel. That sounds unnatural to Romanian listeners. Never say "ba-yet-ee" with two separate syllables at the end. Instead, merge the ending into one sharp, whispered "ts" release. Also, remember to shift the vowel sound from A to E. Practicing the shift from băiat to **băieți** /bəˈjet͡sʲ/ will help your tongue remember the pattern.
articles.summary: In Romanian plurals, the letter T changes to a TS sound before the plural ending.

articles.title: Plural C Becomes CI
articles.body:
## The sound change

In Romanian, singular words often end with a hard *c* sound like in *cat*. When these masculine or neuter nouns form a plural, they add an *i* at the end. That added letter changes the sound completely. The hard *c* becomes a soft *ch* sound, just like the start of the word *chair*. This is an important rule for plural forms.

## How to say it

Touch the tip of your tongue right behind your upper front teeth. Push air out gently to make a quick *ch* sound. At the very end, raise the middle of your tongue toward the roof of your mouth. Do not add a full vowel *ee* sound at the end. The final *i* is whispered and very short, like a soft puff of breath.

## Word stress and example

Stress stays on the syllable before the ending in many of these words. Look at the word for trees: **copaci** /ko.paˈt͡ʃʲ/. The singular is *copac*, with the voice landing on *pac*. In the plural **copaci**, the stress remains strongly on *pa*. Your voice rises slightly on that stressed middle syllable, then drops quickly on the final soft consonant.

## Common mistakes to avoid

Many English speakers try to pronounce a full *ee* sound at the end. They say *co-pa-chee*, which sounds unnatural in Romanian. The final *i* is only a tiny hint of sound that softens the consonant. Another mistake is keeping the hard *k* sound from the singular. Always switch your tongue forward to produce the soft *ch* sound.
articles.summary: In many Romanian plurals, the hard c sound turns into a soft ch sound when plural i is added.
